title: Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) im Unterricht: Chancen und Risiken für das Lernen
subtitle: Die rasante Entwicklung der künstlichen Intelligenz verändert das Lehren und Lernen radikal.
feedText: Knapp die Hälfte der Jugendlichen setzt laut JIM-Studie KI inzwischen regelmäßig bei der Informationssuche ein. Damit ist KI nach Suchmaschinen die zweitwichtigste Anlaufstelle. Neue Kompetenzen sind gefragt, gleichzeitig drohen Fähigkeiten verloren zu gehen. articleBody:
# KI in der Bildung: Neue Trendanalyse zu Chancen und Risiken

KI-Systeme bieten neue Möglichkeiten der individuellen Förderung oder der Entlastung von Lehrkräften, gleichzeitig stellen sie die gesamte bisherige Lern- und Prüfungskultur in Frage. © Heiko Rebsch/dpa Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) ist die Fähigkeit einer Maschine, menschliche Fähigkeiten wie logisches Denken, Lernen, Planen, Problemlösen und Kreativität zu imitieren. Die sprachbasierte Anwendung über Chatbots wie ChatGPT macht den Austausch mit der KI möglich.

Diese und andere Anwendungen sind längst im Alltag angekommen und verändern Schule nachhaltig. Knapp die Hälfte der Jugendlichen (47 Prozent) setzt KI inzwischen regelmäßig bei der Informationssuche ein – ein Zuwachs um 8 Prozentpunkte gegenüber 2025. Damit ist KI nach Suchmaschinen (68 Prozent) die zweitwichtigste AnlaufstelleDie Lesezeit der Jugendlichen schrumpft, die KI-Nutzung wächst: Nur noch ein Drittel der 12- bis 13-Jährigen liest in der Freizeit regelmäßig ein Buch – vor einem Jahr war es noch fast die Hälfte. Das zeigt die am 13.11.2026 veröffentlichte JIM-Studie 2026 des Medienpädagogischen Forschungsverbunds Südwest. Drei von vier Jugendlichen, die KI verwenden, nutzen diese für Hausaufgaben und zum Lernen.

## Trendmonitor KI in der Bildung

Auch im Unterricht und in der Schulorganisation selbst spielt KI eine immer größere Rolle. Innerhalb nur eines Jahres hat der KI-Einsatz an deutschen Schulen massiv an Fahrt aufgenommen. Das konstatiert der „Trendmonitor KI in der Bildung 2026“. Deutsche Telekom Stiftung veröffentlichte am 23. September 2026 die zweite Trendanalyse zur Nutzung von künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) in Schulen.

Text-, bild- und videogenerierende Systeme, zum Beispiel ChatGPT, bleiben demnach die mit Abstand wichtigsten KI-Tools im Schulbetrieb. Allerdings stünden 2026 deutlich mehr bildungsspezifische LLM-basierte Plattformen und Chatbots wie fobizz oder AIS.chat zur Auswahl als noch 2025.

Für den Trendmonitor 2026 hat das mmb Institut zusammen mit dem Deutschen Forschungszentrum für Künstliche Intelligenz (DFKI) insgesamt 258 KI-Anwendungen für Schulen recherchiert und systematisiert. Von den untersuchten Anwendungen sind 87 Entwicklungen aus dem deutschsprachigen Raum. 104 Anwendungen (Vorjahr: 88) sind Produkte US-amerikanischer Technologieunternehmen. Damit habe sich der deutschsprachige Markt zwar gut entwickelt, es bestehe aber nach wie vor eine große Abhängigkeit vom US-Markt, urteilt das Autorenteam der Studie.

### Status quo und Potenziale von KI in der Schule

Darüber hinaus wurden 81 Bildungs- und KI-Fachleute zu ihren aktuellen Einschätzungen und Prognosen befragt. Der KI-Einsatze in deutschen Schulen sei laut Analyse der Expertinnen und Experten derzeit noch stark von Experimenten mit bekannten generativen Tools wie ChatGPT geprägt ist. Es gehe dabei vorrangig darum, den Status quo zu optimieren, KI werde hierzulande eher als softwarebasierter Assistent für Lehrkräfte genutzt.

Das Potenzial, das KI für mehr Bildungsgerechtigkeit biete, werde in Deutschland bislang nur in Einzelinitiativen sichtbar. China dagegen setze KI gezielt und im großen Stil dafür ein: Über Fernunterricht und intelligente Infrastruktur werde dort das Leistungsniveau strukturschwacher und ländlicher Schulen massiv gehoben.

Den größten Nutzen von KI für Schülerinnen und Schüler sehen die Fachleute in assistiven Systemen zur Inklusion und zum individuellen Lernen, nur geringes Potenzial wird etwa in Robotik und auch, was die Potenziale der KI bei Korrekturen von Klassenarbeiten angeht, zeige sich eine gewisse Ernüchterung.

### Die größten Risiken von KI-Anwendungen in der Schule

Aktuell nehmen die Befragten die Abhängigkeit von marktführenden KI-Unternehmen und damit die Frage der digitalen Souveränität als größtes Risiko wahr.

An zweiter Stelle stehen das Deskilling und Skill Skipping . Die Sorge, dass durch den Einsatz von KI Grundkompetenzen wie Recherche, Textproduktion, kritisches Denken oder Problemlösungsfähigkeiten verloren gehen oder gar nicht erst gelernt werden, hat im Vergleich zu 2025 weiter zugenommen. Die Expertinnen und Experten gehen davon, dass sich die Schere zwischen digital kompetenten und weniger kompetenten Lernenden in Deutschland weiter öffnen werde: Medienkompetente Schülerinnen und Schüler würden stark profitieren, andere nutzten KI oft rein aus Bequemlichkeit.

Auf Platz drei der größten Risiken sehen die Expertinnen und Experten die Überforderung der Lehrkräfte bei der Unterscheidung , ob eine Leistung von der KI erstellt ist oder nicht.

Das 2026 erstmals abgefragte Risiko-Item „Psychische Probleme durch allgemeinen KI-Einsatz“ (zum Beispiel Abhängigkeit von Chatbots) schätzen die Expertinnen und Experten aktuell noch als sehr gering ein.

## Befragung von Lehrkräften zu KI

Die große Mehrzahl der Lehrkräfte in Deutschland hat sich bislang kaum oder überhaupt nicht mit den Regelungen auseinandergesetzt, die für den Umgang mit Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) an Schule gelten. Das zeigt eine repräsentative Forsa-Umfrage unter rund 1.000 Lehrkräften an allgemeinbildenden Schulen im Auftrag der Deutsche Telekom Stiftung, die am 11. März 2026 veröffentlicht wurde. 88 Prozent der Befragten geben an, sich bislang weniger intensiv bis gar nicht (jeweils 44 Prozent) mit KI-Regelungen beschäftigt zu haben. 78 Prozent begründen dies damit, dass es zusätzlich zu ihren regulären Aufgaben nicht zu leisten sei. 50 Prozent empfinden das Thema als zu komplex. Insgesamt wünschen sich 87 Prozent verständliche und gut umsetzbare KI-Regelwerke für ihren Schulalltag.

Diese und weitere Ergebnisse der Forsa-Befragung ergänzen den Trendmonitor Spezial „Regelwerke zu KI an Schulen”. Die Studie wurde vom Deutschen Forschungszentrum für Künstliche Intelligenz (DFKI) und dem mmb Institut im Auftrag der Telekom -Stiftung erarbeitet.

## Deutsches Schulbarometer: Skepsis der Lehrkräfte überwiegt

Im Rahmen des Deutschen Schulbarometers 2026 , einer repräsentativen Befragung der Robert Bosch Stiftung, wurden Lehrkräfte in November 2025 zur Nutzung und Bewertung von künstlicher Intelligenz befragt. Die Ergebnisse wurden im Juni 2026 veröffentlicht. Lehrkräfte nutzen demnach immer häufiger künstliche Intelligenz (KI) für ihre berufliche Arbeit, vor allem für die Erstellung von Unterrichtsaufgaben (64 Prozent) und zur Unterstützung bei der Unterrichtsplanung (58 Prozent). Im letzten Befragungszeitraum Ende 2024 gaben knapp ein Drittel (31 Prozent) der Lehrkräfte an, KI-Tools in den zurückliegenden 12 Monaten nie genutzt zu haben. Ein Jahr später sank dieser Wert auf 10 Prozent.

Der Anteil der Lehrkräfte, die KI-Tools mehrmals im Monat verwenden, steigt von 20 Prozent im Jahr 2025 auf 27 Prozent im Jahr 2026. Und der Anteil der Befragten, die KI-Tools mehrmals pro Woche einsetzen, hat sich sogar mehr als verdoppelt und stieg innerhalb eines Jahres von 9 auf 19 Prozent an. Am häufigsten greifen Lehrkräfte an beruflichen Schulen auf KI zurück, am wenigsten nutzen Lehrerinnen und Lehrer an Förderschulen entsprechende Tools.

Befragt nach den Chancen, erwarten Lehrkräfte vor allem eine bessere individualisierte Lernunterstützung durch KI-Anwendungen (59 Prozent). Insgesamt überwiegt jedoch die Skepsis. Mit Blick auf die Kompetenzen der Schülerinnen und Schüler befürchtet eine Mehrheit der befragten Lehrkräfte eher negative Auswirkungen durch die Nutzung von KI-Tools, etwa auf Sprach- und Schreibkompetenzen (57 Prozent erwarten eher negative Folgen), auf die Problemlösefähigkeit (62 Prozent), kritisches Denken (67 Prozent) oder auf soziale und kommunikative Fähigkeiten (67 Prozent).

Im Rahmen des Schulbarometers wurden die Lehrkräfte auch zu den größten Fortbildungsbedarfen befragt. An erster Stelle stehen hier Fortbildungen zum Einsatz von künstlicher Intelligenz. 52 Prozent sehen hier großen Bedarf.

Auch der Campus des Schulportals bietet regelmäßig Fortbildungs-Veranstaltungen zum Thema Künstliche Intelligenz im Unterricht.

# Gesellschaft - "Flächendeckende Vernachlässigung": Verbände rufen Politik zum Tag der Kinderrechte zum Handeln auf

"Wer bei den unterschiedlichen Entwicklungsphasen von Kindern und Jugendlichen spart, verschiebt die Probleme gesellschaftlich, politisch und wirtschaftlich." (picture alliance / Connect Images / Pancake Pictures) Der Berufsverband Deutscher Psychologinnen und Psychologen warnte in einem Brandbrief an die Mitglieder des Deutschen Bundestags , der Bundesregierung und der Landesregierungen vor Kürzungen bei Bildung, Jugendhilfe und psychosozialer Versorgung. Er fordert langfristige Investitionen. Wer bei den unterschiedlichen Entwicklungsphasen von Kindern und Jugendlichen spare, verschiebe die Probleme nur gesellschaftlich, politisch und wirtschaftlich. Das Deutsche Kinderhilfswerk erklärte , die Interessen der Jüngsten würden bei politischen Entscheidungen noch immer zu wenig berücksichtigt. Man nehme eine fast flächendeckende Vernachlässigung ihrer Belange in Deutschland wahr. Auch UNICEF Deutschland forderte mehr Mitbestimmung für Kinder und Jugendliche . Mit einer bundesweiten Schulaktion will die Hilfsorganisation auf deren Recht aufmerksam machen, bei Entscheidungen, die sie betreffen, angehört zu werden. Diese Nachricht wurde am 20.11.2026 im Programm Deutschlandfunk gesendet.

articleBody:
[Art Movements,](https://hyperallergic.com/tag/art-movements/) * published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.*

### Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence

The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced **Laura Hoptman**, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told *Hyperallergic* in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”

title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
subtitle: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of su…
feedText: In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.
articleBody:
# Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

## Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

A new approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have identified a compound that increases the amount of energy the body uses rather than simply reducing how much food a person eats.

In experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass. It also increased energy expenditure by up to 18%, even though the mice did not become more physically active or experience an increase in body temperature.

The findings, published in Science Advances , suggest a promising new direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease. The experimental compound also appeared to enhance the benefits of popular weight-loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy when the treatments were used together. However, its effectiveness and safety have not yet been established in humans.

A Different Approach to Weight Loss Than Ozempic

Over the past five years, medications known as GLP-1 drugs have transformed the treatment of obesity and other metabolic conditions, including diabetes and fatty liver disease. Drugs marketed as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound have helped many patients achieve substantial weight loss while improving their ability to regulate blood sugar.

Despite these benefits, the medications have important limitations. Nausea and other digestive problems can make treatment difficult for some patients. Because these drugs reduce appetite and food consumption, they can also increase the risk of inadequate nutrition and loss of muscle mass. Over time, losing too much muscle can contribute to weakness, frailty, and other health complications.

Berkeley researchers wanted to investigate a fundamentally different strategy. Rather than focusing on reducing calorie intake, they explored whether it would be possible to increase the amount of energy the body burns.

This process, known as energy expenditure, includes the calories used to maintain basic bodily functions, regulate metabolism, and support everyday activities. Increasing energy expenditure could potentially help people lose weight without relying exclusively on eating less.

"Body weight responds to two levers: taking in fewer calories, or spending more energy," said Anders Näär, a professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at UC Berkeley and senior author of the study. "GLP-1s work almost entirely on the first, so we went after the second."

A Compound That Burns Fat While Preserving Muscle

The researchers focused on a molecule called 5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid (TOFA), which has an unusual combination of effects on the body's metabolism.

TOFA interferes with the production of lipids, a broad category of fatty substances that includes cholesterol and triglycerides. These molecules serve important functions, but excessive levels of certain lipids can contribute to metabolic disorders and cardiovascular disease.

At the same time, TOFA activates genes involved in taking up and burning fat for energy. This combination allows the compound to influence both how the body produces fat and how it uses fat as fuel.

In mice, treatment with TOFA produced several encouraging results. The animals became more sensitive to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. Improved insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to control blood sugar, an important benefit for people with diabetes or insulin resistance.

The compound also lowered triglyceride levels and improved characteristics of fatty liver disease, a condition in which excess fat accumulates inside liver cells and can eventually interfere with liver function.

Perhaps most notably, obese mice treated with TOFA lost weight primarily through reductions in body fat, without experiencing significant losses of lean muscle mass. This distinction could be especially valuable because maintaining muscle is important for strength, mobility, and long-term metabolic health.

How TOFA Increases Energy Burning by 18%

Although TOFA was originally discovered in the 1970s, the new research uncovered additional properties that could make it particularly useful for treating metabolic disease.

The compound belongs to a group of substances known as ACC inhibitors. These compounds interfere with enzymes that help the body manufacture fatty acids, effectively slowing the production of certain fats.

Other ACC inhibitors have previously advanced to mid-stage clinical trials, but none has been approved to treat metabolic diseases. One major obstacle has been an unexpected side effect: many of these compounds increase triglycerides in the blood, potentially raising the risk of heart problems.

The Berkeley team discovered that TOFA does more than inhibit ACC. It also activates two cellular receptors called PPARα and PPARδ, which help regulate the genes responsible for fat metabolism.

These receptors function as molecular switches. When activated, they stimulate processes that allow cells to absorb fatty acids and break them down to produce energy. In effect, TOFA simultaneously reduces the production of certain fats and encourages the body to burn fat that is already available.

In mice, this activity increased energy expenditure by as much as 18%, without requiring additional physical activity or raising body temperature. Unlike other ACC inhibitors, TOFA also did not cause triglyceride levels to rise, potentially because of its additional effects on fat metabolism.

"TOFA appears to engage a coordinated metabolic response," said study first author Justin Y. Lee, a postdoctoral student at UCSF who conducted the research as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley. "It is not simply blocking lipid synthesis. It is also activating energy expenditure pathways that may help the body handle excess lipid and glucose more effectively."

To understand whether these effects could be reproduced with separate treatments, the scientists gave mice a combination of two different compounds. One blocked lipid production, while the other stimulated energy expenditure.

Surprisingly, this two-compound approach was less effective at improving overall metabolic health than TOFA alone. The finding suggests that TOFA's ability to influence multiple metabolic processes through a single molecule may be an important part of its effectiveness.

Could TOFA Make Ozempic and Wegovy More Effective?

The researchers also investigated whether TOFA could improve the results of existing GLP-1 medications.

They tested the compound alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, as well as tirzepatide, which is marketed as Mounjaro and Zepbound.

These medications primarily help people lose weight by reducing appetite and food intake. TOFA, by contrast, targets the other side of the energy balance equation by increasing how much energy the body expends.

When the researchers combined TOFA with these medications in mice, the results were more favorable than those produced by either treatment alone. The combinations led to greater improvements in body weight, blood glucose regulation, insulin levels, and triglycerides.

This suggests that treatments targeting calorie intake and energy expenditure could potentially work together to produce stronger metabolic benefits.

"In our combination experiments, TOFA worked additively or synergistically with the GLP-1 appetite-suppressing drugs, so we view it as complementary rather than as a replacement," Näär said.

In other words, the researchers do not necessarily envision TOFA replacing medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy. Instead, it could eventually become an additional treatment that helps address obesity and related metabolic conditions through a different biological mechanism.

A Promising Discovery, but Human Trials Are Still Needed

Despite the encouraging results, the researchers emphasize that TOFA remains an experimental compound. All the findings so far come from animal studies, and scientists have not yet established whether it is safe or effective in humans.

Further research will be necessary to determine whether the same metabolic improvements can be achieved in people and whether the treatment could offer meaningful advantages over existing medications.

To help move the research toward potential clinical applications, the Berkeley scientists have established a biotechnology company called ReRx Therapeutics. The effort has received support from the university's life sciences entrepreneurship network, including Nucleate and Berkeley SkyDeck.

If the findings eventually translate to humans, TOFA could represent an important addition to the growing range of treatments for obesity and diabetes. By encouraging the body to use more energy while helping preserve muscle, the compound points toward a potentially different way to achieve healthier weight loss.

The research was funded through discretionary resources provided by UC Berkeley, with additional support from the UCSF Liver Center and the University of Michigan Animal Phenotyping Core.

Additional authors include Chi Zhu, Melissa A. Boldridge, Rachelle L. Stark, Lei Xu, Federico Gonzalez, Xin Tang, Kaitlyn T. Dang and Kook Son of Berkeley; Gracia Bonilla, Kashish Chetal and Ruslan I. Sadreyev of Massachusetts General Hospital; Kosuke Watari and Michael Karin of the University of California, San Diego; Christina Papa and Bilal N. Sheikh of the Helmholtz Center Munich; Prabha Ibrahim of ReRx Therapeutics.

title: Fact Check: FAKE Photo of Xi, Putin and Trump Resembling Yalta Image of Churchill, FDR and Stalin Is AI-Generated
subtitle: Does a real photo of Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S.
feedText: President Donald Trump resemble the Yalta photo of British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt? No, that's not true: AI detection tools concluded that the supposed photo is an AI-generated fabrication, not a genuine photograph of the three leaders together. The clothing worn by the three men at the Nov. 19, 2026, summit in Shenzhen, China, does not match the clothing depicted in the AI-generated image. The claim appeared in a post by the @MrPool_…
articleBody:
Does a real photo of Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump resemble the Yalta photo of British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt? No, that's not true: AI detection tools concluded that the supposed photo is an AI-generated fabrication, not a genuine photograph of the three leaders together. The clothing worn by the three men at the Nov. 19, 2026, summit in Shenzhen, China, does not match the clothing depicted in the AI-generated image.

The claim appeared in [a post](https://x.com/MrPool_QQ/status/2123126862352101768) by the @MrPool_QQ account on X on Nov. 18, 2026. The date is a day earlier than the summit because of the time difference between the United States and China. It read:

> 🔻 THIS IS HUGE.
> TWO PHOTOGRAPHS. EIGHTY-ONE YEARS APART. THE SAME THREE CHAIRS.
> February 1945, Livadia Palace, Crimea. Roosevelt, Churchill, Stalin. They sat exactly like this for the cameras -- and then they moved Poland's borders while Poland was still burning, and signed a protocol nobody in Warsaw had read.
> Roosevelt died two months later. Churchill was voted out within six months. Stalin outlived them both by eight years. The photograph outlived all three.
> Now look at the bottom frame. Shenzhen. Xi, Putin, Trump. Same chairs. Same order. Same arrangement of bodies.
> Nobody staged this. Or somebody did -- and that is worse.
> Look at the middle seat. In 1945 it belonged to a man who was already dying. In 2026 it belongs to the man neither host invited and neither host can remove.
> Look at the hands. In 1945 they were the hands that had just carved a continent. In 2026 they are the hands that will decide whether the next carve is Ukraine.
> And notice the single absence. There is no fourth chair. There was no fourth chair in 1945 either -- and the countries whose borders were drawn that week were not in the room then, and will not be in the room Thursday.
> The chairs are identical. That is not design. That is instruction.
> They will not sign a map on Thursday. They will pose for one. The signature comes later, in a document you will read about after it is already binding.
> SZX-1119 / YALTA-2 / SEAT-2-CENTRE / 81-YR / NO-SIGNATURE / NO-4TH-CHAIR
> Eighty-one years. Same three chairs. The world is being arranged again while everyone watches the handshake.
> ⟁

This is what the post looked like on X at the time of writing:

*(Image source: post by @MrPool_QQ on X.)*

#### Image analysis

Lead Stories ran the image through the [Hive Moderation AI-Generated Content Detection tool](https://hivemoderation.com/ai-generated-content-detection), which concluded that it was 88% "Likely to be AI-Generated Image":

Lead Stories also ran the AI-generated image of the three leaders through the [UncovAI verification tool](https://uncovai.com/image-detection/). The tool concluded with 100% confidence that the image was AI-generated:

*(Image source: UncovAI.)*

Additional evidence that the image is fabricated comes from discrepancies between the leaders' clothing in the fake photo and what they actually wore that day. In the composite image below, the fabricated photo is between the authentic summit photos. At the time, Trump was wearing a medium-blue tie, not a red one; Putin was wearing dark slacks and a plum-colored tie, not gray slacks and a dark-colored tie; and Xi was wearing a red tie, not a dark-colored one:

*(Image sources: video by C-SPAN on YouTube, post by @MrPool_QQ on X and a pool photo by Win McNamee via AFP-Getty.)*

[The video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bDhxojEdu6E) of the three men at the summit by C-SPAN on YouTube on Nov. 19, 2026, is embedded below:

#### News searches

Lead Stories searched [Google News](https://news.google.com/search?q=%22Xi%2C%22%20%22Putin%2C%22%20%22Trump%2C%22%20and%20%22Yalta.%22&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) and [Yahoo News](https://news.search.yahoo.com/search;_ylt=A2RRm1yfeP9qCQMAC1LQtDMD;_--?fr=uh3_news_web&.tsrc=uh3_news_web&fr2=sb-top&p=%22Xi%2C%22+%22Putin%2C%22+%22Trump%2C%22+and+%22Yalta.%22) and found no matching reports about the claim from established news outlets using the search terms: "Xi," "Putin," "Trump" and "Yalta."

feedText:

articleBody:
The Landing, a beloved Los Angeles gallery whose program was defined by its unique pairings of historical and contemporary artists, announced that it had closed. Its last exhibition was a one-night only solo for Maxwell Hendler staged on October 29.

On the gallery’s website, founder and owner Gerard O’Brien wrote, “the Landing Gallery at 5118 W Jefferson Blvd is now closed. We are no longer programming at this location. We are deeply grateful to the artists, collectors, collaborators, and community who have been fellow participants in our engagements. It has been a privilege to champion extraordinary artists, present ambitious exhibitions, and create a space for meaningful exchange and discovery.”

In an [Instagram post](https://www.instagram.com/p/Df7rFoCvlzd/?bqrl=ZmZoYmgzejNzcnEy), Gerard O’Brien put it more simply, “End of an era … 22 years of Gallery spaces in Los Angeles, Reform Galley 2004-2019 … the Landing Gallery 2012 -2026 … onwards. thank you Los Angeles❣️”

O’Brien founded the Landing in 2012 as an off-shoot of his design-focused Reform Gallery. “I never really thought there was a big difference,” he said of the distinction between art and design. He chose the name for its original location, a spot within Reform: “he cleared out the landing atop a short staircase in his furniture gallery and dedicated it to shows of art, bringing in work by artists both contemporary and historical to display just above his design wares,” as a 2016 blog post by book publisher Phaidon [reported](https://www.phaidon.com/en-us/blogs/stories/meet-the-dealers-the-landing-s-gerard-o-brien?srsltid=AYCX9vIWBuPWzpUxHKJVRoEDEhUnIDJ0cluQ_tFNg9kSjya0bCEjQ6Pt).

In 2015, O’Brien decided that it was time for the Landing to grow, opening in a 2,800-square-foot gallery space on Jefferson Boulevard with a solo show for the late California artist JB Blunk.

Over the years, the Landing would become known for its pairings of historical and contemporary artists. At the time of its closing, its roster included four deceased artists (Jeremy Anderson, Richard Bowman, Leslie Kerr, and Fred Reichman) and five living contemporary artists (Yevgeniya Baras, Ryan Fenchel, Matt Phillips, Jonathan Ryan, and Amanda Valdez).

The gallery was also known for regularly staging off-kilter group exhibitions, with titles like “Rat Bastard Protective Association” (2016), “The Useful and the Decorative” (2017), “New Iconography: Artists Raising Children” (2021), and “Consensual Ennui (2023). The first of these, “3 Women” (2016) took its name from a 1977 Robert Altman film as a way “to create a cross-generational dialogue that explores the intersections of craft and fine art, influence and homage,” per a release. It featured the work of Lenore Tawney from the 1960s and ’70s paired with textile pieces by Tanya Aguiñiga and paintings by Loie Hollowell. The exhibition marked the first time Tawney’s work had been exhibited in LA in nearly 50 years.

In an *[Artforum review](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/55f04045e4b0a5f28738e951/t/57ffb553579fb3fe7189f985/1476375892928/Artforum-3Women.jpg)*, Erin Kimmel wrote, “The Landing’s handsome, restrained exhibition showcased the exquisite detail of [Tawney’s] works, which reward prolonged scrutiny with seemingly boundless formal revelations.”

To mark its 10th anniversary at its Jefferson Boulevard space, the Landing mounted a two-part anniversary exhibition. The first part, which opened in November 2025, focused on contemporary art and design and featured the work of Ruth Asawa, Wallace Berman, Bruce Conner, Lyne Foulkes, and Doyle Lane. The second part, which opened this past April, featured gallery artists as well as others who had exhibited there, including Brenda Goodman, Sam Jablon, and Lukas Geronimas.

In a release for part one, O’Brien wrote, “10 Year brings together the feeling of the earliest days of the Landing Gallery when two years of exhibitions took place inside Reform Gallery on Melrose Avenue. Exhibiting art in a salon style in dialogue with decorative arts is how tL began.”

The Landing’s closure is the latest in an [extended wave of closures](https://www.artnews.com/t/gallery-closures/) that began in mid-2025. Los Angeles galleries have particularly been affected, with Murmurs, the Box, LA Louver, and Blum all shuttering, along with the LA outposts of Marian Goodman Gallery and Tanya Bonakdar.

In his statement on the gallery’s website, O’Brien added, “While our gallery doors have closed, our commitment to art and artists continues. Watch this space for news of future offsite exhibitions, activations, and special projects. Thank you for being part of the Landing’s ongoing narrative.”

subtitle: Maybe we shouldn’t be giving this release more attention, since it was “recorded entirely without permission,” which makes us suspect a similar thi…

articleBody:
Maybe we shouldn’t be giving this release more attention, since it was “recorded entirely without permission,” which makes us suspect a similar thing about the cover photo.  But it’s impossible to resist.  zakè and Akira Film Script tell us “iykyk” and we didn’t know until we read the liner notes; we thought Bellscapes referred to musical bells, when it instead refers to Taco Bells; yes, you read that right.  These tracks were recorded in two Taco Bells, so now it’s time to drop the Gordita and give them a spin.

Taco Bells can be many things: fast, fun, cheap, loud, colorful, grungy.  One thing they are not (at least to adults) is cool.  (They do, however, offer Cool Ranch® Doritos® Locos Tacos. We should probably put ® all over this article, but we don’t want to be annoying.)  However, if they wanted to be cool, or at the very least, hipster, they might consider playing this album as restaurant ambience.  It is, after all, ambient music: the true-to-life sounds of Taco Bell, beginning with zakè’s “Taco Bell, Whitestown, Indiana, April 21st, 2026 (Order 326).”  The number 326 speaks of fast food, high volume, and relative anonymity, which is likely why nobody noticed or cared about zakè’s recording equipment.  Is this ambient music over the sounds of the dining room: the clinks and scrapes and chairs and plates?  Or is this ambient music under such sounds?  We love this description, so we’re printing it in full:

Every sound heard across these sprawling compositions was sourced organically from the field: soda dispensers sputtering with divine carbonation, tortilla wrappers crackling like distant bonfires, ice machines collapsing into metallic avalanches, fluorescent lighting frequencies, parking lot wind, muttered order confirmations, tray impacts, fryer resonance, and the spiritually transformative ambience of fire sauce dropping in slow motion onto a crunchwrap supreme.

Fast food music is meant to enhance the diner’s experience, but also to subtly manipulate the mood: it tends to be upbeat, popular and innocuous.  But what if it were this music?  Would the diner want to stay longer?  Would deeper conversations take place?  Would the patrons begin to discuss the actual food instead of using it as an inexpensive, convenient source of padded calories?  Removed from its original setting, the music also becomes an odd meditation, offering a nostalgic gloss over something that one would never expect to provoke nostalgia – unless, of course, Taco Bell was a favorite teen hangout.  And what if, God forbid, the chain were ever to fold?  Then this album would become its prescient elegy.  Side A sounds like a long, lonely meal, but also sounds like rumination: from “I shouldn’t have eaten that burrito” to “What have I done with my life?”

Akira Film Script’s “Taco Bell Cantina, Pacifica, California, April 18th, 2026 (Order 155) shifts the location to the West Coast, raising questions of geography as they pertain to the chain’s desire to offer a universally analogous experience.  The food at this Taco Bell should taste like the food in any Taco Bell, and the restaurant should feel and sound the same, but it does not, because like the old adage says, “You cannot step into the same Taco Bell twice.”  Akira Film Script calls this branch “the Pacific coast’s most spiritually active Taco Bell location,” but who knows if this is true?

The piece begins with pure field recordings: the sounds of traffic and turn signals, a distant hum, the ambience of real life.  One can hear the sound of the sea, children laughing, adults corralling them in.  What could be more satisfying after a day of catching barrels than a Cantina Chicken Rolled Quesadilla and Olivia Rodrigo x Pretty Pink Baja Blast®?  The seagulls are chirping happily, anticipating discards.  In this piece, the ambient music comes rolling in like a slow wave, a vast drone, a pleasant shelter.  The children’s hellos are particularly endearing; if Side A is adulthood looking back, Side B is the childhood of the now.  When one hears the sound of wrappers being crumpled, one knows that an adult is doing it, and that the children have gone back to play.

In the twelfth minute, the track begins to transcend its sources.  Gorgeous piano tugs the mind upward, away from beef and beans and cheese and grain.  One begins to feel grateful for the little things, which may include the restaurant, the family, the day.  There’s certainly a tongue-in-cheek nature to this release, but there’s also love, which is why the chain, should it ever learn about this release, should not trust their first reaction but recognize what a compliment it is.  Bellscapes is as much a tribute to the chain as “Fancy Like” is a tribute to Applebee’s.  We’d love to see a picture disc featuring a full-vinyl image of a quesadilla, but that’s probably asking too much.

Taco Bell always has value meals, the latest being the $5 Classic, $7 Supreme, or $9 Discovery Luxe Box®.  zakè and Akira Film Script have a value meal of their own; as of this writing, the album is only $1.  Hurry to Bandcamp today to take advantage of this limited time offer!  (Richard Allen)

articleBody:
## Ava Roth and the art of Kintsu-Bee

One of Ava Roth’s most valuable collaborators is not human. In fact, it’s the bees. In her series, Kintsu-Bee, she places broken ceramics into a [hive of bees](https://www.designboom.com/tag/beeswax-art-design/) who, through the formation of honeycombs, create a new bond between the cracked pieces. The method is named after the Japanese repair method,[kintsugi,](https://www.designboom.com/tag/kintsugi/)which uses lacquer and gold leaf to create a shining new seam in broken dishware, turning what was once considered waste into a valuable new form. From this, Roth’s work expands beyond cups and plates. She has experimented with frames, [textiles](https://www.designboom.com/tag/textile-and-fabric-art/), and even embroidery hoops to create structures in collaboration with the planet’s busiest[insects](https://www.designboom.com/tag/insects/). In this extraordinary interspecies project, the Canadian artist and artisan creates a powerful meditation on the power of the natural world, craft, and more-than-human intelligence. Her work has gone on to be recognized by Homo Faber and has been exhibited internationally, including in Canada, where she’s from.

**In conversation with designboom,** artist [Ava Roth](https://www.avaroth.ca/) shares what brought her to the hives, her multimedia works, and her relationship with the bees. She says of her process, *‘I am committed to sharing the labor equally, meaning that in each piece I try to give as much of my own time and effort as I am hoping the bees will offer.’*

Kintsugi/Kintsu-Bee Cup #1 ceramic plate by Satoshi Yoshikawa and natural honeycomb | all images courtesy of [Ava Roth](https://www.instagram.com/avarothart/?hl=en)

Cherry Beach Salvage on Paper Salvaged garbage, rocks, encaustic medium, paper, wire and natural honeycomb

## Busy bees and interspecies art

Famed American poet Emily Dickinson wrote in [To make a prairie](https://www.emilydickinsonmuseum.org/to-make-a-prairie-1755/) (1779), one of her poems about bees, *‘To make a prairie it takes a clover and one bee,/ One clover, and a bee./ And revery.’* In this musing on the creation of plains, the wonder bees can inspire comes to life. From their essential role as a pollinator species to their intricate hexagonal combs and the sweet honey they produce, bees are not only invaluable to the functions of the natural world, but the complex worlds they create in their hives continue to inspire artists.

Seeing their value as a keystone species, one that’s critical to the greater functioning of their environment, has inspired many artists like Roth. For example, Pierre Huyghe’s Untilled (Liegender Frauenakt) [Reclining Female Nude] (2012) features an actively maintained beehive atop a human body and is held in the collections of MoMA in New York. In this sculpture, the artist comments on the collective thinking capacity of bees. There’s also the work of [Pollinator Pathmaker](https://www.designboom.com/art/pollinator-pathmaker-brings-back-buzzing-bees-foliage-filled-artworks/) by Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg, which seeks to bring pollinating species back to specified regions through an algorithmically generated plot of pollinator-optimized plants. These works, just a few in a world of bee-forward art, show how the insects have inspired creatives both with their incredible intelligence and their importance to the cycles of the environment.

honeycomb and mesh hanging structures by Ava Roth inspired by the works of Ruth Asawa

## Roth and Beeswax

One form of art particularly linked to the legacy of bees is encaustic painting. Using a mixture of melted, pigmented beeswax and resin, an artist can build pigmented layers similar to those of an oil painter. *‘I was working with encaustic as my primary media,’* Roth says of the technique. Some of these works incorporate the golden ginkgo leaf and embroidery floss, while others feature horsehair and photographs of expansive bodies of water. ‘Being immersed in wax naturally led to a curiosity about bees. And the more I learned about bees, the more that knowledge began to inform my work, which in turn led me to take a beekeeping course. During this period of learning, I found myself incorporating pieces of burr comb into my work and building encaustic paintings inside hive frames.’

Self Portrait Photography (image by Joana Betzner), encaustic, embroidery floss and natural honeycomb in embroidery hoop by Ava Roth

## Arriving at a collaboration with the bees

After working with encaustics, Roth notes that her next big leap was training with Master Beekeeper Mylee Nordin. On this experience, she notes, *‘Her expertise and oversight provided me with the confidence to keep an apiary in my backyard. At that point, the final move to putting my work directly into hives was almost inevitable!’* She points out that this body of work wasn’t the intention. It was more, what she calls, *‘a process of playful experimentation born out of genuine curiosity and deep respect,’* for her insect collaborators.

As a multimedia artist, much like in her work with encaustics, Roth’s bee sculptures start with an arrangement of embroidery, paintings, photographs, and other materials. When creating these structures, she works with space in mind for the honeycombs and other alterations that will eventually occur once they’re placed in the hive. *‘Control is also something I try hard to share equally,’* she says of the collaborative nature of her work. *‘Importantly, I don’t force the bees to engage with the art in any way. In other words, whether or not the bees build their comb on any given piece, let alone how much and in what shapes, is left entirely to them.’*

after working with encaustics, Roth notes that her next big leap was training with Master Beekeeper Mylee Nordin

As a multimedia artist, much like in her work with encaustics, Roth’s bee sculptures start with an arrangement of embroidery, paintings, photographs, and other materials

## More-than-human creativity abounds

After Roth creates this structure, it’s up to the bees to finalize the form. Though the structure of a comb is fairly regular in shape and color, Roth admits that *‘Most of the pieces surprise [her] in some way, which is one of the great delights of this project.’* She highlights two pieces in particular: ‘One was a two-dimensional beaded piece that, for some reason that is beyond me, the bees built a massive and undulating armature of comb over. The structure of the comb is really gorgeous, much more complex and massive than on anything else I’ve seen in the decade I’ve been working on this project. Another is a small piece of driftwood and knitted wire, where the bees collectively decided to trace and mimic the pattern of the wire with their comb, which is truly remarkable.’

Inherent in Roth’s work is a juxtaposition between the man-made and the forces of nature. Through these small meditations on the logic of bees, their combs bulging, bonding, and restructuring her objects, she sheds light on how the intelligence of these little insects is at once comparable to our own and entirely beyond our comprehension. Yet, rather than attempting to understand or control this intelligence, Roth makes space for it to unfold. Her work asks us to reconsider what it means to create, and whether art-making must remain an exclusively human act. By sharing both the labor and the authorship with her bees, Roth offers a different model of artistic collaboration, one rooted in patience, reciprocity, and respect for the natural world.

Roth says she continually finds herself amazed by the creation of the bees

articleBody:
[Open video on YouTube ↗](https://youtu.be/x0VSm6IjcDQ?si=ux2et_X2fIVnHUHL&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled["Issue tracking is dead."](https://linear.app/next?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) In this episode, we chat with[Cristina Cordova](https://linear.app/blog/welcoming-cristina-cordova-to-linear?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), COO of[Linear](https://linear.app/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way.

Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp.

When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold[$99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation](https://linear.app/now/sharing-growth-with-the-people-building-linear?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv).

We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else.

### Half the work on Linear is now created by agents

Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents.

That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app.

So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work.

[Jump to the MCP discussion →](https://youtu.be/x0VSm6IjcDQ?t=1200&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

### "Issue tracking is dead"

When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues.

Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear.

Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads.

[Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion →](https://youtu.be/x0VSm6IjcDQ?t=1419&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

### The AI budget behind $100M in months

The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high.

It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing.

When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real.

[Jump to the AI budget discussion →](https://youtu.be/x0VSm6IjcDQ?t=2806&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

### Linear threw out its 2025 enterprise roadmap

Three weeks after joining in 2023, Cristina crossed "move upmarket to enterprise" off Linear's company goals. It had one salesperson. She went after growth-stage companies that would have to rip out an existing tool instead, the same way Stripe won new businesses long before it won switchers.

Linear finally declared an enterprise push in 2025, with a roadmap full of features for large organizations. Then agents happened. Linear built an MCP server, an agents platform with a whole new set of APIs, and integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot. None of it was planned, and a lot of the enterprise work never got done.

Cristina chose to race ahead anyway. Competitors waited, and enterprises started putting Linear on their shortlists.

[Jump to the enterprise roadmap discussion →](https://youtu.be/x0VSm6IjcDQ?t=3427&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

### No SDRs, no forward deployed engineers

Linear has never hired a single SDR. Cristina thinks the qualification call wastes the customer's time: they want a demo, not questions about their budget. AEs do their own outbound, with tooling to keep it personal.

It doesn't do forward deployed engineering either. Linear should be easy enough to adopt that nobody needs access to your systems. Solutions engineers sell alongside enterprise AEs instead, sometimes building a working ServiceNow integration overnight to show a prospect it can be done. Cristina adds that an opinionated tool gives agents cleaner data than one where every team defines "bug" differently.

Support stays in-house, and Linear won't let an LLM answer tickets on its own. AI drafts replies and a human decides what goes out. Customers sometimes assume the replies are AI because they arrive so fast. In three and a half years, Cristina has never had an escalation over a bad support experience.

[Jump to the sales team discussion →](https://youtu.be/x0VSm6IjcDQ?t=2080&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

### Everyone wants outcome-based pricing

Cristina would love a model like Intercom's Fin, which charges for each support conversation its AI resolves. It's harder for Linear. What is auto-triaging a bug to the right team worth when one company thinks that's the PM's job and another doesn't?

Until someone cracks that, Linear charges for what costs it money and keeps the rest free. Seats stay. Linear Agent chat is free even though it runs on frontier models. In coding sessions, users pick OpenAI or Anthropic models and harnesses, and Linear passes through the published API price plus a small markup. Loops run on AI credits.

Linear doesn't start charging for things that used to be free. New AI features launch as free betas with notice that pricing is coming, and prices start high and come down rather than the other way around.

[Jump to the pricing discussion →](https://youtu.be/x0VSm6IjcDQ?t=3006&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

### Why not hire 100 salespeople?

Cristina says Linear runs on about half the headcount of companies at its stage and revenue. A sales team bigger than the rest of the company would have cost it the trust engineering now has in sales.

From Stripe she brought a 40% rule: at least 40% of the company should be engineering, product, design and data. If sales wanted more people, it helped recruit engineers first. Linear has no hard rule, but one of the first things she built was a headcount spreadsheet by function, and she still watches the ratio.

Hiring is slow on purpose. Candidates do a work trial on a real problem. Hers was writing Linear's go-to-market plan for the next six to twelve months, which then became her job. At about 170 people, the only C-suite is the founders and her.

[Jump to the hiring discussion →](https://youtu.be/x0VSm6IjcDQ?t=3954&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

## Show notes

- [Linear](https://linear.app/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — the product development system where Cristina is COO.
- [Sharing Linear's growth with the people building it](https://linear.app/now/sharing-growth-with-the-people-building-linear?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — the August tender at a $2.5 billion valuation, with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention.
- [Issue tracking is dead](https://linear.app/next?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — Karri's March post on why Linear is building for agents.
- [Linear MCP server](https://linear.app/changelog/2025-05-01-mcp?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — the May 2025 launch Cristina says was basically a first for the category.
- [Introducing Linear Agent](https://linear.app/changelog/2026-03-24-introducing-linear-agent?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — the built-in agent whose chat Linear keeps free.
- [How we built Triage Intelligence](https://linear.app/now/how-we-built-triage-intelligence?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — the feature that suggests labels and catches duplicates in incoming issues, Cristina's example of AI that doesn't need to be an agent
- [Coding sessions in Linear](https://linear.app/changelog/2026-06-11-coding-sessions?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — the June launch that ended Linear's all-seat pricing, running Claude Code and Codex on AI credits.
- [Introducing Loops](https://linear.app/changelog/2026-07-20-introducing-loops?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — recurring agent jobs, also billed with AI credits.
- [Intercom Fin pricing](https://www.intercom.com/help/en/articles/8205718-fin-pricing?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — $0.99 per resolved conversation, the outcome-based model Cristina wishes fit Linear.

## Transcript

**0:00** Karri writing this blog post, like issue tracking is dead. So like how do you explain to your customers that like, hey, you know, our entire business was issue tracking before and now our CEO just wrote this blog post? The great thing about our business is that we're not like so big to like kill ourselves. Right? Yeah. Like, it's probably really hard if you're Google to, like, kill the search business. Yeah. Right? And put an AI, you know, box at the top of every search result, and maybe no one's gonna look at the ads. Right? So your entire business is upended. And, like, yes, the unit of the issue still exists, but we probably shouldn't have a world where people are, like, manually tracking work. Yeah. So, like, that's what's dead. Right? So in a lot of cases, when we were talking to various customers as this, you know, blog post came out, most of our customers were like, yeah. Tracking is dead. And by the way, like, what are you guys? What am I buying? Right? Cristina Cordova, you're the COO of Linear. Could you introduce yourself? Yeah. Yeah. So I'm Cristina. I've been at Linear for about three and a half years now. Joined as COO, and I'm still COO today. Prior to Linear, I spent time at Notion leading our platform, so the build out of our APIs, and then our partnerships and self serve growth initiatives as well. And then before that, I was at Stripe for seven and a half years. And there, I led a lot of our early partnerships and go to market, and then moved over to the product side and built out some new products for early stage companies. So I've been probably anywhere from like the product side of a company and like managing engineers all the way to, managing, you know, the business side of a company as well, which has been really fun.

**1:30** So why did Linear hire a COO at, like, 40 employees? Is that, like, odd or is that pretty normal? I mean, I I generally don't believe every company needs a COO. Yeah. Right? Like, when I talk to founders and they're like, hey, like, I think I found product market fit. Like, how do we start to scale, like, the business side of the company? I am often, I feel like, cautioning against maybe hiring someone like me. So I think for every company, it's a little bit different. I think you have to really understand as, like, a founder, like, what are the things you need and what are the things you're looking for and the people that you bring on to the team. Often early on, it's just like I need someone to, like, sell something. Right? We have expanded beyond the capability of the founder CEO to sell every net new customer. Right? So there, I generally talk about, well, you should hire folks in sales. Maybe hire a sales leader to build out a team. Right? But if you're not exactly sure what you're looking for in, like, marketing or operations or other parts of the company, then it may very well not make sense to hire someone like me. You know, I think with the Linear founders, you know, they were incredibly focused on, like, design and engineering and product. And I think they had a really great, you know, kind of combination of skills between the three of them. But as we were starting to scale the business side of the company, they didn't necessarily look at, like, the next salesperson that we hired and said, I know exactly what we're looking for here, and I know whether or not sales is performing really well. Right? So if you don't look at different parts of your company and say like, okay, I know what great is, and I feel like I have a good sense of, like, how to get to great, it can sometimes be helpful to hire someone like me or, like, a functional leader, like, when it comes time to do that.

**3:00** Yeah. So, like, what did the business look like at that point? Like, can you talk about, like, what revenue they were at? Or Yeah. We were probably... I wanna say, you know, we had some large customers, but no, like, public company customers. Probably no customer above, I wanna say, like, maybe 500 seats or something like that. So I would say, like, we mostly tapped out at, like, mid market. And we were probably best well known for being a great product for startups, but not necessarily a great product for other companies Yeah. At that time. You know, and I think at that point in time, we were we're doing well with like a product led growth model where most people were using our product because they signed up self serve. Mhmm. And then grew with us over time. So companies like Vercel and Ramp and many other customers like that, you know, really never talked to a human being at Linear. Signed up for the product, started using it, and then started scaling, which was great. Like, you know the product can do a lot of work on its own. But it was also start... Like, time to start selling to, you know, the company that is not even gonna put, like, a lick of data into your service without, you know, signing a contract Yeah.

**4:30** And doing a pilot and surveying their team on, you know, what tool they're using before and what... You know, what tool is this and what's better. Right? That also means that we can be a lot more nimble than other companies because you're not moving this, like, gigantic ship whenever you need to change direction. But I don't think we would have done well with, like, having a sales team that was bigger than, like, the entire company. You know? So, you know, I think at the beginning, I think... And this was true when I was at Stripe too. Like, there was this impression of salespeople that I think for a lot of tech companies can be pretty negative. Right? It's like, oh, like, who are these people? These, like, car salesman Yeah. Coming in to, like, sell our product. I never thought about it that way. We don't think about it that way at Linear, but that was like maybe the impression of salespeople maybe of like, you know, tech in the twenty twelves. You know? I view it very differently because I do believe that like sales has a lot of power to help inflect a business that requires human interaction Yeah. And persuasion. And I I would say that, like, for us, you know, doing it small and steady built the kind of trust that was required in different parts of the organization.

**1:07:30** So like engineering really trusts sales. Like when our sales team is like having trouble in a particular segment and, you know, gets on calls with, like, PMs on our team and things like that. Like, there's a lot of trust in that salesperson really understanding the need of the customer, what they're asking for, sometimes even helping solution when necessary. I don't think he would have done that. Like, we would have been able to do that particularly well by hiring a ton of people really quickly. And again, a lot of startups take that approach, but I think they have probably more of like a hire fast, fire fast Yeah. Type of mentality. And I think with hiring, you know, we do work trials. Like, what signal does that send to you? That signal sends to you. Like, we like to, take our time and really understand if someone's a good fit. We want to get them into the, problem scope that Linear operates in and test to see, like, that their great experience somewhere else is going to translate well into our company. You know? So I think it's like a philosophy difference and, you know, every company does things differently. And I would say a lot of the great companies, you know, in the world do things their own way for a reason. Yeah. Do you guys take inspiration from any other companies?

**1:09:00** I mean, I I spent seven and a half years at Stripe. And certainly, there are things I take inspiration from. I'll give an example. What... Because we were talking about hiring. You know, at a certain point, we were hiring, like, business people at Stripe faster than we were hiring, like, engineers and product folks and designers. And, you know, the founders were like, this has to come to a stop. Right? And it's like, well, you know, what kind of, you know, ratio would you like? Right? So you then take a step back and you're like, yeah. What what do we want this company to be? If we want this company to be like an engineering and product driven company, probably at least like 40% of the company should be like engineering product design, data, etcetera. And so we basically were like, okay. That's the, like, watermark. And, like, we can't It was just like an arbitrary number. Like It was 40%. 40%. And it was like, we can't go under that number. So if sales wants to hire more people, have sales help us hire engineers so that sales can then hire more people. I see. Right? And I think, like, yes, it's an arbitrary number, but I think it's important for you to understand, like, how do you want your company to be constructed? Right? Like, there are a lot of companies like... And Uber that are, like, heavy on operations, but that's because they're moving like humans and things. Right? We're a very different kind of company. We're like a software business. Right? And for us, we don't necessarily have to have, like, an operations component of the business that is, like, that huge because we're not dealing with those kinds situations. So like understand your business really well, understand what you want to be, and then figure out what model makes sense for you. So like, we don't have like that hard and fast rule at Linear of like 40%, but like I I watch that number. I like created a headcount spreadsheet. Was, like, one of the first things I did. Like, put everyone into their categories of, like, what function they're in, like, calculated the percentage, and, like, you know, I watch it.

**1:10:30** And I'm, like, we really need to, like, step up our game on, like, engineering recruiting. It is always going to be harder to hire engineers than it's going to be to hire salespeople. Yeah. And so, like, what are we going to do to like make that easier for us? So a lot of it is just like the philosophy and what you want to be. And knowing that I've been at companies that like, you know, wanna do things the same way, but also, you know, for example, don't wanna outsource support or, you know, wanna treat different aspects of the product in a different way. And I think that's the challenge. There are a lot of things that like I get to bring with me from like my previous experience. And then at the same time, there are a lot of things that I wanna do in a new way that I haven't seen anyone else do. Yeah. I was gonna ask that next. Like, were there like certain things that you specifically did not wanna bring over from like Stripe or Notion? Maybe one example. I think I think Stripe did so well as a company that I think in a lot of ways when, you know, you're a 140, $160,000,000,000 company and you're like on that rise, sometimes you believe you can always hire better than what you have today. So you have a leader in a given function that's doing well. And sometimes your first reaction to that could be like, well, it's because the business is doing well, not because that person necessarily is that great. Yeah.

**1:12:00** And it's It's like, oh, I'm at Google. I helped increase revenue by, you know, $20,000,000,000. Exactly. But what did you really do? Right? And and so sometimes it goes really well. Is it, you know, because of that person or is it because the business was going really well? And then if the company is doing so well that you can attract really high quality talent. Right? So someone like two levels above that person, and then a year later, you're able to attract a person who's two levels above that person. And... Right? You're kind of always going to be seeking, like, someone better than who you haven't seen because you can. And I think, like, for a lot of companies, like, being able to say, like like, I've said this to our founders. I'm like, we can get someone better. Like, we're a good company. Company that people want to work for and then are excited about. Like, we don't have to settle. Right? And I think that's, like, great. And then at the same time, sometimes you also have to, like, really recognize, like, the great people that you have. And I think for Stripe, it took a longer time to, like, come around to that. Like, Stripe's been having a lot of, like, boomerangs. Like, you know, people left the company because maybe they, you know, weren't on the rise, you know, in the way that they wanted to be. And then, you know, came back and are doing like amazingly well. And I think sometimes I would like to look back on my time at Linear and say like the right people were, like, promoted and excelled. And we didn't hire above them unless the company needed to. Right? Unless we needed to get to that a different stage. We needed something that that person didn't have. And not just because, like, we weren't willing to let them try to, like, be better than they are, to, like, scale at that next stage. Because, you know, in running startups, this is true of founders. Like, you don't... Like, almost no founder who has a lot of success has, like, done it exactly before. Right? And that's probably going to be true of a lot of the early team. Like, they're leaders at the company, but they've never scaled a support team to like 200 people or 500 people or whatever. That doesn't mean that they can't. Right? Just like it doesn't mean that that founder can't be a great founder at a thousand people and also a great founder at like 50 people. Mhmm. And so, like, I just fundamentally believe that like people can grow and scale, and that you should like reward that over time.

**1:13:30** And, you know, I have some time... Like different parts of of the company, like, I'm like, I don't know if they always believe that. I I think... And I think a lot has changed since then, for what it's worth. But maybe that's one thing. On support, that would be the other thing. I think it's incredibly difficult to scale support to that degree. And I think that we emphasize a higher level of quality than I've seen in vast majority of support organizations I've operated in. And so it's something that we care about. We're willing to pay more for it. And we believe it's like the right thing to do by our customers. And I love that I've literally never in three and a half years gotten an escalation because someone had a poor experience with our support team. So that's like a company that like I see and I love to be part of. Yeah. Know, and that's not true for every other company I've worked for.

**1:15:00** So, okay, you were at Stripe, then you went to Notion for a little bit, and then you became an investor. Yes. Why did you make that transition to becoming an investor? Yeah. When I was at Notion, I enjoyed my job, but the parts that I enjoyed were almost the parts that I wasn't really hired to do. So I I joined around maybe 40 people or so, and we were, you know, we were scaling. We didn't have like a single recruiter. We didn't have a head of people. We didn't have anyone working on growth. So, you know, what did I do? I, like, raised my hand and was like, I'll help hire our head of people. Like, I'll help hire our first recruiter. I'll find our first product manager and, like, hire them. And I did all of those things, and then I kind of, like, hired my way out of, like, jobs that I had. Right? And then got to a point where I was like, wait. I'm, like, back at the job. I was, like, actually hired to do. Yeah. Like, I don't really Which was what? Like, head of platform and partnerships. Okay. And I was like, I'm not really excited about this job anymore. Like, I was having more fun doing all that other stuff Yeah. That I wasn't really hired to do. But it's just like, it's company building. Mhmm. Right?

**1:16:30** And at the time, I was just like, I I I think I need a new role at like a different company. And I don't know what that role exactly looks like. Right? And so I thought that venture might be a great way to kind of get the breadth that I was looking for, really, by spending time with, like, a bunch of different kinds of companies in different spaces. And, you know, I think for me, it's it's it's very different being an investor than, like, coming into a company and actually doing the work. Mhmm. It's really, like, different to, like, advise a company like, oh, you should go spend more time with your customers. And you, you know, should think about this business model or, you know And you were doing early stage? Or Early stage. Yeah. And a lot of the early stage stuff is like you're investing like pre product market fit. And like, I don't know anything about your market. Like, you sell to like, I don't know, procurement leaders or like construction workers or like like, you know, you have to be in that to really understand. And I actually felt like I was more helpful when companies had that product market fit. If I think about every single company I've ever joined, it like just was finding like product market fit, and then I joined. And then I can be a lot more helpful and like build out the business. But, you know, I think for pre product market fit, a lot of it's just like investing in the right people and like getting out of the way. Yeah. And being supportive and helpful with intros and things like that. But what I... Like, I actually really love execution. Yeah. Being inside a company and, like, helping get stuff done. And I think I'm kind of known as a person who will, like, run through walls to get things done even, you know, if that might rub people the wrong way in certain larger organizations. But, you know, for a startup, it works really well. Yeah. And so that's Are worked for

**1:18:00** there certain things that you noticed, like being an operator made you a better investor at? And then also vice versa, like what did you learn from being an investor that made you better at, you know, your current role at Yeah. At Linear? I think I was speaking from, like, a place of, like, knowledge and truth. And I think a lot of investors have, like, never worked at a startup before. And there's nothing wrong with that. You can be an amazing... They're amazing investors who've never worked at a startup before, and it doesn't matter. Like, you invest in the right people. And, again, let them do their thing. And, you know, as long as you invest in the right people, that strategy works. Right? But, you know, I think also doing VC is sales. Like, you are selling money. And every other investor, like, has money to sell too. Right? So you're kind of selling the same product in some ways, but you are trying to sell yourself. Right? And, like, you are trying to differentiate yourself as a product beyond the money to that founder. And I found it much easier as someone who had, like, been operating at some great companies to be able to go to a founder and say, like, I can credibly help your business. Yeah. What would maybe other investors could.

**1:19:30** What would be, like, the the pitch for an investor who's never worked at a company? It'd be, like, oh, I have a lot of intros. I've already invested in a lot of like really cool companies. Is that like kinda their selling point? I think a lot of it is like sometimes like pattern matching. Right? Like I've been on the boards of these great companies and I've seen success from zero to, you know, a 100 or whatever. It may have been several times over. And, you know, maybe I can tell you when it's time to do x or when it's time to do y because I've pattern matched my way here. I, you know, in a lot of cases, you work with certain investors and they have, like, a very large Rolodex. They know lots of great people at great companies and Yeah. You know, can introduce you to people who are more knowledgeable than they are in certain areas. So, you know, often investors will come to me and be like, can you help this founder who's team up building a sales team Yeah. You know, from zero? And, well, I can tell you about building it from one. You know? And, you know, because they know me, you know, that's like an access point that helps the founder. Right? So I think for every investor, it's like it's like something different. But, you know, what I take back now as, like, an investor, you know, going back into working at a company is, like, just having more of that understanding when I'm, like, in a board meeting, you know, of, like, what are the investors thinking? Like, oh, right. I I was an investor. Like, I I have a sense of, like, what they're thinking and what data they wanna see and what are the metrics that they care about. And if we're thinking about raising, like, a new round, like, what are my expectations for their help? If we need more customers, what are my expectations for, like, their introductions? And I have a better sense of, like, what I should be getting out of that person as an investor or board member or something like that. And I think that's, yeah, again, like helpful to the company in a lot of ways.

**1:21:00** Yeah. I guess you're COO, so you have to, like, interface with investors a lot. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And, you know, we we work with some great investors and, you know, are very helpful and have referred people. But, know, in a lot of situations, like, closed mouths don't get fed. So if you don't ask for things, they're not gonna give them to you. Yeah. So... So Linear doesn't have any other c suite other than the founders in you? Yes. Why is that? It's a good question. I mean, I think, again, we we operated this way at Stripe for a very long time. So again, I take a bias towards it. But I think it's been true actually, for a lot of companies. Like, you might have, like, one executive who's, like, hired in on the business side who who has this title or something similar. And I would say at the beginning, a a lot of it is just, you know, my role is kind of a catchall for like a really small company for like lots of different functions and things over time. But I expect that to change. I don't think that's going to be like the way it is forever. You know, if we build out like the right team, you know, the right leadership in the right places, like people will earn that level of title. And I think for us right now, because we still feel so small, like we're about a 170 people, in a lot of ways, wanna remain pretty flat rather than, like, adding a lot of layers when we are still pretty small.

**1:22:30** Yeah. And, I think that's been helpful for us so far. But that doesn't mean that we haven't, like, promoted people and given people more responsibility, more ownership, more scope. But we tend to focus on things like, you know, head of titles for, like, wide areas of ownership. Yeah. Yeah. I mean, that's all I had. Is there, like, any... Anything else that, you know, you wanted to talk about? No. No. This was a great conversation. I feel like we went into a lot of different different areas Cool. Of of of a business. So thanks. You had great questions. Yeah. Thank you.

body: Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova, COO of Linear, about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber…
