articleBody:
PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — [Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/voyager/1-light-day-from-earth-nasas-voyager-1-probe-hits-huge-milestone-in-interstellar-space), something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary.

Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's [Jet Propulsion Laboratory](https://www.space.com/16952-nasa-jet-propulsion-laboratory.html) (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, [Voyager 2](https://www.space.com/voyager-2), flew past Neptune. The gathering served to celebrate [Voyager 1](https://www.space.com/17688-voyager-1.html)'s distance milestone: At 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 18), the probe reached one light-day from Earth — the distance a photon travels in one day, which is about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). That means it now takes a full day for a signal to travel from Earth to Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object out in space.

"I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day. What an incredible milestone," Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker said during Thursday's event.

## An unexpected, but manageable, anomaly

While this day and this week have been chock-full of excitement over the distance milestone, the Voyager mission team has been hard at work, as usual, keeping the two nearly 50-year-old spacecraft alive and functioning.

Unfortunately, as JPL spokesperson Raquel Villanueva shared at this celebration, on Saturday (Nov. 14), Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 while investigating the issue, and they are confident that they'll be able to solve it soon.

NASA and Voyager team members celebrate Voyager 1's light-day milestone at NASA JPL on Nov. 19, 2026. From left to right: Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate; Jonathan Lunine, chief scientist, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager; Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager; Jamie Rankin, Voyager deputy project scientist. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd)

"We listen to each spacecraft every day," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd told Space.com at the event. Regarding Voyager 1, "we have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," Dodd said. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We currently don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently."

"But if you recall," Dodd added, "one light-day is very far from us. [It takes] 24 hours to get the signal to the spacecraft, 24 hours for the signal to come down, so it takes two days to diagnose anything on the spacecraft … So we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low."

According to Dodd, this anomaly isn't a major cause for long-term concern. Rather, it's likely just part of the natural aging process for spacecraft.

"These spacecraft are old," she said. "All of us old people have our aches and pains, and you know, sometimes it takes longer to stretch out your muscles and remember things, and so we are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager just due to the distance and the age."

"But we feel Voyager 1, although it's not sending us the telemetry data, it's pointed at the [Earth](https://www.space.com/54-earth-history-composition-and-atmosphere.html). It's sending us a strong carrier signal, and I'm confident that it won't be too long, and it will send us data back."

And, for anyone curious how Voyager 1's slower twin Voyager 2 is faring, Dodd shared that it is doing very well on its own journey through [interstellar space](https://www.space.com/interstellar-space-definition-explanation). "Voyager 2 is very healthy. It's continuing its mission. It has three scientific instruments on it," she told Space.com.

"Each spacecraft is basically setting a record every day for longevity or distance," Dodd added about the twin probes.

A Voyager 1 photo of Saturn, which the probe flew by in November 1980. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

## A heartfelt celebration

Despite the communications anomaly — and even though most of the team had been up all night to confirm the one-light-day signal from Voyager 1 — the room was alive with excitement. The Voyagers have been flying for nearly 50 years on a mission expected to last just five years, so the team was beyond ready to celebrate.

Amidst the more technical updates about the mission and its current status out in interstellar space, the event included footage of Voyager light-day celebrations from around the world. From children cheering on Voyager to iconic landmarks lighting up gold in honor of the mission's [Golden Record,](https://www.space.com/34223-voyager-golden-record-space-messages-in-pictures.html) the Voyager love echoed around the world in photos and videos. The footage of this international celebration was enough to move Nicky Fox, NASA's associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate, nearly to tears.

"I actually thought I was going to start sobbing," Fox joked to Space.com after the media briefing. "I think just hearing children's voices and people saying 'We love you, Voyager,' 'Go Voyager' — it just was amazing."

And Fox and the mission team members weren't the only ones sharing their love for Voyager. NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins beamed down her own video message to the Voyager 1 spacecraft from the [International Space Station](https://www.space.com/16748-international-space-station.html), sharing in the celebration.

"Dear Voyager 1," Watkins said. "As an orbiting outpost just 250 miles [400 kilometers] above Earth, we often feel distant yet deeply connected to our home planet. The International Space Station has had crew continuously living off of the Earth for 26 years, seen hundreds of visitors from around the world, and enabled thousands of experiments to advance space exploration.

"While you have been traveling into the unknown for nearly half a century, helping pave our path, together, our two journeys tell a single story of exploration," she continued. "One remains close to home, and the other reaches ever outward. Voyager 1, you have been a beacon of light, a symbol of exploration, a seeker of truth, a carrier of hope, a brave explorer, traveling further than any human hand has ever reached. You represent the very best of what humanity has to offer.

"As you reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, the entire crew of Expedition 75 and people across the planet send you our admiration and our wishes for a safe and continued journey as you begin your post-one-light-day era. There are so many amazing milestones and discoveries to come. You have a [universe](https://www.space.com/52-the-expanding-universe-from-the-big-bang-to-today.html) ahead of you, and you carry with you our collective hopes and dreams. When we look up from Earth, we will always think of you as you continue forward into the great unknown. May you continue shining bright for all of us. Go Voyager 1!" Watkins said, ending her message with a weightless backflip from aboard the station.

In concluding the media briefing, the mission team invited those in the room who, over the past 50 years (or more, with one person sharing their excitement having worked on Voyager before it was even called Voyager) have worked on the mission in one way or another, to stand up to a round of applause. With mission team members today ranging from those in their 20s to their 90s, the people behind this enduring mission span many generations.

## A golden moment

Interestingly, Fox actually began her light-day celebrations earlier in the week. She, alongside writer/producer Ann Druyan — who was the wife of the late astronomer [Carl Sagan](https://www.space.com/15994-carl-sagan.html), whose work helped create the mission's Golden Record and who took the now-famous "[pale blue dot](https://www.space.com/pale-blue-dot-voyager-1-photo-30th-anniversary.html)" Voyager image of Earth to the public — together lit up the Empire State Building gold.

Nicky Fox's Voyager-inspired golden nails. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd)

"I was actually very privileged to flick the switch and turn on the Empire State Building lights on Tuesday evening [Nov. 17]," Fox, wearing golden Voyager-inspired nail polish crafted by her daughter, told Space.com. "That was just spectacular … I was there with Ann … we were both so giddy with the excitement of doing it … It was amazing. And then going up and standing underneath and seeing the tower was just really, really special."

## Looking to the future

While the room lit up with excitement for Voyager's light-day milestone on Thursday, the team was also brimming with anticipation for what lies ahead. As Voyager hurtles toward another major milestone, turning 50 in 2027, it remains an active science mission, and the team remains hard at work to push the boundaries of exploration with these aging probes.

"Voyager right now — the two Voyagers — they're in an area of space that we've never been into. So every single bit of data that comes back is precious because it's unique," Fox said.

"Now we're in a region where the sun's influence is a lot different, and we're in this region where we can start to understand: What is it like out past [our sun](https://www.space.com/58-the-sun-formation-facts-and-characteristics.html)? What is it like in the space between the [stars](https://www.space.com/57-stars-formation-classification-and-constellations.html)?" Voyager deputy project scientist Jamie Rankin told Space.com. "We're at a very exciting time of starting to connect what we know and what we've seen, living with this star [our sun] to what is out there."

"What's next? Voyager is just going to keep on going. You know, people sometimes think, 'When's the mission going to end?' It's never going to end," Fox added to Space.com. "Even when we can no longer talk to Voyager, they're both going to keep going … So there's no end for the Voyager mission."

title: Outage Chaos: Who Turned Off All The Computer?
subtitle: It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email, fly, spend money, use an Apple device*, or do signals intelligence.

articleBody:
It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email, fly, spend money, use an Apple device*, or do signals intelligence. Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it?

Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the Microsoft cloud outage on November 12, any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the Air Traffic Control problems anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the PlayStation Network might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless.

One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service.

While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI (or to malicious hackers), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and reportedly attributed at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse.

Vulnerabilities are a type of software bug that affects security. Once a vulnerability is found in a given piece of software and disclosed, typically the software maker will release a patch fixing that vulnerability. That’s why so many update notes say things like “performance improvements and security fixes” — the security fixes are patches to vulnerabilities.

Companies and governments that run infrastructure face a challenging tradeoff: deploy patches quickly or slowly and cautiously? Patching quickly is important to keep systems secure. But every software update runs a risk: any change to a deployed system can have unintended consequences that snowball into a disastrous outage.

This exacerbates a much deeper problem long discussed in the engineering culture of many, if not most organizations. Keeping networks, servers, and applications not just secure but resilient in the face of patches, reboots, and capacity changes requires an investment in staff, time, hardware, and processes for frequent maintenance, redundant systems, realistic staging environments, automated rollbacks, monitoring, and pre-deployment testing. These investments are rarely as attractive to decision-makers as a new product or feature, or at times, sadly, as layoffs.

This should come as no surprise when we think of our apps, web sites, airlines, and bank cards as supported by electronic infrastructure. As in the more visible physical world, maintenance can only be deferred for so long before the costs become immediate and dramatic. We accept the cost of an occasional short term bridge closure to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse, and highway departments schedule road work nearly every night of the year to repair and prevent the worst potholes.

When this kind of work is endlessly deferred in the world of software, we speak of technical debt: issues we already know about that aren't causing a big enough problem right now to divert us from other work, but that, if left unaddressed, can easily multiply and interact to cause outages or other complications. This can show up as routine steps that have to be done by hand instead of automatically on a schedule, a programmer's shortcut that works well in one specific situation but is more fragile in general, an operating system six months (or years) overdue for a reboot, or a piece of networking hardware no longer supported for patches by its manufacturer. On the other hand, when maintenance work is well-resourced and routine, it should be rare for even major security updates to cause significant issues.

What’s needed in the short term is a big investment in the people and training needed to roll out patches promptly and safely. What’s needed in the long term is a big investment in software security, eliminating entire classes of vulnerabilities, like memory safety, before they are ever written.

For organizations that have gotten used to patching slowly and cautiously, suddenly switching gears to patching quickly is a big challenge. And the flood of vulnerability disclosures enabled by AI means that everyone is being asked to switch gears like that at once.

Fortunately, it’s not a zero-sum game: patches can be rolled out quickly and cautiously, with investments in reducing technical debt and expanding maintenance budgets as described above. These measures are expensive and time-consuming, but necessary. For governments asking how to respond to AI-enabled cybersecurity threats, investing in the people and training necessary to stay on top of patches will pay big dividends in reliability and security.

For individuals, consider the trade-offs when relying on a single provider for many services you rely on. Consumer cloud and device offerings tie together many of the things we need to function on a daily basis like email, messaging, file storage, and even payments, but that convenience and simplicity comes with the risk of losing access to it all if that service goes offline (or suspends your account). Trying out interoperable alternatives is a great way to reduce your reliance on a single company.

Finally, for any critical data, learn the 3-2-1 rule for backups: Keep three different copies on two different types of storage with one copy in a different physical location. For many users, a laptop or other personal device, cloud storage, and a local backup disk exemplify this rule, as long as the laptop stores data on its own drives, not only in the cloud.

Among other things, the accelerated rollout of AI has made it all the more critical to reinvest in people and systems to keep our software, networks, governments, and interconnected world stable.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

The Cincinnati Zoo hippopotamus named Fiona [swallowed a knit cap](https://www.neatorama.com/2026/11/17/Fiona-the-Hippo-is-on-Poop-Watch-Tonight/) that was accidentally flung into her enclosure nine days ago. While many people thought an animal as large as a hippo would be able to pass the cap, zoo veterinarians were worried. After a couple of days, Fiona's appetite changed. The vets sedated her for examination, and she was given an untrasound scan and blood tests, which initially came back normal. As Fiona deteriorated, she became dehydrated and was given IV fluids. Other care included enemas, medication, and therapy that included [standing on a vibrating plate](https://www.nbcnews.com/pop-culture/pop-culture-news/fiona-hippo-dies-cincinnati-zoo-rcna610297). Surgery was ruled out for several reasons, including her size, the pressure of the blockage, and the fact that thick hippopotamus skin doesn't heal well.

The zoo announced today that Fiona did not make it. The nine-year-old hippo will be fondly remembered by all those who knew here. Read more about [Fiona's last days](https://people.com/fiona-the-hippo-receives-24-hour-care-after-swallowing-a-hat-12261997)at People magazine.

## You Can Catch, Collect, and Learn About Animals in teamLab’s New Interactive Digital Forest

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/teamlab-catching-and-collecting-extinct-forest/)

teamLab, Catching and Collecting Extinct Forest, 2025, from the series of Catching and Collecting Forest – A Whole Year per Year, 2020- © teamLab
*Composite image *Not an actual exhibition photo.

The teamLab Forest Fukuoka museum by Tokyo-based art collective [teamLab](https://www.teamlab.art/) is a one-of-a-kind space that invites you to immerse yourself in a digital wonderland. Opening Nov. 21, [Catching and Collecting Extinct Forest](https://www.teamlab.art/ew/extinctforest-forest/forest/) is the collective’s latest interactive artwork. Its permanent installation features a mythical forest inhabited by various animals that respond to the actions of visitors.

The new educational experience is based on the concept of “Catch, Collect, Research.” Visitors are invited to explore the digital forest and use their smartphone cameras to spot the virtual animals and launch a virtual “Research Eye” to “capture” them. Each creature is then added to their digital collection book, where they can learn more about it. Participants can also release animals back into the forest by swiping them towards a location on their screen. Alternatively, they can also throw a virtual “Research Net” onto the floor and work together to herd animals into it, adding them to their collections.

The *Extinct Forest* is home to a variety of [extinct animals](https://mymodernmet.com/footage-of-extinct-animals/), but it isn’t always easy to catch them. As visitors approach or touch them, the creatures can react by either running away or turning to face them.

Check out footage of the magical *Catching and Collecting Extinct Forest* installation below, and learn about the art collective behind this immersive experience on [teamLab’s website](https://www.teamlab.art/).

articleBody:
# Dudes Online Are So Mad That ‘GTA VI’ Makes Them Respect Women

The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.

This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue ), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.

“RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded . “Killed by women.”

In case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. Living together in a fictionalized version of South Florida, they look to get by on the wrong side of the law—but the player must also negotiate their emotional bond through domestic chores and acts of affection.

“This game is such woke slop,” wrote one blue-check user on X who has posted almost nothing besides negative reactions to the game for the past week. The post included a screenshot of a fully optional GTA VI mission that describes how the Lucia character will appreciate a flower delivery and indicates with a heart icon that the action will strengthen feelings between her and Jason.

Other choices you can make as Jason to get closer to Lucia (sex is very much on the table) include picking up groceries, getting a haircut or beard trim, gifting her a piece of jewelry, and repainting walls in the house.

The concept of role-playing as a nice and non-performatively masculine boyfriend has come as a rude shock to those more interested in explosions and mayhem. The right-wing streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold, was dumbfounded to find himself unclogging a sink in a scene where Jason is trying to collect back rent from a tenant who refuses the money until the plumbing is fixed. “I actually have to fucking fix this bitch’s sink?” Hoyt asked on stream. “Why can’t she do this?” Elsewhere, when running errands for Lucia as Jason, Hoyt referred to GTA VI as a “cuck simulator.” (That Hoyt thinks caring for a romantic partner makes someone a cuckold is perhaps an unfortunate glimpse into his dating history.)

More frustrated responses to the massively popular GTA VI came from looksmaxxing influencer Braden Peters, aka Clavicular, (the game required too much “simping for girls,” the streamer, currently facing multiple rape charges , complained on X), anti-woke gamer activist Mark Kern, aka Grummz (he called the housework “mundane crap”), and misinformation superspreader Dom Lucre, who falsely claimed that Rockstar had specifically made it impossible to open fire in a gay nightclub. (Washington Post critic Gene Park pointed out that the club in question was not LGBTQ-specific and that the mechanics of the game don’t allow you to shoot anyone in any kind of club.) These comments came alongside the predictable gripes over supposedly “overweight” female characters with insufficiently large breasts.

And Andrew Tate himself denounced the game in a Thursday email blast to his newsletter subscribers. “The establishment does not understand the male spirit,” he wrote from prison in Miami, where he and his brother Tristan Tate are fighting extradition to the UK on charges of rape, human trafficking, and assault. “No man wants to be a slave who breaks his back and gets nothing back.” Promoting a link to classes for building “AI systems,” he exhorted his readers: “Put down the game controller.”

If the Tates, incels, and other far-right reactionaries of the world are so bent out of shape, it’s probably because whereas GTA once punched down at marginalized groups like sex workers and transgender people , bigots and self-styled alpha males are now the butt of the joke. The Vice City of GTA VI is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout MAGA-coded conspiracy theories and call you a “libtard” or “commie socialist” if you walk into them. These touches seem to have made the game into “a bug zapper for chuds,” as one Bluesky user put it . (That hasn’t stopped Republicans and Trump allies from trying and failing to score political points with the game.)

Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element of GTA VI .

It’s not that games like The Sims haven’t explored this territory before, and Rockstar’s own Red Dead Redemption franchise paid similar attention to quotidian detail. In those frontier-set narratives, your cowboy character had to make coffee over campfires and even clean up manure in barns. By addressing characters’ most basic needs—you can even manage personal hygiene by showering— GTA VI recalls some of the slower and quieter aspects of that franchise.

What’s truly remarkable, though, is that adult men who grew up indulging their most selfish and sociopathic instincts in the older GTA games have had their nostalgia for those escapades cleverly complicated with real-life problems. They can still steal cars, sell drugs, and rise through the ranks of a seedy underworld. That will always be the appeal of the series, which is now asking eternally aggrieved culture warriors to consider a vital question: What if you didn’t have to do it alone?

The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.

This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue ), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.

“RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded . “Killed by women.”

In case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. # The U.S. and Iran Are Back to Trading Strikes

## The U.S. and Iran Are Back to Trading Strikes

## A roughly two-month lull in the fighting is seemingly over.

- United States
- Iran
- Middle East and North Africa
- Rishi Iyengar
- John Haltiwanger
### Iran War

Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report. We sincerely thank all of you for reading this week’s edition when you could be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. As a quick note, SitRep will be off next week for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Iran and the United States engage in a new tit-for-tat , Pete Hegseth makes an unexpected visit to Venezuela , and Donald Trump meets with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China .

Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report. We sincerely thank all of you for reading this week’s edition when you could be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. As a quick note, SitRep will be off next week for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Iran and the United States engage in a new tit-for-tat , Pete Hegseth makes an unexpected visit to Venezuela , and Donald Trump meets with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China .

### Past the Expiration Date

The Iran war appears to be heating up (again), as diplomatic talks have hit a wall (again). The United States and Iran resumed strikes over the past week, ending a roughly two-month lull in the conflict.

The renewed fighting has come as Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and amid an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports.

Tit-for-tat. Over the past six days, Iran launched a series of strikes on U.S. assets in Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, and an air base in Kuwait that hosts U.S. forces.

Iran targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in Bahrain on Friday and took aim at a radar system at a helicopter base in the tiny island nation on Sunday. No damage was reported. Tehran said the attacks were in retaliation for U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers as well as ongoing drone surveillance operations.

On Tuesday, Iran targeted another radar facility in Bahrain with drones, which were reportedly intercepted; the United States retaliated with a strike on an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island. Iran responded on Wednesday with an attack on Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait. There were no reports of damage. Bahrain also said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday.

Under pressure. U.S. President Donald Trump has been vague about his plans in the war, and some reports suggest he is mulling over ordering expansive strikes. But Trump on Thursday indicated that he’s not in a hurry to escalate. “I am not rushing into any decision. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year,” Trump told Axios.

Trump’s comments came as Israel is reportedly pressing the White House to escalate with a fresh bombing campaign. Roman Gofman, the director of the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad, visited Washington this week, where he is said to have expressed concerns to U.S. officials over alleged Iranian chemical weapons development.

The United States also has intelligence that Iran has drawn up plans to potentially use a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington, according to a CNN report . Trump on Tuesday said the United States was looking into the dirty bomb report and takes it “very seriously.” But he later downplayed the prospect of Iran actually using such a weapon in Washington, and he warned that “if it does happen, we’ll wipe them out.” Trump this week also told Fox News there’s “indication that Iran is looking at gasses, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear.”

“And they’re looking at gas and biological weapons. Not nice. And we’ll see,” he said.

Expired. If Trump does decide to ramp up the war, experts have warned that it would be a huge gamble and would undoubtedly lead to further retaliatory attacks on U.S. forces and assets in the region. The U.S. intelligence community reportedly assesses that Iran has a stockpile of up to 2,500 missiles in its arsenal, despite prior claims from the Trump administration of such capabilities being destroyed. Iran also remains defiant in the face of continued U.S. economic pressure, and Tehran appears emboldened by major Republican losses in the midterm elections.

The United States still has significant military assets in the region, including two aircraft carriers (after yet another reshuffling that saw the USS George Washington leave the Middle East this week, following the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt ). But the United States is also facing significant constraints, and the war has depleted stockpiles of key munitions. Due to such shortages, acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao this week told senators that U.S. forces resorted to firing expired munitions in the war.

### Let’s Get Personnel

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a surprise trip to Venezuela, where he signed a defense cooperation agreement with the country that the United States invaded in January. The Defense Department did not share details of the trip with the U.S. press, with the main images and details coming from Venezuelan state media.

Meanwhile, Politico reported that Hegseth’s personal lawyer, Tim Parlatore, also works for the son of a Libyan warlord who has been accused of war crimes.

The Pentagon nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be permanent chief of staff of the U.S. Army, a role that he has been carrying out in an acting capacity since the ouster of Gen. Randy George in April.

Democrats on Wednesday officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House, making him the first black person to serve in that role should he be confirmed.

### On the Button

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

Rohingya genocide verdict. The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed a genocide against its Rohingya ethnic minority population, the first time that the court has found a state responsible for genocide. The judgment is expected to set a number of international legal precedents, including those concerning standards of evidence and reparations, as journalist Andrew Nachemson wrote in FP.

Trump’s big trilateral. Trump capped off his Asia visit this week by meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. In a joint “peace declaration” following their meeting, the three leaders committed to “reform” the United Nations, vowed to increase the supply of petroleum products “for the benefit of all nations,” and warned that the International Criminal Court and other similar entities “must not abuse their jurisdiction.” They also agreed to “conduct a dialogue” on nuclear risk and nonproliferation, saying that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”

Huang’s defenders. It’s been one week since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal over multiple extramarital affairs, but some of the United States’ most powerful individuals—including Trump—are calling for his return to the helm of the $4 trillion semiconductor company.

A petition to “Bring Jensen Back” has received more than 200,000 signatures, including from the world’s richest man, Elon Musk. Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang came back, and Huang himself fueled the fire with a lengthy post on X in which he wrote: “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

The board, however, appears uninterested. Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said during the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that the board “unanimously accepted his [Huang’s] resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

The scrutiny of Huang and Nvidia will continue in the meantime. Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on Dec. 1, and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating the company.

### Snapshot

In a photo provided on Nov. 17, 2026, by the North Korean government, leader Kim Jong Un inspects a tourist zone under development during a visit to Samjiyon city, North Korea. Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

### Put On Your Radar

Friday, Nov. 20: The European Union hosts the EU-United Kingdom summit in Brussels.

Wednesday, Nov. 25: The EU-Western Balkans summit takes place in Brussels.

Saturday, Nov. 28: Taiwan is set to hold local elections.

Sunday, Nov. 29: Spain will hold snap parliamentary elections

Monday, Nov. 30: The International Criminal Court trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is set to begin.

### Quote of the Week

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

—Trump, when asked if he was worried about the series of major software outages this month. (Read John’s smart explainer on the tech outages here .)

### FP’s Most Read This Week

- Lame-Duck Trump Heads to Asia by Rishi Iyengar
- The Middle East Is Finally on Its Own by Stephen M. Walt
- How Netanyahu Lost His Bet on Trump by Azriel Bermant
### Whiskey Tango Foxtrot

Would you commit to your current job for two to six more years if it meant getting a four-day weekend to play the hottest new video game on the market? It’s not just about the video game—many of them had other reasons to reenlist anyway, and some also got hefty cash bonuses—but one of the soldiers told Task and Purpose that he now had “a good 24 hours to waste on it.”

# The U.S. and Iran Are Back to Trading Strikes

## The U.S. and Iran Are Back to Trading Strikes

## A roughly two-month lull in the fighting is seemingly over.

- United States
- Iran
- Middle East and North Africa
- Rishi Iyengar
- John Haltiwanger
### Iran War

Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report. We sincerely thank all of you for reading this week’s edition when you could be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. As a quick note, SitRep will be off next week for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Iran and the United States engage in a new tit-for-tat , Pete Hegseth makes an unexpected visit to Venezuela , and Donald Trump meets with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China .

Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report. We sincerely thank all of you for reading this week’s edition when you could be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. As a quick note, SitRep will be off next week for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Iran and the United States engage in a new tit-for-tat , Pete Hegseth makes an unexpected visit to Venezuela , and Donald Trump meets with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China .

### Past the Expiration Date

The Iran war appears to be heating up (again), as diplomatic talks have hit a wall (again). The United States and Iran resumed strikes over the past week, ending a roughly two-month lull in the conflict.

The renewed fighting has come as Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and amid an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports.

Tit-for-tat. Over the past six days, Iran launched a series of strikes on U.S. assets in Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, and an air base in Kuwait that hosts U.S. forces.

Iran targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in Bahrain on Friday and took aim at a radar system at a helicopter base in the tiny island nation on Sunday. No damage was reported. Tehran said the attacks were in retaliation for U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers as well as ongoing drone surveillance operations.

On Tuesday, Iran targeted another radar facility in Bahrain with drones, which were reportedly intercepted; the United States retaliated with a strike on an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island. Iran responded on Wednesday with an attack on Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait. There were no reports of damage. Bahrain also said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday.

Under pressure. U.S. President Donald Trump has been vague about his plans in the war, and some reports suggest he is mulling over ordering expansive strikes. But Trump on Thursday indicated that he’s not in a hurry to escalate. “I am not rushing into any decision. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year,” Trump told Axios.

Trump’s comments came as Israel is reportedly pressing the White House to escalate with a fresh bombing campaign. Roman Gofman, the director of the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad, visited Washington this week, where he is said to have expressed concerns to U.S. officials over alleged Iranian chemical weapons development.

The United States also has intelligence that Iran has drawn up plans to potentially use a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington, according to a CNN report . Trump on Tuesday said the United States was looking into the dirty bomb report and takes it “very seriously.” But he later downplayed the prospect of Iran actually using such a weapon in Washington, and he warned that “if it does happen, we’ll wipe them out.” Trump this week also told Fox News there’s “indication that Iran is looking at gasses, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear.”

“And they’re looking at gas and biological weapons. Not nice. And we’ll see,” he said.

Expired. If Trump does decide to ramp up the war, experts have warned that it would be a huge gamble and would undoubtedly lead to further retaliatory attacks on U.S. forces and assets in the region. The U.S. intelligence community reportedly assesses that Iran has a stockpile of up to 2,500 missiles in its arsenal, despite prior claims from the Trump administration of such capabilities being destroyed. Iran also remains defiant in the face of continued U.S. economic pressure, and Tehran appears emboldened by major Republican losses in the midterm elections.

The United States still has significant military assets in the region, including two aircraft carriers (after yet another reshuffling that saw the USS George Washington leave the Middle East this week, following the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt ). But the United States is also facing significant constraints, and the war has depleted stockpiles of key munitions. Due to such shortages, acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao this week told senators that U.S. forces resorted to firing expired munitions in the war.

### Let’s Get Personnel

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a surprise trip to Venezuela, where he signed a defense cooperation agreement with the country that the United States invaded in January. The Defense Department did not share details of the trip with the U.S. press, with the main images and details coming from Venezuelan state media.

Meanwhile, Politico reported that Hegseth’s personal lawyer, Tim Parlatore, also works for the son of a Libyan warlord who has been accused of war crimes.

The Pentagon nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be permanent chief of staff of the U.S. Army, a role that he has been carrying out in an acting capacity since the ouster of Gen. Randy George in April.

Democrats on Wednesday officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House, making him the first black person to serve in that role should he be confirmed.

### On the Button

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

Rohingya genocide verdict. The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed a genocide against its Rohingya ethnic minority population, the first time that the court has found a state responsible for genocide. The judgment is expected to set a number of international legal precedents, including those concerning standards of evidence and reparations, as journalist Andrew Nachemson wrote in FP.

Trump’s big trilateral. Trump capped off his Asia visit this week by meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. In a joint “peace declaration” following their meeting, the three leaders committed to “reform” the United Nations, vowed to increase the supply of petroleum products “for the benefit of all nations,” and warned that the International Criminal Court and other similar entities “must not abuse their jurisdiction.” They also agreed to “conduct a dialogue” on nuclear risk and nonproliferation, saying that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”

Huang’s defenders. It’s been one week since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal over multiple extramarital affairs, but some of the United States’ most powerful individuals—including Trump—are calling for his return to the helm of the $4 trillion semiconductor company.

A petition to “Bring Jensen Back” has received more than 200,000 signatures, including from the world’s richest man, Elon Musk. Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang came back, and Huang himself fueled the fire with a lengthy post on X in which he wrote: “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

The board, however, appears uninterested. Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said during the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that the board “unanimously accepted his [Huang’s] resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

The scrutiny of Huang and Nvidia will continue in the meantime. Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on Dec. 1, and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating the company.

Friday, Nov. 20: The European Union hosts the EU-United Kingdom summit in Brussels.

Wednesday, Nov. 25: The EU-Western Balkans summit takes place in Brussels.

Saturday, Nov. 28: Taiwan is set to hold local elections.

Sunday, Nov. 29: Spain will hold snap parliamentary elections

Monday, Nov. 30: The International Criminal Court trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is set to begin.

### Quote of the Week

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

—Trump, when asked if he was worried about the series of major software outages this month. (Read John’s smart explainer on the tech outages here .)

articleBody:
[Cosentino](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/cosentino/) aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with [Cosentino](https://www.cosentino.com/)’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

Ēclos is designed to support three-dimensional compositions

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”

Its patterning runs right through the slab for refined exposed edges

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an important part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”

Details can suggest a continuous volume or highlight its assembly

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”

Cosentino facilitates collaboration between designer and fabricator

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos launched earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

Ēclos can be used on walls, worktops and other surfaces

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the company’s [website](https://www.cosentino.com/).

articleBody:
Mark Gurman, [reporting for Bloomberg today](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-19/apple-s-iphone-camera-and-photos-software-chief-jon-mccormack-leaves-company?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5NTEwOTM1MSwiZXhwIjoxNzk1NzE0MTUxLCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUT1IzMlJUOU5KTTUwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiJDNEVEQ0FFMUZBMDU0MEJFQTI0QTlGMjExQzFFOTA4MCJ9.aeSQbn794aHs3B5ecmfYGppiDoPtcY_FXRHn7Hbe76Y) (gift link):

> Jon McCormack retired at the end of October after more than eight
> years at the company, according to people with knowledge of the
> matter. He oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying
> technology that determines how users capture, view and edit their
> pictures and video.
> Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to take over McCormack’s
> exact role. Instead, his former deputies are assuming his
> responsibilities under another executive, said the people, who
> asked not to be identified while discussing internal moves. An
> Apple spokesperson declined to comment.
> His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the
> iPhone 17 lineup last year.

I’ve met McCormack a few times. He frequently led media briefings for new iPhone camera features. He was always thoughtful, insightful, and fair. Like, sometimes his demonstrations would involve comparisons between photos of the same subjects and scenes captured on iPhones and ones captured with flagship Android phones. The photos were *all* good. It was never “ *Here are some beautiful images captured on iPhones and some dogshit ones from a Samsung and OnePlus* ”. The differences were often subtle. He’d even make the case for why someone might prefer the Android ones. But he could explain why Apple — and he personally — preferred the ones from the iPhone. Not just how the iPhone camera captures and processes images, but why. He also knew when to let the images speak for themselves.

McCormack was deeply informed at a technical level. He reported directly to Craig Federighi and that level of engineering acumen showed. I can’t recall any question being too technical for him to have a ready answer. One of the best iPhone camera innovations in recent years is the redesigned [Center Stage selfie camera](https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/take-a-selfie-iph1b88429a6/ios) introduced with the iPhone 17 (and Air) lineup last year. The square sensor is hardware, and McCormack was a software VP, but the feature exemplifies the way hardware and software are developed in tandem at Apple. McCormack was [the public face for that feature](https://www.businessworld.in/article/exclusive-jon-mccormack-on-how-apple-reinvented-the-selfie-for-the-iphone-17-575523) — and internally, pushed to make it happen. That square sensor is bigger, which means (a) it’s more expensive; and (b) it takes up more space internally. Both of those require winning hard-fought arguments inside Apple in order to ship. The bottom line is that it helps iPhone users take better photos of themselves — and [according to McCormack himself](https://www.instagram.com/helloapple/reel/Daiat9bNtiF/), over 1 billion selfies are taken with iPhones *every day*. The influence Apple’s Camera team has on the daily lives of *billions* of people is significant; McCormack understood that.

But what really struck me about McCormack, right from the start, is that he is clearly a serious photographer himself. That’s perhaps understating it. He recently published a book of his own nature and travel photography: *[Patterns: Art of the Natural World](https://jonmccormack.com/book/)*. He [discussed the book in an hour-long interview](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chenpamela/) with his Apple colleague Pamela Chen, whose [job title](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chenpamela/) is one of the coolest I’ve ever heard: Chief Aesthetics Scientist. (Chen, unsurprisingly, is also [a talented photographer](https://www.instagram.com/chenpamela/).)

Gurman:

> His departure comes at a time when Apple is navigating a
> fundamental shift in photography. Competitors such as Alphabet
> Inc.’s Google and Samsung Electronics Co. have increasingly
> embraced generative AI features that allow users to make
> substantial changes to images. That has blurred the distinction
> between capturing a real moment and creating an artificial one.

Two years ago [in his iPhone 16 Pro review](https://www.theverge.com/24247538/apple-iphone-16-pro-review), returning to his repeated theme of “What is a photo?”, Nilay Patel quoted, at length, the answer he got from McCormack. I, in turn, [quoted Patel quoting McCormack](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2024/09/23/nilay-patel-iphone-16-pro-review), and added:

> McCormack’s response is genuinely thoughtful, and resonates deeply
> with my own personal take. But it’s worth noting that Apple is the
> conservative company when it comes to generative AI and
> photography — and yet they’re still shipping Clean Up. I’m not
> complaining about Clean Up’s existence. I’ve already used it
> personally. I’m just saying that even Apple’s stance involves
> significant use of generative AI.

This year, Apple added [“extend” and “reframe”](https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/clean-up-extend-and-reframe-photos-xy0grrlxue5w/ios) alongside Clean Up. I don’t love either of those features simply because I don’t like how they change the meaning of “What is a photo?”, but I don’t *hate* them either. We can’t put the generative AI genie back in the bottle. Apple, still, is the conservative company in the generative AI phone photography space.

Jon McCormack had a knack for shepherding good new features *into* the Camera app. But also, based on conversations I’ve had with multiple people who worked with him at Apple, McCormack was *great* at keeping stupid ideas *out* of the Camera app. Good new features that ship get more recognition than stupid new features that never ship — but the latter, I would argue, is the rarer and more important management skill. It’s far more important to keep stupid ideas out of any app than it is to add good new features. McCormack was the protector of the Camera app. Under his leadership, it remains focused on the craft and art of photography.

Lastly, everyone I know who worked with him loves the guy. McCormack was the perfect guy for an essential job, and he leaves big shoes to fill.

title: AI helps researchers investigate how thousands of medical studies share code
subtitle: The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how.
feedText: In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated? articleBody:
The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated?

Access to a study's data and code help researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods, and to build on the work.

“Studies involve many choices about how to prepare data, develop models, and evaluate performance. These are sometimes called ‘researcher degrees of freedom,’” says Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. “The choices we make affect the results, and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail.”

While sharing code can be a first step, in order for code to be understood and reused, it must be sufficiently structured and described. The problem is that, right now, there is little guidance for researchers on what constitutes a well-organized, well-described collection of code.

This is where an international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute sought to help, by examining how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies. Such studies develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes, such as the risk of developing a disease. Because these models inform decisions about patient care, researchers need to be able to scrutinize how they were built and tested.

Using large language models (LLMs), the researchers examined nearly 4,000 papers to identify statements about shared code. They then followed the statements to assess hundreds of associated code repositories.

Their review revealed two key gaps: Code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings, recently [published in Nature Medicine](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04691-1), are informing [TRIPOD-Code](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12888484/), a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share.

**Following the code**

TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. To understand current code-sharing practices, the team identified studies citing either guideline. The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models, and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central’s open-access collection.

“The challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent. First, we had to identify whether or not a paper shared code” says Thomas Sounack, the study’s first author. He adds that authors “discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways.”

The team used an LLM to help screen papers, identify statements about code availability, and extract links. Software then retrieved the linked repositories — online collections of code and related files — for further assessment.

The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed. It also assessed repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse.

“The real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text. These models helped us work with information that was scattered across papers and software repositories, rather than neatly organized in a table,” says Pollard, who is a senior author of the study. “That allowed us to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies.”

Human reviewers evaluated the work of the LLMs. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results.

Agreement was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Because classification errors remain possible, the authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact.

**Inconsistent code sharing**

Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Where code was shared, the contents of repositories varied widely.

Some repositories were “extremely well-organized and -documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all,” Sounack says. Good code sharing, he explains, means “giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper.”

Practices also varied substantially across journals and countries. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing.

The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice. Some researchers, for example, provided synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where the original patient records could not be shared publicly.

**Setting a standard for code sharing**

Researchers who share code are already making an effort to make their work transparent. But clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ.

TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential.

“We want to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code, and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors,” Pollard says. “The review gives us evidence to inform those discussions."

articleBody:
In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.

When I log into Amazon today, I’m met with a vertical banner that reads: “ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order” with a button that says “Act now.”

A screenshot of the top of Amazon's homepage.

I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon's website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-19/amazon-ups-pressure-on-nyc-delivery-bill-with-threat-to-move-out) reported. Amazon hasn't specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I'm logged into Amazon.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/11/amazon-takes-its-fight-against-nyc-delivery-bill-to-shoppers-with-in-app-pop-up/)

[Comments](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/11/amazon-takes-its-fight-against-nyc-delivery-bill-to-shoppers-with-in-app-pop-up/#comments)

title: Promotions Gallery in Paris, France
subtitle: Historically, a secret entrance at the School of Mines, known as the “Mines staircase,” provided students access to the Paris Catacombs.
feedText: Although this private access is no longer available for use due to safety reasons, the General Inspector of Quarries still grants students permission to uphold this artistic tradition. articleBody:
# Promotions Gallery in Paris

## About

Historically, a secret entrance at the School of Mines, known as the “Mines staircase,” provided students access to the Paris Catacombs .

Although this private access is no longer available for use due to safety reasons, the General Inspector of Quarries still grants students permission to uphold this artistic tradition.

Each year, on the occasion of Sainte-Barbe, celebrated on December 4th in honor of the patron saint of miners, first-year students create a painting representing their class, continuing the tradition.

title: Korg’s phase8 acoustic synthesizer adds companion app, updated firmware
subtitle: Korg's phase8 remains an acoustic, resonating fascination, just at a time when everything seems lost in a sea of software.
feedText: The companion app we saw first at Berlin's Superbooth is now public this week, expanding sequencing capabilities and providing tools for arranging and storing ideas, alongside tweaked device firmware. The post Korg’s phase8 acoustic synthesizer adds companion app, updated firmware appeared first on CDM Create Digital Music.
articleBody:
# Korg's phase8 acoustic synthesizer adds companion app, updated firmware - CDM Create Digital Music

- Korg's phase8 acoustic synthesizer adds companion app, updated firmware - CDM Create Digital Music Gear Music tech Tech Korg’s phase8 acoustic synthesizer adds companion app, updated firmware Peter Kirn - November 19, 2026 Add comment Korg’s phase8 remains an acoustic, resonating fascination, just at a time when everything seems lost in a sea of software. The companion app we saw first at Berlin’s Superbooth is now public this week, expanding sequencing capabilities and providing tools for arranging and storing ideas, alongside tweaked device firmware. If you’re new to the phase8, Korg has just published a new video: The free phase8 companion apps is shipping as a Chrome/Chromium-compatible Web application; connect your device via USB-C and go. The tool expands the step sequencing storage up to 32 steps (from 16), but quite a lot more than that. Originated by Korg’s Iarla Scaife (Berlin) and Keisuke Nohara (Tokyo), it’s essentially a pattern editor and librarian, with additional onscreen tools for developing your ideas: 8-, 16-, and 32-step sequences
- Unquantized sequencing option
- Euclidean pattern generator (an algorithm for creating balanced patterns, equally distributing beats and silences across a cycle)
- Voice editing
- Control automation
You can use it to store your patterns on your computer or the device, and there’s a facility for updating your firmware.

That makes this useful even if you just want to manage more patterns and save your work, but it’s really nice being able to see what you’re doing visually. More on this soon; I’m preparing a demo.

phase8 companion: A web-based editor for phase8

Or head straight to the app:

phase8.korg.com

Check this nice overview video:

Speaking of firmware, version 1.3 is out now, too. Most importantly, it corrects the phase8’s sometimes-wonky resonator behavior (I think I just went with it in my set), adds support for this app, and improves sync and MIDI behavior. Full release notes on the Korg site:

phase8/System Updater

Now, no word on if two other projects we saw at Korg’s woodland Superbooth booth will see a wider release. There were custom bass resonators on-hand, plus a unique set of 3D-printed “physical effects” by Hadrien Costrejean. Fingers crossed.

articleBody:
Apple TV überträgt ab 2027 jedes Qualifying und jedes Rennen der F1 Academy und erweitert damit sein Formel-1-Angebot in den USA.

Fotocredit: Apple

## Nachwuchsserie für Rennfahrerinnen

Seit ihrem Start 2022 fördert die F1 Academy als Nachwuchsserie auf Formel-4-Niveau junge Rennfahrerinnen. 2027 geht sie in ihre fünfte Saison. Laut der Global F1 Fan Survey von 2025 ist die F1 Academy unter den befragten Formel-1-Fans die am zweithäufigsten verfolgte Rennserie. Zu den Fahrerinnen, die sich in der Serie einen Namen gemacht haben, gehören Alba Hurup Larsen, Alisha Palmowski und Emma Felbermayr.

Susie Wolff, Geschäftsführerin der F1 Academy, spricht von einem wichtigen Schritt für die Serie. Ihr ist wichtig, dass die Rennen ein möglichst großes Publikum erreichen, weil Mädchen sich selbst mehr zutrauen, wenn sie im Fernsehen sehen, wie Frauen Rennen fahren und gewinnen. Apples Sportchef Jim DeLorenzo will den jungen Fahrerinnen eine größere Bühne bieten, damit sie neue Fans für sich gewinnen.

In den USA hält Apple bereits seit dieser Saison die exklusiven Übertragungsrechte an der Formel 1. Den Vertrag über fünf Jahre schloss das Unternehmen nach dem weltweiten Erfolg seines Kinofilms „F1“.

articleBody:
this album has been in the works off and on for most of the year

the final track includes drums partially generated by machine learning tool trained on mike gao beats and even though i started the experiment and felt comfortable enough to use it in a session based on what i heard from him…i wasn’t completely sure if i wanted anything remotely ai related representing me or folded into my art (maybe we can have conversation about how the sausage was made)

for full disclosure, while on topic, the loop variations underpinning track 5 were made on te sp1 running ai assisted custom firm ware as well as ableton live

full gear list for the geeks (click for more details)

here’s the rough timeline of how this came together:

for some reason i tend to get creative juices flowing quick if i make an album cover before the music OR make a list of wip song titles to easily draw inspiration from when recording and editing tracks on computer

i have daydreampt about projects under the title vandal eyes and recorded a brief beat mixtape 5 or 6 years ago that took the original concept i had as a teen (looking for spots to write on walls / the ear it takes to dj and make sampled based beats) just exemplifying my passion for the essence of good hip hop

they were meant to be vandal flips of sound, made quickly with no special effort to hide source material or get permission before chopping

so again, i had the concept, an album cover and 3 songs done made by may 2026 (tracks 1, 2 and 8) then i sat on them and experienced something like beat block where i couldn’t find a sampling workflow i enjoyed and could create with quickly

during this phase i returned to my roots, using only a DAW and trackpad, to make the drum loops for underscore two and colour grade

colour grade is actually a great description of my artistic process…i don’t see my other skills as very special but i treat mixing and stacking fx like the lens or lighting choices in cinematography and colour grading done in post production

it’s around this time that i linked with mike gao on IG after seeing he’d shifted from ios dev and m4l devices into full fledged vst plugin design

the result of adopting one of his newer tools was another daw & trackpad track, rush 4 none

_________________________________________

in subsequent months, the tape looper firmware for te stem players became quite advanced and i sold my ep133 to acquire two units (they now dwarf most of my portable tools in sample time with a total of 512 minutes storage on each sp1)

feeding an old unreleased loop made on ipad w/ koala sampler led to timeline / cleanse; the bassline was flipped with my launchpad mini during a break at work and then later refined with push 3

but i forgot before that more recent session i found two incredible beats on the usb i record tx6 loops on…those got extended and arranged into dent stutter & nx2g (additional parts played with synths and samples on opxy)

they both a have a texture and quality born from tx6 fx and internal converters imho

so — i’ve given bts info on tracks 1 & 2 plus 5-8; what else?

third track numaabi, is a typical glia ableton flip done mostly with trackpad, playhead loop function and copy/paste to flesh out the structure; drums and percussion done in a similar way but some parts were fingerdrumming on push

fourth track was the last one made and a subtle hint at an old weezer track; it feels like it might fall apart at the seams…multiple layers of gauze and drums all played by push with sampler vsts and simpler

hope yall enjoy one or two beats

as always i welcome feedback, question or comments about anything: process choices, mixing and FAT (final audio treatment), cover design bts, or geeking out about hardware and software used

peace!

articleBody:
# Trump warnt Musk vor Absprung bei MAGA

Bild vergrößern US-Präsident Trump, Milliardär Musk: Wenn jemand vom MAGA-Kurs abkommt, »läuft es für sie nicht so gut«

Mit seinem Versuch, sich von Donald Trumps MAGA-Bewegung abzusetzen, hat sich Tech-Milliardär Elon Musk eine ominöse Mahnung des US-Präsidenten eingehandelt. »Für mich bedeutet MAGA etwas ganz Bestimmtes – und wenn Leute davon abweichen, läuft es für sie nicht so gut«, sagte Trump dem Sender NBC. Zugleich versicherte er: »Er ist ein Freund von mir.« MAGA - »Make America Great Again« – ist der Slogan, um den sich treue Anhänger Trumps scharen.

Musk hatte im jüngsten Midterms-Wahlkampf nahezu 500 Millionen Dollar an Kandidaten von Trumps Republikanern gespendet. Ein Schwerpunkt dabei war der Bundesstaat Texas, in dem seine großen Unternehmen wie der Elektroautobauer Tesla und die Raumfahrtfirma SpaceX ihren Sitz haben. Trotz der Riesenspenden setzten sich in wichtigen Rennen Kandidaten der Demokraten durch – wie Gina Hinojosa, die den republikanischen Gouverneur Greg Abbott aus dem Amt drängte.

Musk selbst schien das Ergebnis am Morgen nach der Wahl erst einmal mit Humor zu nehmen: »Ich schätze, meine wahlbeeinflussenden Weltraumlaser haben diesmal nicht funktioniert«, schrieb der Raumfahrt-Unternehmer auf X .

### Dunkles gothisches MAGA – reine Geldverschwendung?

Aber nun schlägt er andere Töne an: Er komme sich »ziemlich dumm vor, so ‌viel Geld ausgegeben und dafür so wenig bekommen zu haben«, sagte der reichste Mann der Welt am Mittwoch auf einer Konferenz der »New York Times« . Um dann noch hinterherzuschieben: Womöglich hätten die Republikaner ohne ​seine Spenden noch ‌schlechter abgeschnitten.

> View this post on Instagram

Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung.

## »Dunkles, gothisches MAGA«

Allerdings versuchte er auch, seine Verbindung zu MAGA herunterzuspielen: »Ich bin nicht MAGA.« Auch sei er nicht sicher, »was MAGA bedeutet«. Aber wenn es dabei darum gehe, »blind« bestimmter Politik der Republikanischen Partei zu folgen, treffe das auf ihn nicht zu.

Bild vergrößern Da stand er noch auf MAGA: Elon Musk 2025 bei seinem Auftritt auf der Conservative Political Action Conference

Musk war in den vergangenen Jahren jedenfalls auf vielen Fotos mit Trumps MAGA-Kappen auf dem Kopf zu sehen. Zudem stand er im Oktober 2024 auf der Bühne eines Trump-Wahlkampfevents im damaligen Rennen um das Weiße Haus und verkündete: »Ich bin nicht nur MAGA, ich bin dunkles, gothisches MAGA.«

Nach den Midterms wurmt ihn seine Investition in die dunkle Seite der Macht: Das Wahlergebnis zeige, ‌dass ​Geld allein keine Wahlen entscheide, sagte Musk. »Wenn ich die Zeit zurückdrehen könnte, würde ich wahrscheinlich weniger ​Geld ausgeben.«
