title: Militärökonom Keupp: Putin "ist ein Vasall Chinas"
subtitle: Der Gipfel in China habe zwischen zwei Großmächten stattgefunden - und einer, die gerne dazugehören würde, sagt der Militärökonom Keupp.
feedText: Der Gipfel in China habe zwischen zwei Großmächten stattgefunden - und einer, die gerne dazugehören würde, sagt der Militärökonom Keupp. Xi habe Putin gezeigt, was seine Rolle sei. Zwei Gipfeltreffen an einem Tag: Während Trump, Putin und Xi über die internationale Sicherheitslage diskutieren, empfängt Merz in Berlin Selenskyj und Vertreter aus 40 Ländern. Beim Dreiergipfel im chinesischen Shenzhen haben die Staatschefs der USA, Russlands und Chinas über internationale Konflikte gesprochen. Doch obwohl sich die Atommächte auf eine "Erklärung zum Frieden" einigten, sei das Treffen rein symbolisch zu werten, sagte der Militärökonom Marcus Keupp bei ZDFheute live. Spannend sei es jedoch im Hinblick auf die Dynamiken zwischen den drei Teilnehmern Donald Trump, Wladimir Putin und Xi Jinping gewesen.
articleBody:
# Militärökonom Keupp: Putin "ist ein Vasall Chinas"

## Neue Weltordnung? : Militärökonom Keupp: Putin "ist ein Vasall Chinas"

Der Gipfel in China habe zwischen zwei Großmächten stattgefunden - und einer, die gerne dazugehören würde, sagt der Militärökonom Keupp. Xi habe Putin gezeigt, was seine Rolle sei.

Zwei Gipfeltreffen an einem Tag: Während Trump, Putin und Xi über die internationale Sicherheitslage diskutieren, empfängt Merz in Berlin Selenskyj und Vertreter aus 40 Ländern. ZDFheute live

Beim Dreiergipfel im chinesischen Shenzhen haben die Staatschefs der USA, Russlands und Chinas über internationale Konflikte gesprochen. Doch obwohl sich die Atommächte auf eine "Erklärung zum Frieden" einigten, sei das Treffen rein symbolisch zu werten, sagte der Militärökonom Marcus Keupp bei ZDFheute live. Spannend sei es jedoch im Hinblick auf die Dynamiken zwischen den drei Teilnehmern Donald Trump, Wladimir Putin und Xi Jinping gewesen.

Sehen Sie das Interview oben im Video in voller Länge oder lesen Sie es hier in Auszügen. Das sagte Keupp über ...

## ... die Bedeutung des Dreiertreffens in Shenzhen

Eine neue Weltordnung entstehe aus dem Treffen zwischen Putin, Xi und Trump nicht, stellte Keupp klar.

> Es gibt eine deutliche Diskrepanz zwischen dem, was die Beobachter da so hinein interpretieren, und dem, was an Substanz aus diesem Treffen eigentlich herauskommt. „

Marcus Keupp

So trage die etwa von Bundeskanzler Merz gezogene Parallele zur Konferenz von Jalta im Jahr 1945 nicht: Damals hatte Deutschland den Zweiten Weltkrieg verloren und saß als Aggressor - anders als heute Putin - nicht mit am Konferenztisch.

Am 4. Februar 1945 gelingt es dem roten Zaren mit List und Tücke, seine Verbündeten zu täuschen. Der Film zeigt, wie Josef Stalin in Jalta den Zweiten Weltkrieg gewinnt.

Das Treffen in Shenzhen sei "etwas völlig anderes". "Es ist eine schöne Inszenierung, es ist ein großer Gewinn für China , würde ich sagen." Die kleinen, feinen Details seien zwar "sehr schön gemacht", aber es gebe "wenig Ergebnis".

- Trump, Xi und Putin: Große Worte, wenig Konkretes
## Dr. Marcus M. Keupp

Quelle: ZDF … ist Dozent für Militärökonomie an der Militärakademie der ETH Zürich, der Ausbildungsstätte für Berufsoffiziere der Schweizer Armee. Zuvor hat er an der Universität Mannheim und der Warwick Business School Betriebswirtschaftslehre studiert und an der Universität St. Gallen promoviert. In seiner Forschung beschäftigt sich Keupp insbesondere mit militärischer Logistik. Seit Beginn des Kriegs in der Ukraine 2022 analysiert Keupp das Geschehen an der Front, die russischen und ukrainischen Nachschublinien sowie die wirtschaftlichen Auswirkungen des Krieges.

## ... Putins Rolle in der Welt

In Russland selbst möge Putin zwar mächtig sein, verglichen mit Xi und Trump sei er aber "die kleinste Macht", sagte Keupp. Zwar fabuliere der Kreml-Chef von sich selbst als Großmacht. Doch es gelte, zwischen purer Symbolik und den wirtschaftlichen und militärischen Fakten klar zu trennen.

Schließlich schaffe Putin es seit viereinhalb Jahren "nicht einmal, die beiden großen Städte Brjansk und Kramatorsk einzunehmen". Trotzdem gebe es bisher keinerlei Anzeichen, dass Putin von seinen Kriegszielen und seiner imperialen Weltsicht abrücken könnte.

Wenn es nach Trump geht, ist es ein Treffen für die Geschichtsbücher. Doch Konkretes gibt es am Ende nicht. Betont wird etwa die Vermeidung eines Atomkriegs und eine Reform der UN.

Das "Gerede" über Verhandlungen für ein Ende des Ukraine-Kriegs bestärke das Kreml-Narrativ, warnte Keupp. Damit würde man einen Kriegsverbrecher, nämlich Putin, aufwerten.

> So lange Putin nicht ernsthaft einen Druck spürt, wo er merkt, er kommt hier militärisch in diesem Krieg nicht weiter, und er kommt auch wirtschaftlich in diesem Krieg nicht weiter, so lange wird es keine ernsthaften Verhandlungen geben, sondern viel mehr diese ständigen Finten, Pseudo-Angebote. „

Marcus Keupp

Dazu zählt laut Keupp auch die jüngste Einladung Putins an die Europäer zu Gesprächen nach Moskau. "Wir sollten dringend weg davon, uns so konditionieren zu lassen", appellierte Keupp.

Stattdessen sollte die Ukraine so ausgestattet werden, dass sie "Putin in jeder Form klar machen kann, dass er keine Chance hat". Etwa habe die Ukraine bisher keine vollständige Kontrolle über ihren Luftraum. Europa agiere weiterhin zu passiv und "viel zu zögerlich" - trotz der nun zugesagten weiteren Hilfen von 45 Milliarden Euro sowie bei der Flugabwehr.

Beim Dreier-Gipfel in China spielte der Ukraine-Krieg quasi keine Rolle, berichtet Miriam Steimer. Derweil tagt die "Koalition der Willigen" in Berlin weiter, so Diana Zimmermann.

## ... das Verhältnis zwischen Xi und Putin

Aufschlussreich sei, wie Putin bei dem Treffen von Xi Jinping behandelt worden sei, sagte Keupp. Auf Fotos habe der chinesische Präsident den Kreml-Chef auf die Seite gedrängt.

> Putin wird sehr klar gemacht, wie hier seine Position ist unter den Dreien, nämlich, er ist ein Vasall Chinas. Er ist nicht gleichberechtigt. „

Marcus Keupp

Das ärgere den russischen Präsidenten auch sichtlich. Wenn überhaupt, entstehe gerade eine neue bipolare Ordnung aus China als aufstrebender Großmacht und den USA als "eher stagnierender Großmacht", in der Russland nicht gleich bedeutend sei.

China, Russland und die USA treffen sich zu einem Dreiergipfel. Ist das der Beginn einer neuen Weltordnung? Mirko Drotschmann erklärt, wie das Treffen China in die Karten spielt.

Aktuell profitiere China zwar vom Ukraine-Krieg, da es Russland nun sämtliche Konsumgüter liefere, die zuvor aus den USA importiert wurden. Doch Russland sei für China kein wichtiger Markt. Vielmehr halte China Russland über die Belieferung in Abhängigkeit.

Derzeit sei Moskau für China nützlich als "böser Kettenhund gegen den Westen". Doch China denke langfristiger: Wenn ihm Russland irgendwann nicht mehr nütze, werde es womöglich mit dem nächsten amerikanischen Präsidenten versuchen, "irgendeine Art von stabilem Kompromiss auszuhandeln", so Keupp.

## ... mögliche Folgen aus dem Treffen von Putin, Xi und Trump

Während Xi ohnehin kein Interesse daran habe, "aktiv irgendwas zu tun", stehe Trump mit den neuen Senatoren und Kongressabgeordneten ab Januar unter sehr großem Druck und werde seine Energie auf innenpolitische Fragen richten müssen. Und die Ukraine werde unterdessen weiterkämpfen.

Das schüre die Hoffnung, dass sich die Weltordnung in diesem Kriegswinter womöglich auch "zum Positiven wenden" könnte, sagte Keupp. "Vielleicht haben wir den Höhepunkt der autoritären Verehrung des Rechtspopulismus und so weiter gesehen."

> Diese drei autoritären Herren sind vielleicht eher dann Fußnoten des 20. Jahrhunderts und nicht die Zukunft des 21. Jahrhunderts. „

Marcus Keupp

Klar sei aber, dass sich Europa seinen "bequemen Wohlstandspazifismus" nicht mehr leisten könne. Der Ukraine-Krieg habe bei allem Schrecken auch etwas Gutes, findet Keupp: "Er erzeugt Anpassungsdruck."

Die Europäer spielten bei der Neuordnung der Welt nur eine „nachgeordnete Rolle“, so Politikwissenschaftler Stefan Bierling. Der Ukraine-Gipfel habe vor allem Geschlossenheit demonstriert.

Die Europäer würden merken, dass es so nicht weitergehen könne, weil sie sonst aus der Weltpolitik verschwinden würden. "Ich hoffe sehr, dass es für Europa noch nicht zu spät ist."

Das Interview führte ZDFheute live-Moderator Philip Wortmann. Die Zusammenfassung ist von Anja Engelke.

# Militärökonom Keupp: Putin "ist ein Vasall Chinas"

## Neue Weltordnung? : Militärökonom Keupp: Putin "ist ein Vasall Chinas"

Der Gipfel in China habe zwischen zwei Großmächten stattgefunden - und einer, die gerne dazugehören würde, sagt der Militärökonom Keupp. Xi habe Putin gezeigt, was seine Rolle sei.

Zwei Gipfeltreffen an einem Tag: Während Trump, Putin und Xi über die internationale Sicherheitslage diskutieren, empfängt Merz in Berlin Selenskyj und Vertreter aus 40 Ländern. ZDFheute live

Beim Dreiergipfel im chinesischen Shenzhen haben die Staatschefs der USA, Russlands und Chinas über internationale Konflikte gesprochen. Doch obwohl sich die Atommächte auf eine "Erklärung zum Frieden" einigten, sei das Treffen rein symbolisch zu werten, sagte der Militärökonom Marcus Keupp bei ZDFheute live. Spannend sei es jedoch im Hinblick auf die Dynamiken zwischen den drei Teilnehmern Donald Trump, Wladimir Putin und Xi Jinping gewesen.

Sehen Sie das Interview oben im Video in voller Länge oder lesen Sie es hier in Auszügen. Das sagte Keupp über ...

Eine neue Weltordnung entstehe aus dem Treffen zwischen Putin, Xi und Trump nicht, stellte Keupp klar.

> Es gibt eine deutliche Diskrepanz zwischen dem, was die Beobachter da so hinein interpretieren, und dem, was an Substanz aus diesem Treffen eigentlich herauskommt. „

Marcus Keupp

So trage die etwa von Bundeskanzler Merz gezogene Parallele zur Konferenz von Jalta im Jahr 1945 nicht: Damals hatte Deutschland den Zweiten Weltkrieg verloren und saß als Aggressor - anders als heute Putin - nicht mit am Konferenztisch.

Am 4. Februar 1945 gelingt es dem roten Zaren mit List und Tücke, seine Verbündeten zu täuschen. Der Film zeigt, wie Josef Stalin in Jalta den Zweiten Weltkrieg gewinnt.

Das Treffen in Shenzhen sei "etwas völlig anderes". "Es ist eine schöne Inszenierung, es ist ein großer Gewinn für China , würde ich sagen." Die kleinen, feinen Details seien zwar "sehr schön gemacht", aber es gebe "wenig Ergebnis".

## Dr. Marcus M. Keupp

Quelle: ZDF … ist Dozent für Militärökonomie an der Militärakademie der ETH Zürich, der Ausbildungsstätte für Berufsoffiziere der Schweizer Armee. Zuvor hat er an der Universität Mannheim und der Warwick Business School Betriebswirtschaftslehre studiert und an der Universität St. Gallen promoviert. In seiner Forschung beschäftigt sich Keupp insbesondere mit militärischer Logistik. Seit Beginn des Kriegs in der Ukraine 2022 analysiert Keupp das Geschehen an der Front, die russischen und ukrainischen Nachschublinien sowie die wirtschaftlichen Auswirkungen des Krieges.

In Russland selbst möge Putin zwar mächtig sein, verglichen mit Xi und Trump sei er aber "die kleinste Macht", sagte Keupp. Zwar fabuliere der Kreml-Chef von sich selbst als Großmacht. Doch es gelte, zwischen purer Symbolik und den wirtschaftlichen und militärischen Fakten klar zu trennen.

Schließlich schaffe Putin es seit viereinhalb Jahren "nicht einmal, die beiden großen Städte Brjansk und Kramatorsk einzunehmen". Trotzdem gebe es bisher keinerlei Anzeichen, dass Putin von seinen Kriegszielen und seiner imperialen Weltsicht abrücken könnte.

Wenn es nach Trump geht, ist es ein Treffen für die Geschichtsbücher. Doch Konkretes gibt es am Ende nicht. Betont wird etwa die Vermeidung eines Atomkriegs und eine Reform der UN.

Das "Gerede" über Verhandlungen für ein Ende des Ukraine-Kriegs bestärke das Kreml-Narrativ, warnte Keupp. Damit würde man einen Kriegsverbrecher, nämlich Putin, aufwerten.

> So lange Putin nicht ernsthaft einen Druck spürt, wo er merkt, er kommt hier militärisch in diesem Krieg nicht weiter, und er kommt auch wirtschaftlich in diesem Krieg nicht weiter, so lange wird es keine ernsthaften Verhandlungen geben, sondern viel mehr diese ständigen Finten, Pseudo-Angebote. „

Marcus Keupp

Dazu zählt laut Keupp auch die jüngste Einladung Putins an die Europäer zu Gesprächen nach Moskau. "Wir sollten dringend weg davon, uns so konditionieren zu lassen", appellierte Keupp.

Stattdessen sollte die Ukraine so ausgestattet werden, dass sie "Putin in jeder Form klar machen kann, dass er keine Chance hat". Etwa habe die Ukraine bisher keine vollständige Kontrolle über ihren Luftraum. Europa agiere weiterhin zu passiv und "viel zu zögerlich" - trotz der nun zugesagten weiteren Hilfen von 45 Milliarden Euro sowie bei der Flugabwehr.

Beim Dreier-Gipfel in China spielte der Ukraine-Krieg quasi keine Rolle, berichtet Miriam Steimer. Derweil tagt die "Koalition der Willigen" in Berlin weiter, so Diana Zimmermann.

Aufschlussreich sei, wie Putin bei dem Treffen von Xi Jinping behandelt worden sei, sagte Keupp. Auf Fotos habe der chinesische Präsident den Kreml-Chef auf die Seite gedrängt.

articleBody:
A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist [Jean-Michel Basquiat](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/jean-michel-basquiat/) (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate.

In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was. Simply titled *[Jean-Michel Basquiat](https://www.netflix.com/title/82820725)*, the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world.

As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.

articleBody:
# Börsengang: Anthropic schließt 17 Prozent im Plus – Kursrückgang im Handelsverlauf

Dario Amodei beim Anthropic-Börsengang: Der KI-Gründer applaudiert auch sich selbst. Foto: REUTERS Zusammenfassung Nutzen Sie komprimierte Kernaussagen für maximale Effizienz in Ihrem News-Alltag – verfügbar im H+ Standard Abo. Jetzt für 1 € testen Düsseldorf, Frankfurt, New York, San Francisco. Dario Amodei steht auf dem Parkett der Nasdaq und wippt hin und her. Der Anthropic-CEO spricht schnell, abgehackt, schaut immer wieder auf das Redemanuskript in seiner Hand, während er von „wissenschaftlichen Durchbrüchen“ und „realen Risiken“ der Künstlichen Intelligenz (KI) spricht. Der 43-Jährige hat am Donnerstag gemeinsam mit anderen Anthropic-Mitgründern und Mitarbeitern den Handel an der New Yorker Technologiebörse eingeläutet – und Börsengeschichte geschrieben.

Anthropic ist mit einem deutlichen Kursplus in den Handel an der Nasdaq gestartet. Die Erstnotiz lag bei 111,50 Dollar. Das war ein Plus von 34 Prozent im Vergleich zum Emissionspreis, der bei 83 Dollar lag.

Damit brach der KI-Anbieter gleich zwei Rekorde. Das Unternehmen sammelte mit 107,3 Milliarden Dollar mehr Geld bei Investoren ein als jeder andere Börsenkonzern zuvor. Anthropic erzielte zudem eine Marktkapitalisierung von gut zwei Billionen Dollar. Auch dies ist eine Höchstmarke. Im Juni war SpaceX , das Raumfahrtunternehmen von Elon Musk, mit der bisherigen Rekordbewertung von 1,8 Billionen an die Börse gegangen.

title: Susan Sontag: Eine Frau, die das Meer pflügte?
subtitle: Mehr Impact in Schwaben und darüber hinaus: Das DLA Marbach startet eine Reihe zu „Schriftstellerinnen im Archiv“.
feedText: Ein Typoskript aus dem jüngst nach Marbach gegebenen Vorlass Sigrid Löfflers zählt zu den interessantesten Stücken dieser Ausstellung: Darin protokolliert die österreichische Kritikerin ein Gespräch, das sie im August 2003 in Edinburgh mit der amerikanischen Intellektuellen und Schriftstellerin Susan Sontag für ein Porträt in der Zeitschrift „Literaturen“ geführt hat, also im Sommer vor Sontags Frankfurter Paulskirchenrede, die damals schon in eine für transatlantische Beziehungen schwierige Zeit fiel. Die Friedenspreisträgerin Sontag macht sich darin Gedanken über die Bedeutung und Resonanz ihrer Rede als „Botschafterin zweier Kontinente“, die sich zugleich amerikanisch und europäisch fühle, sagt im Hinblick auf die (tatsächlich nicht mehr existierende) Kanzel dieser Kirche, diese sei „a great pulpit and I want to use it well“. Und, ehrfürchtig weiter: „I feel very much a disciple of German Literature.“ Diese Literatur sei stets von großer Bedeutung für sie gewesen. Dann folgen noch Satzfetzen über eine „magical week in Tübingen“, „first time in Schwaben“ und „a great opportunity to say something that will have some impact“. Die gehaltene Rede im Oktober 2003 hatte dann tatsächlich „impact“; der damalige amerikanische Botschafter sagte seine Teilnahme ab, weil Sontag als scharfe Kritikerin der Regierung unter George W. Sie kritisierte in der Paulskirche zwar dessen „imperiales Programm“, widmete sich dann aber der Literatur, der sie die Fähigkeit zusprach, Grenzen zu überwinden, während sie auch über Selbstzweifel und Rollenkonflikte sprach.
articleBody:
# Ausstellung über Susan Sontag im Deutschen Literaturarchiv

Ein Typoskript aus dem jüngst nach Marbach gegebenen Vorlass Sigrid Löfflers zählt zu den interessantesten Stücken dieser Ausstellung: Darin protokolliert die österreichische Kritikerin ein Gespräch, das sie im August 2003 in Edinburgh mit der amerikanischen Intellektuellen und Schriftstellerin Susan Sontag für ein Porträt in der Zeitschrift „Literaturen“ geführt hat, also im Sommer vor Sontags Frankfurter Paulskirchenrede, die damals schon in eine für transatlantische Beziehungen schwierige Zeit fiel. Die Friedenspreisträgerin Sontag macht sich darin Gedanken über die Bedeutung und Resonanz ihrer Rede als „Botschafterin zweier Kontinente“, die sich zugleich amerikanisch und europäisch fühle, sagt im Hinblick auf die (tatsächlich nicht mehr existierende) Kanzel dieser Kirche, diese sei „a great pulpit and I want to use it well“. Und, ehrfürchtig weiter: „I feel very much a disciple of German Literature.“ Diese Literatur sei stets von großer Bedeutung für sie gewesen. Dann folgen noch Satzfetzen über eine „magical week in Tübingen“, „first time in Schwaben“ und „a great opportunity to say something that will have some impact“.

Die gehaltene Rede im Oktober 2003 hatte dann tatsächlich „impact“; der damalige amerikanische Botschafter sagte seine Teilnahme ab, weil Sontag als scharfe Kritikerin der Regierung unter George W. Bush bekannt war. Sie kritisierte in der Paulskirche zwar dessen „imperiales Programm“, widmete sich dann aber der Literatur, der sie die Fähigkeit zusprach, Grenzen zu überwinden, während sie auch über Selbstzweifel und Rollenkonflikte sprach. Knapp ein Jahr vor ihrem Tod stand Susan Sontag damals in gewisser Weise auf dem Höhepunkt ihrer öffentlichen Wahrnehmung in Deutschland, die von Anfang an zwischen Wertschätzung und Kritik pendelte.

### Zu kompliziert und avantgardistisch?

Diese Wahrnehmung versucht die Wechselausstellung „Susan Sontag – Erfindung einer Klassikerin“ in fünf Stationen nachzuzeichnen. Obwohl es an Wahrnehmung Susan Sontags bis heute nicht mangelt, wirkt die Marbacher Schau komplementär gewinnbringend, auch weil sie die im Deutschen Literaturarchiv befindlichen Verlagsarchive fruchtbar macht.

So lassen sich mehrere Zeugnisse intensiver Korrespondenz mit dem langjährigen Hanser-Verleger Michael Krüger zeigen, in dessen Haus Sontag 1978 eine deutsche Heimat fand und dort Werke wie „Krankheit als Metapher“, „Über Fotografie“ oder „Kunst und Antikunst“ veröffentlichte. Zuerst war sie in Deutschland bei Rowohlt verlegt worden, wo der damalige Cheflektor Fritz J. Raddatz 1967 gegenüber Sontags New Yorker Verlegerin Lila Karpf brieflich versicherte: „There is no doubt that she will develop as one of the important modern American authors.“ Um dann hinzuzufügen, was Deutschland betreffe, sei er weniger zuversichtlich, „because Susan Sontag’s books are rather difficult and avantgarde“.

Dass Sontag sich selbst gern wie hier beschrieben in Szene setzte, verschweigen die von Sandra Richter, Anna Kinder und Vera Hildenbrandt kuratierte Ausstellung und das zugehörige „Marbacher Magazin“ nicht, während darin zugleich die ambivalenten Haltungen der männlichen Förderer und Kritiker Susan Sontag gegenüber dokumentiert und zugespitzt werden.

Marcel Reich-Ranicki sieht man in einem Video aus dem „Literarischen Quartett“ die These aufstellen, Susan Sontag sei nur erfolgreich geworden, weil sie eine Frau, jung und hübsch gewesen sei. Fritz J. Raddatz geriet über Sontag ins Schwärmen („Eine Frau, die das Meer pflügte“), mehr aber noch über eine von ihm bei sich zu Hause für Sontag organisierte Party 1993, die wiederum sie dann von seinem „spectacular apartment“ schwärmen ließ. Dass Raddatz dennoch Kritik an Sontags Roman „The Volcano Lover“ für berechtigt hielt, muss nicht per se empören – und ihrem Impact hat auch andere Kritik nicht unbedingt geschadet. Dieser wird in Marbach zugleich für den Aufschwung zu einer von der Wüstenrot-Stiftung geförderten Reihe von fünf Ausstellungen zu „Schriftstellerinnen im DLA“ genutzt, in der als Nächste im Herbst 2027 Helga M. Novak gewürdigt werden soll.

Ein Typoskript aus dem jüngst nach Marbach gegebenen Vorlass Sigrid Löfflers zählt zu den interessantesten Stücken dieser Ausstellung: Darin protokolliert die österreichische Kritikerin ein Gespräch, das sie im August 2003 in Edinburgh mit der amerikanischen Intellektuellen und Schriftstellerin Susan Sontag für ein Porträt in der Zeitschrift „Literaturen“ geführt hat, also im Sommer vor Sontags Frankfurter Paulskirchenrede, die damals schon in eine für transatlantische Beziehungen schwierige Zeit fiel. Die Friedenspreisträgerin Sontag macht sich darin Gedanken über die Bedeutung und Resonanz ihrer Rede als „Botschafterin zweier Kontinente“, die sich zugleich amerikanisch und europäisch fühle, sagt im Hinblick auf die (tatsächlich nicht mehr existierende) Kanzel dieser Kirche, diese sei „a great pulpit and I want to use it well“. Bush bekannt war. Fritz J. Raddatz geriet über Sontag ins Schwärmen („Eine Frau, die das Meer pflügte“), mehr aber noch über eine von ihm bei sich zu Hause für Sontag organisierte Party 1993, die wiederum sie dann von seinem „spectacular apartment“ schwärmen ließ. articleBody:
ICIJ’s [China Capital](https://www.icij.org/investigations/china-capital/) investigation revealed how the London units of the world’s largest bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC), routinely financed companies to push Beijing’s geopolitical agenda, sometimes flouting their own compliance rules in the process.

ICIJ, in collaboration with 23 media partners, obtained 4.8 million internal documents leaked from ICBC London, including loan application forms, due diligence reports, know-your-client documents and internal email exchanges.

To better understand ICBC’s London operations, the ICIJ data team dissected more than 200 loan agreements and amendments dated from 2010 to 2024. ICIJ found that ICBC London partnered with at least one other Chinese state-owned commercial bank in more than half of the agreements and amendments reviewed. Among the Chinese lenders, Bank of China stands out as the main Chinese partner of ICBC London: They joined forces in 102 agreements.

ICIJ’s analysis shows that the London units of the Chinese banking giant usually partnered with other Chinese and international banks on loan agreements often worth hundreds of millions of dollars—or more. ICIJ identified 36 loan agreements and amendments for which half or more of the money was provided by Chinese lenders. In 16 of those cases, the financial commitments were entirely from Chinese banks.

ICBC documents prepared as part of the due diligence process on the bank’s clients show how the bank at times downplayed compliance problems or otherwise justified continued business with clients it had classified as high risk, an ICIJ review found. In Zambia, ICBC played a role in exacerbating the country’s debt burden, creating dependency on Chinese loans and contributing to years-long difficulties for Zambians. In the U.K., ICBC bank officers disregarded legal risks faced in a U.S. court by one of their Chinese clients so the bank could finance the company’s acquisition of a British competitor and consolidate its market share.

The case studies below reveal the inner workings of a bank balancing the advancement of the agenda of the Chinese party-state with its own global commercial ambitions.

## Ignoring Red Lights

01

In May 2024, ICBC’s high-risk client list included the financing arm of global fuel trader and distributor Puma Energy, along with a major shareholder Trafigura Pte. Ltd., a trading giant registered and headquartered in Singapore with major trading operations in Switzerland, and two other Trafigura entities. Despite ICBC's concerns about Puma and Trafigura dating back to at least 2015, ICIJ identified 19 syndicated credit facility agreements involving Puma and Trafigura, between 2015 and 2024, with a combined value of $38.7 billion. ICBC's London entities committed a total of $1.4 billion across those facilities. In 2015, ICBC escalated its due diligence of Puma’s financing vehicle, Puma International Financing; in its May 2015 Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) report, it rated the company’s bribery risk as high. At the time, Puma's shareholders included Angola's state-owned oil company Sonangol and Cochan Holdings LLC, an investment company founded and chaired by Angolan presidential adviser Leopoldino Fragoso do Nascimento. The report acknowledged extensive adverse media coverage alleging bribery and corruption involving senior Angolan officials, including then-President José Eduardo dos Santos and his children, as well as Sonangol, Cochan and Nascimento. Still, ICBC characterized much of the adverse reporting as “rumour based and unfounded” and continued the relationship, subject to enhanced monitoring. In February 2020, ICBC’s EDD report again identified allegations centered on Nascimento’s close ties to former President dos Santos and speculation in media reports and elsewhere that he had used political connections to acquire a stake in Puma Energy while serving as a public official. The report also noted that Nascimento had faced investigations into alleged corruption, conflicts of interest and money laundering in several countries. Yet ICBC cited reasons for discounting the risks, noting that Nascimento did “not appear to have been convicted” of wrongdoing. In December 2021, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned Nascimento and Cochan, saying Nascimento and another Angolan official had embezzled billions from the Angolan government. In 2025, an Angolan court convicted Nascimento of fraud, document forgery, money laundering and influence peddling. Likewise, ICBC's October 2019 Enhanced Due Diligence report came after a highly public Brazilian corruption investigation into allegations that commodity traders, including Trafigura, had bribed employees of Petrobras, Brazil’s state-owned and state-controlled oil company. A month earlier, Reuters reported allegations that senior Trafigura executives Mike Wainwright and José Larocca knew about the bribes. But ICBC's EDD report referred only to "two high-ranking executives” at Trafigura, without identifying them, despite separately listing both men as key controllers of Trafigura. Wainwright's adverse-media assessment was marked "No." ICBC continued the relationship, citing Trafigura's status as a longstanding "strategic client," the participation of major international banks in syndicated loans, its compliance controls and the absence of suspicious activity detected by ICBC. In 2024, Trafigura Beheer B.V., the Dutch-registered former parent company of the Trafigura Group, pleaded guilty in the U.S. to conspiring to violate U.S. anti-bribery laws in a scheme that ran from approximately 2003 to 2014. The companies also reached a settlement agreement with Brazilian authorities. Read responses Responses Trafigura: In response to ICIJ's questions, a Trafigura spokesperson said lender due diligence was a normal part of doing business and that the company cooperated with lenders' reviews, supported by its public financial and sustainability disclosures. Regarding the Petrobras bribery case, the spokesperson referred to Trafigura's 2024 statement announcing the resolution of the U.S. investigation, in which the company said the misconduct involved former employees or agents and was inconsistent with its principles and code of conduct. The statement said U.S. authorities had recognized improvements to Trafigura's anti-corruption compliance procedures. Puma: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Nascimento: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Angolan government: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Cochan: ICIJ could not successfully contact Cochan for comment. Sonangol: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. A legal representative for Mike Wainwright didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. José Larocca: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. ICBC: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Main borrowers Puma International Financing S.A., Trafigura Group Pte. Ltd., Trafigura Pte. Ltd., Trafigura Trading LLC Amount $1.4 billionTotal loan commitments Start dates of loans 2015-2024 From the China Capital files PUMA In their own words: There is a wealth of adverse news in the public domain citing the Angolan Government's bribery and corruption and monopolisation of various industries in Angola.Risk From the China Capital files TRAFIGURA In their own words: The risks of money laundering, sanctions and bribery and corruption are heightened [...] and thus this poses an increased reputational risk to the Bank.Risk Trafigura is an existing and strategic client of the Bank.Mitigating factors

Financing Kleptocrats 02 ICBC started lending to Socar, Azerbaijan’s state oil and gas concern, in 2015 when ICBC London took part in a revolving credit facility to one of the company’s subsidiaries, Socar Trading SA. Even though the bank decided to exit this facility in 2019 because of the company's “underperformance and ongoing restructuring," a review of ICBC documents shows that under the head office’s encouragement, ICBC’s London and Turkey offices maintained close connection with Socar. Bank officers in an internal memo noted “Azerbaijan's geopolitical importance in the area's political and economic landscape, and its longstanding partnership with super oil majors,” adding “SOCAR is a strategically important client for ICBC in view of supporting China's 2013 One-Belt One-Road policy." ICBC London committed to at least three additional loans, each between $25 million and $89 million, even as the bank continued to list Socar among high-risk clients, with one document stating: “the risks of money laundering, sanctions and bribery and corruption are heightened." Corporate bank officers underlined the risks presented by the nature of Socar’s business and its jurisdiction, Azerbaijan; the fact that all the members of its board of directors were, at the time, identified as politically exposed persons, including the president and 12 vice presidents; Socar’s lack of transparency and accountability; and that the company had recently featured in major international corruption scandals. Yet the same year that ICBC listed these risks, 2021, the bank agreed to lend Socar $89 million. ICBC and Socar had deepened their ties in 2018, when the bank’s London branch listed $1.58 billion worth of green bonds on the London Stock Exchange, and Azerbaijan's State Oil Fund, SOFAZ, decided to invest $150 million. Socar, which sells oil and gas on the state’s behalf, contributed about 90% of SOFAZ’s 2017 revenue. The Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project later reported that leaked documents from inside British Petroleum exposed that two Socar subsidiaries were set to siphon off more than $1.7 billion from the Shah Deniz 2 gas project through padded contracts and fake charges. Socar denied the allegations. Read response Response Socar: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. SOFAZ: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. ICBC: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Main borrower Socar and its subsidiaries Amount $217 million (4 loans)Total loan commitments Start dates of loans 2015-2021 From the China Capital files In their own words: Given Azerbaijan’s geopolitical importance in the area’s political and economic landscape, and its longstanding partnership with super oil majors, SOCAR is a strategically important client for ICBC in view of supporting China’s 2013 One-Belt One-Road policy aimed at creating infrastructure and establishing links among the Eurasian countries.Risk

Consolidating Market Share 03 ICBC records show bank risk management officials looking past the potentially illegal actions of a Chinese customer seeking a loan to buy out one of its competitors. In 2017 ICBC London Branch agreed to back China’s Hytera Communications Corp. Ltd.’s acquisition of Sepura PLC, a British telecommunications competitor in the mobile radio communications sector. Hytera designs and manufactures professional mobile communications devices commonly used by law enforcement agencies worldwide — including two-way radios, a market that at the time was expected to be worth $7.3 billion by 2025. The agreement with ICBC London, which was the only lender involved, allowed Hytera to borrow up to $57.1 million over three years. Sepura shareholders had approved the $92.7 million acquisition in January 2017 but antitrust authorities in the UK and Germany, where governments relied on Sepura’s technology, stalled the acquisition. Spanish antitrust authorities also assessed the transaction, which was eventually approved in May of that year. While conducting their due diligence work to approve the loan in early 2017, ICBC London employees discovered that Motorola Solutions Inc., another competitor in the mobile telecommunications market, had filed a lawsuit pending against Hytera in a U.S. federal court for alleged patent infringement and industrial espionage. The bank’s compliance officers allowed the loan to go forward anyway, adding a handwritten note on a printout of an article about the suit that the case wasn’t related to any major financial crime. The article mentioned, however, that Motorola accused Hytera of hiring ex-Motorola employees after they had allegedly stolen thousands of pages of confidential documents. By early 2020, while Hytera was repaying the loan ICBC employees flagged a problem — Hytera had lost its U.S. case. In a briefing note to the bank’s credit committee at the end of April, they wrote that the verdict “confirms that Hytera engaged in illegal trade secret theft and copyright infringement, validating Motorola's global litigation against Hytera.” Following the U.S. court verdict ICBC London received an injunction from a British court ordering the bank to freeze Hytera assets, potentially stopping the repayment of the loan. Seven Hytera employees were later indicted for their alleged roles in the thefts from Motorola; one pleaded guilty in 2022 to charges of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and is awaiting sentencing. Hytera pleaded guilty in 2025 to “conspiracy to steal trade secrets” and was fined $50 million. Hytera was also ordered to pay Motorola more than $400 million in a separate lawsuit. In 2021, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission published a list of Chinese manufacturers, including Hytera, which “pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States.” The same year, the British government passed the National Security and Investment Act which gave heightened power to the government to proactively review acquisitions in 17 sensitive sectors, including communications. Hytera sold its entire shareholding in Sepura in July 2022. Read responses Responses Hytera: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. In an email to ICIJ, Sepura said that "neither Sepura PLC nor its shareholders or management at the time were involved in Hytera’s choice of funding for its acquisition of Sepura” and that the company “had no customer relationship with ICBC and held no accounts with the bank” following the acquisition. It also said that it was not “a party to the litigation brought by Motorola against Hytera concerning Motorola’s intellectual property” and that “the technology at issue was distinct from that developed and used by Sepura in its own products”. “Sepura's proprietary technology and IPR were ring-fenced by statutory undertakings, as mandated and defined by the UK government and accepted by Hytera.” Sepura said it “has had no further interaction with Hytera since the sale” in 2022. ICBC: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Borrower Project Shortway Ltd. (ultimately owned by Hytera Communications Corp. Ltd.) Amount up to $57.1 millionTotal loan commitments Start date of loans May 2017 From the China Capital files In their own words Handwritten note on an article: Not major financial crime issues relatedRisk

Buying your backyard 04 ICBC participated in syndicated loans — financing provided by a group of lenders who share the risk — for a Chinese commercial real estate venture that went bust and defaulted on its loans, according to internal loan agreements and property assessments reviewed by ICIJ. In 2017, Chinese real estate tycoon Chen Hongtian and his wife bought two office towers in London’s trendy Canary Wharf commercial district, hoping to convert their $900 million investment into a profitable venture. ICBC London described the area as “one of the world’s premier commercial districts,” with “24 office buildings with around 200 shops, bars, and restaurants” according to a 2022 assessment of 5 Churchill Place’s value by the real estate company managing the asset. The real estate firm’s assessment came as the bank and other creditors looked to liquidate the assets of the embattled tycoon who had found himself short on cash and unable to make payments. By then, ICBC London Branch had committed $205 million out of roughly half a billion in loans made with other banks to Chen’s companies in the British Virgin Islands, through which he and his family owned the London properties. One of those properties, at 20 Canada Square, was mainly occupied by two Western firms, according to a 2022 ICBC internal credit report. But the properties couldn’t compete with more modern and energy-efficient real estate, and their value plummeted. By April 2023 ICBC London had reclassified the loan to Cheung Pang Holdings Ltd., a BVI company through which Chen owned some units of the Canada Square property, as “non performing” and added the borrower to its watchlist. Around the same time that ICBC was reviewing the properties, the UK government passed the Economic Crime (Transparency and Enforcement) Act which required overseas entities that hold property in England and Wales to file beneficial ownership information with the company registry. A report published in 2017 by the U.S. Government Accountability Office warned that leasing space in foreign-owned buildings "could present security risks such as espionage and unauthorized cyber and physical access.” The UK’s National Security and Investment Act took effect in January 2022, but real estate was not among the sensitive sectors subject to its mandatory screening requirements for acquisitions. Read responses Responses Chen Hongtian/Cheung Kei group: The Cheung Kei group didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. In statement posted on its website in 2023 the group said that “like all heavy asset holders”, it was “experiencing a phase of cash problems” and that its “overall asset scale and asset quality” were “very high, with a low debt ratio among peers.” At the time the group was “selling some equity in some assets and actively negotiating repayment arrangements with relevant financial institutions” and said it “believed that subsequent financial institution issues will be properly resolved.” ICBC London: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Main borrowers Jovial Link Holdings Ltd. for 5 Churchill Place; Cheung Pang Holdings Ltd., Cheung Kwan Holdings Ltd. for 20 Canada Square (London properties) Start dates of loans 2022 Amount $61.7M / $143.5MTotal loan commitments From the China Capital files In their own words: About 5 Churchill Place, from a credit loan application: The deal as outlined herein offers ICBC London an ideal opportunity to assist an incoming Chinese client in the purchase of a major “trophy” asset that is both well let to tenants of significant covenant strengths and well located within the popular Canary Wharf developmentRisk

Trapping In Debt 05 ICBC records on Zambia show a lender watching a borrower facing growing financial risks, while quietly putting protections in place for its own loans. ICBC financed a range of major projects in the country, providing loans for government-owned housing, a hospital, an airport and power projects running to hundreds of millions of dollars. Among them was a $285 million loan approved in 2010 to ZESCO, Zambia's state-owned power company, for two power transmission projects. Between 2015 and 2018, ICBC provided or participated in at least six more loans to ZESCO, totaling $1.2 billion according to AidData estimates, even as the bank was aware of mounting financial pressures on both Zambia and ZESCO. By 2017, a sovereign risk assessment in the bank's files described Zambia as facing limited financing options, rising interest costs, and substantial debt—and specifically pointed to financial pressures on ZESCO. Government net debt had climbed from 23% of GDP in 2013 to an estimated 57% in 2017, while debt costs consumed nearly a quarter of government revenue. ICBC had classified ZESCO as a high-risk client since 2018, citing Zambia's country risk, politically exposed persons and historical adverse media coverage including bribery and corruption allegations, according to a 2023 internal report. Despite these concerns, the bank continued its lending relationship with ZESCO, requiring annual reviews. ICBC built protections into its lending. ZESCO maintained a debt-service reserve account at ICBC London for repayments on the $285 million loan. Money deposited into the account could only be withdrawn by ICBC's head office, which was also the lender, agent and security trustee. ZESCO’s financial precarity triggered a cascade of credit problems. By March 2020, its failure to pay Maamba Collieries Ltd., a Zambian power supplier, had left Maamba unable to meet its own loan obligations to ICBC and other lenders. ICBC records show that lenders sent letters to Zambia's Ministry of Finance seeking government support, contacted Chinese state-owned insurer Sinosure and discussed restructuring the loan. ICBC officials warned that Maamba's loan would be classified as non-performing if payments remained overdue for more than 90 days. The documents offer a window into how the bank continued banking a financially strained borrower while using safeguards to limit its own losses. articleBody:
# How Future Lunar Colonists Can Farm Potatoes on the Moon - Nautilus

## How Future Lunar Colonists Can Farm Potatoes on the Moon

A new study discovered a recipe for success

3:00 PM CST on November 19, 2026

In the movie The Martian , Matt Damon’s character (botanist Mark Watley) finds himself stranded on Mars. With any rescue months away and food supplies dwindling, he decides to do what he does best—grow some plants. Watley mixes the Martian soil with fertilizer provided by the crew’s waste and plants potatoes.

It’s a good plan (spoiler alert: it worked). Potatoes are both nutritionally dense and provide a high number of calories per unit of land (they’re also versatile and delicious). According to a new study published in npj Microgravity , they may even be able to feed future lunar colonists.

Read more: “ How Potatoes Shaped the Genes of the First People to Grow Them ”

To establish a baseline for best lunar farming practices, a team of botanists from Oregon State University relied on simulated moon soil, or regolith. Unlike the living soil here on Earth, moon dirt isn’t exactly conducive to plant growth—it’s nutrient-poor and contains higher levels of toxic heavy metals. So to give the regolith a little boost, they mixed it with various amounts of vermicompost (an organic fertilizer produced by red wiggler worms) as well as additional nitrogen.

The team tested five varieties of simulated lunar soil, some that mimicked low-lying lunar mares and some that mimicked the highlands. As a control, they used soil from Hermiston, Oregon, which has one of the highest yields of potatoes globally (there goes your reputation, Idaho).

The team found that the optimum mix was 30 percent vermicompost and 70 percent regolith. Potatoes grown in this soil were the best match for those grown in good ol’ Hermiston, Oregon dirt. Lower levels of the fertilizer (5 to 15 percent) yielded stunted tubers, dwarfed leaves, and shriveled roots. (Which region of the moon the regolith simulated—highland versus lowland didn’t seem to make much of a difference.)

Looking at the chemical composition of the potatoes, the researchers found they were nutritionally similar to those grown on Earth. In fact, the vermicompost seems to have provided some protection against heavy metals like copper in the regolith.

“We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” study author Aymeric Goyer said in a statement . “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”

Of course, these findings mean future lunar farmers will have to bring vermicompost or something like it to kick-start their agricultural project. But once they get started, they can resupply using their own organic material. After all, as the fictional Mark Watley discovered, astronauts make pretty good fertilizer producers.

feedText: Perched on a cliffside between the canopy of white fig trees and palms, it faces the Pacific Ocean. The project responds to the site's unique conditions through an open architecture that accompanies different moments of hospitality: arriving, taking a seat, sharing a drink, and lingering as the sunset transforms the horizon and music extends the experience into the night. Its mixology menu, inspired by the four elements and Náyeri and Wixárika traditions, dialogues with this natural setting.

articleBody:
# What satellites leave behind

It was the lithium that gave it away, says Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium showed they were too late.

The team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data showed way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

“That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy says. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

The data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

The number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

Since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

Researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

At the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a big risk to the space industry, says Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”

## Design for demise

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

Six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies

“Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” says José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” says Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”

SpaceX launched its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX plans to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

> For decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

Historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy says, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”

Operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he says, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”

There are reasons to be concerned.

Aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

Injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering plans. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

“The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy says. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”

## Conflicting models

One reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” says Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

But in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” says Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”

To quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are currently held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross says. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”

To do better, scientists are developing new models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters , the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

But state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

To validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens says. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross says.

Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens says.

But in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — launched in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

In daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. On Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

Some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency plans to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” says Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens says.

## An enterprise risk

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

If research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” says Ross.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

It was the lithium that gave it away, says Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium showed they were too late.

The team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data showed way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

“That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy says. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

The data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

The number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

Since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

Researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

At the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a big risk to the space industry, says Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

Six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. articleBody:
Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

Via Lobste.rs

articleBody:
Elon Musk speaks via video conference during the New York Times DealBook Summit on Nov. 18, 2026, in New York City. Photo: Adam Gray/Getty Images for The New York Times

After the cresting of a blue wave in the midterm elections earlier this month, it’s officially about-face season, and Elon Musk is the latest major figure to predict which way the wind is blowing. During the New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday — which also featured appearances by the [war](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/ai-strikes-project-maven-civilian-deaths/) profiteer [Palmer Luckey](https://theintercept.com/2025/07/09/trump-big-beautiful-bill-anduril/), New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Hailey Bieber, I guess — the chief of Tesla and SpaceX appeared by video to recast himself as a political moderate.

“I’m not MAGA,” Musk [told](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/18/business/dealbook-summit-news) columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties.”

This “both parties” lip service is deeply revisionist recent history for the man who became the largest individual political donor in U.S. history in [the midterms](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midterm-election-results-voters-democrats/) by spending almost $450 million on Republican candidates, particularly in Texas. Reflecting on that complete and utter waste of unfathomable resources, Musk said he feels “pretty foolish” in retrospect.

“Republicans were routed, and the money I spent — I feel pretty foolish having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” he said. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

Musk went on to say the [Democrats winning the governor and Senate races in Texas](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/james-talarico-ken-paxton-texas-results-trans/) is no crisis for the world’s richest man, who infamously moved Tesla from California to Texas to dodge taxes, regulations, and woke. He also expressed his optimism that Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa would actually be “quite moderate” in office.

This reversal is a telling, but not novel, approach as the rats flee the sinking ship of Donald Trump’s presidency and the Make America Great Again ideology made in his image. Just one day after Republicans were shellacked on Election Day, Vice President JD Vance [planted his 2028 flag by distancing himself](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-vance-midterms-republicans-iran-war/) from the administration he’s still part of to declare that the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran was “the reason we lost.” (Trump is reportedly [not pleased](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/us/politics/vance-trump-iran-2028-election-rubio.html) with Vance throwing him under the bus.) Other Republicans who previously cheered the country into war have also picked up the scent, and now we seem to be left with a war that absolutely no one claims to have wanted in the first place, apparently save for Trump, who said the war was worth losing the midterms.

[Related Musk Warns of Killer AI — While He and the Rest of Silicon Valley Cash In on AI That Kills](https://theintercept.com/2026/05/01/elon-musk-openai-lawsuit-trial/)

As with Vance, cozying up to Trump paid [extraordinary dividends](https://theintercept.com/2025/05/07/elon-musk-trump-pentagon-budget-spacex/) for Musk, until it became a political liability. Musk knew exactly what MAGA was when it was lavishly benefiting his bottom line, and infamously [declared himself](https://www.c-span.org/clip/campaign-2024/elon-musk-makes-surprise-appearance-at-trump-rally/5135526) “not just MAGA, but dark MAGA” while tipping his custom black-on-black Make America Great Again hat at a Trump campaign rally.

As a special government employee in the Trump administration, the Tesla CEO launched the Department of Government Efficiency, better known by its epic meme acronym DOGE, which took a “[slash and burn](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2025/may/05/elon-musk-doge-federal-government)” approach to the federal government under the banners of increasing “efficiency” and eliminating “fraud and abuse.” Musk [empowered](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/08/05/trump-administration-staffer-known-as-big-balls-assaulted-in-dc-00494990) a merry band of half-smart [racists](https://www.npr.org/2025/02/06/nx-s1-5289337/elon-musk-doge-treasury) to lay off [federal employees](https://theintercept.com/2025/03/19/18f-tech-federal-workers-musk-trump-doge/) en masse; handed down [devastating cuts](https://theintercept.com/2026/10/31/trump-south-africa-hiv-aids-funding-cuts/) to foreign aid, [killing](https://hsph.harvard.edu/news/usaid-shutdown-has-led-to-hundreds-of-thousands-of-deaths/) hundreds of thousands of people around the world; eliminated jobs that undergird the social promises that the things we eat and the medicines we take [should be safe](https://www.statnews.com/2026/05/07/fda-rebuilding-after-doge-former-regulators-speaking-out/); and [set scientific research back](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/science/how-trump-is-dismantling-americas-scientific-research-machine.html) untold years.

Musk did all this as part of a project to extract even more wealth from the government — he and his businesses have benefited from a staggering [$38 billion](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/interactive/2025/elon-musk-business-government-contracts-funding/) in public loans, subsidies, contracts, and tax credits over the years — with minimal oversight, and to reshape the work of a functioning federal government into a right wing political project.

The South African businessman, who became the world’s first trillionaire this summer, is deeply invested in [eugenics-based](https://www.npr.org/2025/04/25/nx-s1-5371718/pronatalist-birth-rate-musk-natal-conference) causes like the [pronatalist movement](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/10/rfk-jr-pronatalism-birth-control/), which encourages the *right* kind of Americans to have more kids so “humanity” doesn’t die out. He has pushed the notion that “[white genocide](https://theintercept.com/2025/05/21/south-africa-trump-afriforum-white-refugees/)” is well underway. When he launched his AI chatbot’s competitor to Wikipedia’s “propaganda,” Grokipedia [dubbed itself](https://theintercept.com/2025/11/26/grok-elon-musk-grokipedia-hitler/) “MechaHitler,” praised Adolf Hitler, and listed which races it deemed “[good](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2025/07/new-grok-racism-elon-musk/683515/).”

This is who Elon Musk is, and he hopes Americans have the memory of a fruit fly when it comes to everything he’s [said](https://theintercept.com/2023/10/27/elon-musk-twitter-purchase/) and done in public. But like the [public rejected his campaign](https://theintercept.com/2025/04/12/anti-musk-tesla-activists/) to convince us he was cool, we can’t allow this cynical rebrand to proceed as planned.

Musk is an extremist staring down the barrel of years of courtrooms and congressional hearings who knows the Trumpism he once boosted is a spent political force. He’s experienced no dark night of the soul that’s caused him to meaningfully break from the president or from the far right wing, and no serious person should allow him to deploy that fantasy.

articleBody:
From *Museum De Lakenhal*:

Master I.S., *Man with a Blind Eye*, 164[3]. Collection of Museum De Lakenhal.

Master I.S. is one of the most enigmatic painters of the seventeenth century. The artist, who signed his works with the initials I.S., was active in the Netherlands, although he is also associated with Scandinavia and Eastern Europe. His oeuvre, moreover, displays similarities to the work of artists working in Leiden during the same period. Despite more than a century of art-historical research, the identity of this contemporary of Rembrandt remains unknown. Only an estimated 25 to 35 paintings by the artist are known, most of which are held in international and private collections.

*Man with a Blind Eye* is one of the most important works in this modest oeuvre, alongside major pieces in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts, and the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm. The portrait depicts an older man in three-quarter profile; his damaged left eye turned prominently towards the viewer. His face is rendered with extraordinary precision, yet it is the artist’s treatment of the blind eye that is most striking.

Curator of old masters Janneke van Asperen: ‘Whereas seventeenth century convention typically concealed physical imperfections or emphasised them as curiosities, Master I.S. took a different approach: he painted the eye with the same attentiveness and dignity as the rest of the face.’

More [↗ lakenhal.nl](https://www.lakenhal.nl/en/story/news-museum-de-lakenhal-acquires-masterpiece-man-with-a-blind-eye-by-master-i-s).
