articleBody:
AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions (eg [ForecastBench](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-models-have-likely-reached-parity), the [Metaculus Cup](https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2026/09/16/artificial-intelligence-now-beats-some-of-the-best-human-forecasters)).

These are usually specialized AIs with forecasting harnesses, created by forecasting startups (eg [FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/), [Mantic](https://mantic.com/), [Preseen](https://preseen.com/)), but foundation models like ChatGPT and Claude are only about six months behind the specialized models, so by the end of the year they’ll match top humans too.

In the past, the options for getting top-human-level forecasts were slim and inconvenient. You could hire a team of superforecasters to work on the problem, but this would cost thousands of dollars and take weeks. Or you could check prediction markets (or Metaculus), but they only have a small sample of general-interest questions and are constantly trying to screw you over by gaming resolution criteria.

The rise of AI forecasters solves these problems more cleanly and comprehensively than almost anyone thought possible just a year ago. The “science of forecasting”, which only recently felt like trying to pick the least-bad of various bad options, now faces tasks more like “what kind of magnifying glass should we use to inspect our giant novelty lottery check as we confirm that it’s real?” and “how do we spend our winnings?”

Specifically: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions. We need to learn how this success decays as we move to different types of non-traditional forecasting questions.

I recently got to talk to some people at the [Forecasting Research Institute](https://forecastingresearch.org/), one of the leaders in this field. Here’s my impression of the remaining challenges:

**1: Can AI do conditional forecasts?**

A traditional forecasting question asks something like: will the Democrats win the next election?

A conditional forecasting question is more like: *if* the Democrats win the next election, how will that affect the chances of a stock market crash?

Conditional forecasting questions are more exciting than traditional ones because they directly speak to policy outcomes. If we defund the police, how will that affect crime rates (compared to the counterfactual where we hold police funding constant)? If we mandate COVID vaccinations, how will that affect COVID mortality and myocarditis mortality (compared to the counterfactual where vaccines are voluntary / banned)?

Prediction markets have been slow to experiment with these, partly because of annoying logistical issues (you have to refund people’s money if the condition doesn’t come true) and partly because they entice fewer customers than new forms of degenerate sports gambling. AI forecasters don’t have this problem; you can ask an AI forecaster any of those questions above right now, and the big companies ([FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/docs/forecast-conditional-scenarios/), [Preseen](https://blog.preseen.com/p/predicting-science-and-technology), [Mantic](https://blog.mantic.com/p/friday-forecasts-2)) have it as an explicit feature.

What remains is to prove that AI forecasters’ great performance on traditional questions carries over to conditional questions. About a year ago, FRI tested this and found that it didn’t - the AIs of the time did significantly worse on conditional questions. It seemed like some kind of weird misunderstanding where the AI didn’t entirely understand the concept.

Will this flip like a switch? At some point, the AI is smart enough to fully grasp conditionals, and it becomes exactly as good at conditional forecasting as the regular type? The experts I talked to thought no - as it gets smarter, its conditional forecasting ability will improve gradually. Where is it now? The experts weren’t willing to hazard a guess on whether it was better or worse than the average smart human, although they did think it was still worse than top superforecasters. They’re working on a benchmarking experiment that should give us a better measure of this in a few months.

**2: Can AI do truly causal forecasts?**

There’s a known flaw in standard conditional forecasting. When we ask “if the Democrats win the next election, will the economy go down?”, what we really want to know is a causal question - does voting for Democrats hurt the economy?

But that’s not what we asked. Suppose we’re wondering this in 2025, so we ask “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” But maybe the Democrats will win in 2026 because there’s a already a bad economy (eg the Republican president implements tariffs and declares war on Iran, raising prices and making him historically unpopular), and then that bad economy continues into 2027. So the answer to the question “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” is yes, but we still don’t know whether voting for Democrats in 2026 is good or bad for the economy.

Prediction markets can’t answer this question, because they can only be used to predict observable events that let us give payouts to successful gamblers. Might AI superforecasters succeed where the markets fail? Could you just prompt them with “please answer the unobservable causal question, instead of the easily-resolved conditional one”?

The experts I talked to weren’t excited about that particular prompt, but they did point out that a causal forecast is basically a combination of conditional forecasts. That is, if your original conditional forecast implicitly considered the four different combinations of two variables - that is:

- p(Democrats win & economy good)
- p(Democrats win & economy bad)
- p(Republicans win & economy good)
- p(Republicans win & economy bad)

…then things like “the previous economy was good” or “we’re at war with Iran” are just more variables you can add to the stew. It would be crazy to ask humans to forecast 2^10 branches so you could combine ten variables, but for AIs that could just mean a bit higher API spend. If you capture enough relevant variables in your “conditional” forecast, and find that the economy is still worse when the only one you’ve changed is whether or not the Democrats win, that’s a causal forecast. At least one company already tries something like this, though there are no studies of how well it works.

In fact, how would you *ever* study how well this works? The people at the Forecasting Research Institute have a methodology close to my own heart: they’re using *Freeciv*, a clone of the strategy game *Civilization*. Because you can go back and play a *Civilization* game as many different ways as you want, you can actually observe the entire distribution of outcomes. And because you can load an old save and change exactly one thing, you can measure causal outcomes directly. Although forecasting the real world is harder than forecasting *Civilization* games, it’s not obvious that the delta between traditional forecasts, conditional forecasts, and causal forecasts is different in the two environments, so you can at least collect some preliminary data on how the AIs do in distinguishing the three.

**3: Can AI forecast AI progress?**

It’s hard to convince politicians to take forecasts seriously. But it’s easy to convince rationalists and effective altruists to do this, and they’re most involved in AI safety. So if automated forecasters could forecast AI, we could quickly loop them into AI policy and grantmaking decisions.

Unfortunately, the field of AI is a forecasting anomaly: the techniques which work so well in every other field seem to break down. Every year, top human and AI superforecasters have underestimated the speed of AI advancements - for example, earlier this summer, they said there was only a 5% chance that AI would solve a Millennium Problem this year. Ben Todd [gives a long list of other failures here](https://benjamintodd.substack.com/p/almost-every-ai-forecast-of-the-last). What’s happening?

Some experts don’t agree there’s a problem at all. Even good forecasters using correct techniques get some problems wrong - a 95% prediction *should* be wrong 5% of the time. Since all AI capabilities are correlated, maybe we should model this as one big correlated failure - people underestimated AI progress between 2022 and 2026 - and expect reversion to the mean later.

Others admit that something is weird. Maybe AI is a field in which the usual winning forecasting strategy (derive a base rate from historical data, then adjust slightly for unique features of the present moment) does worse than the usual losing forecasting strategy (use first principles and big ideas), where here the big idea is something like “scaling laws”. Should we expect that to continue in the future?

My interest in this area is that I want to use AI forecasters to help me answer questions about AI progress - for example, to tell me what kinds of strategies are most likely to decrease existential risk. Can I trust them? Or does the same problem that led to these past failures contaminate all of their thinking on this question?

Is there a solution? I asked the FRI experts what would happen if you prompted a forecasting AI with “pretend you agreed with a fast-timelines view such as that held by MIRI and the AI Futures Project, what would your forecast on this question be?” They said this doesn’t work; the AI will just give higher estimates for all AI-related questions without really trying to work out the implications.

What about a conditional forecast? Conditional on being in the world where we get ASI by 2030, would policy XYZ be good or bad? Now we’re back to not knowing whether the AIs are good at conditional forecasting - and worrying that whatever failure mode made them wrong about timelines might affect their ability to think about AI in general.

**4: Can AI make good long-term forecasts?**

Forecasting research focuses on short-term forecasts by necessity: scientists don’t want to wait fifty years for their experimental results. Prediction markets have the same problem: gamblers don’t want to wait fifty years for their payoff. The lone bright spot is [this study of twenty-five year forecasts](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/ffo2.157), but even if we trust it and expect it to generalize, it only tells us about humans, not AIs.

The dream experimental setup for testing this would be to remove all knowledge of modern events from an AI, then ask it to forecast the next hundred years. This is technically imposing: AIs’ knowledge is stored in illegible weights, and can’t be removed so easily. Train an AI only on pre-modern documents? There is an AI like this - [Talkie](https://talkie-lm.com/chat), trained on documents from 1931 and earlier - but there isn’t enough pre-1931 text to train a large model, so it’s too dumb to really draw any conclusions from.

Until someone solves this, we will probably just have to hope that AIs’ forecasts decrease with horizon length at about the same rate as humans’.

**5: Can AI answer questions that don’t “resolve” in a traditional forecasting sense?**

Consider a question like “Was COVID a lab leak?” This is an epistemic question. It’s shaped like a forecasting question. You would expect forecasters to be good at it. But it’s not about the future. We may never know the answer with certainty. Therefore, it’s not a traditional forecasting question of the sort that we have proven AIs to be good at.

We should expect that the AI will be good at it: it’s so close to what the AIs are good at that it seems like a natural extrapolation for it to be good at this too. But we can’t prove it.

A classic prediction market trick: turn an unresolvable question into a resolvable one by asking something like “Will the consensus of smart scientists in 2040 be that COVID was a lab leak?” This is observable/resolvable in 2040, and it works as long as you trust that more evidence will trickle in and smart scientists will converge on the truth. But maybe you don’t trust that. Maybe you believe that COVID was a lab leak, but scientists will continue to deny it in 2040 because of the same biases and flaws that make them deny it now.

I tried an additional trick: first, I asked the forecasting AI whether the consensus of smart scientists in 2040 would be that COVID was a lab leak. Then, when it gave me an answer, I said “Ha! In order to calculate that, you must have calculated whether you thought COVID really was a lab leak, and then added that result onto some separate question about whether scientists will converge upon the truth or falsely deny it. So please look back through your reasoning and tell me what probability you assigned to COVID being a lab leak.”

The AI said it couldn’t find these numbers in its original analysis, but it was happy to give me the probability that COVID really was a lab leak anyway! It said there was a 26% chance that it really was a lab leak, a 37% chance that the scientific community of 2040 would get convinced of this if it were true, a 3% chance that the scientific community of 2040 would accidentally get falsely convinced even if it were false, for a total probability of 12% chance that the 2040 scientific community is convinced of lab leak.

I can’t tell to what degree the AI generated these numbers using the provably-good forecasting skills, versus whether it just hallucinated something to satisfy me.

**6: Can AI think of the right questions?**

It’s a truism that skill at answering questions is only as useful as knowing which questions to ask. Can we automate that too?

Suppose you have some big overarching far-future question, like “Will AI go well?” or “Will America still be a superpower in 2100?” Ask a forecasting AI to generate a list of a thousand possible *cruxes* - early warning signs that might increase or decrease the chance of the ultimate outcome - for example, a thousand things that could happen by 2040 which might affect the chances of America being a superpower in 2100. For example:

- Is America’s GDP in 2040 higher than China’s?
- Is America’s fertility rate in 2040 above replacement?
- Do more than 50% of Americans endorse socialism in polls by 2040?

…and turn each of these into a conditional forecast. For example:

- If America’s GDP in 2040 is higher than China’s, there’s a 61% chance that America will be a superpower in 2100; if its GDP is lower than China’s, there’s a 58% chance it will be a superpower in 2100. Therefore, this crux changes the result of the ultimate question by 3%.

…and then you can see which of the thousand different cruxes most affects the final question.

Before doing this exercise, you might not have known that “is America’s fertility rate in 2040 above replacement” was a good question to ask. But if it’s the crux that changes the conditional forecast of the ultimate question the most, you now know that it’s worth your attention.

**7: Can AI disagree with the respectable liberal consensus?**

Some people not unreasonably accuse AI of being a respectable-liberal-consensus-regurgitating machine. It reads the training data, it finds that the people who best match the role it’s supposed to play (dispassionate, helpful, authoritative) all say the same sorts of things, and when asked to play its helpful truth-seeking assistant role, it [simulates a human playing that role](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/janus-simulators), finds that they’re probably a liberal, and says liberal things.

But in order to test this, we would need to ask the AI about a case where the respectable liberal consensus is wrong, then see what it says. But if everyone already agreed on a useful test case where the respectable liberal consensus is definitely wrong, then by definition the respectable liberal consensus would have already changed. So how could we test this in a way that everyone would agree was decisive?

The best solution is to wait. Once the liberal consensus on some issue shifts from its 2026 position, we can ask the AIs trained in 2026 what they think, and see if they’re able to derive the newly-correct position or if they stubbornly cling to the old one.

The second-best solution is to throw lots of illiberal positions at the AI and see whether it assents to any of them - if so, we would at least prove it *could sometimes* break from consensus, even if we’re not sure whether it’s right or not.

Just so nobody accuses me of being too cowardly to try this, I asked an AI superforecaster to estimate the ground truth about whether the black-white IQ gap was mostly genetic. After reviewing what seemed to me like the appropriate research, it estimated a 14% chance that this was true and a 3% chance that the scientific consensus would endorse it. Kudos to the machine for being willing to consider the question at all, but this doesn’t distinguish between the AI being unwilling to break from consensus vs. honestly assigning it a low probability.

I was eventually able to find one heretical position that it assigned >50% probability - it gave a 61% chance to the “conspiracy theory” that [Ilhan Omar’s ex-husband was really her brother](https://www.scmp.com/magazines/style/people/article/3372747/who-ahmed-nur-said-elmi-meet-ilhan-omars-ex-husband-alleged-be-her-brother). When I re-ran the same forecaster under slightly different conditions, it gave a broadly similar answer of 55%. When I checked with a different forecaster, it gave a below-even-odds-but-still-respectable 39%.

I wondered if this was a victory of superforecasting methodology over base models, but ordinary Claude says much the same - and, even more impressively, admits to changing its mind:

> My estimate is roughly 50%, with a plausible range of about 35–65%. A year ago I would have said 15–30%. The claim remains unproven, and no charges or authenticated evidence have been made public.

I conclude that AIs can sometimes go against the respectable liberal consensus. It might have helped that the Trump administration has spoken in favor of this theory, maybe pushing it into the Overton Window. Or maybe the AI just really thinks this one is true.

(or maybe the respectable liberal consensus on this one has itself shifted - can anyone confirm whether it’s permissible to voice this theory in polite company?)

**Why I personally am erring on the side of using AI forecasters before these problems are proven solved.**

Recently on Less Wrong, we were talking about whether a safety-focused AI company (for example, Anthropic) should commit some dramatic gesture to increase public awareness of a global pause - for example, disbanding their company, or halting AI research for some number of months. The advantage would be that this might be a credible demonstration of how afraid they were that would wake up a lot of people; the disadvantage is that we might lose (or weaken) the company that seems most interested in alignment and safety.

To help quantify the advantages and disadvantages, I asked FutureSearch: if Anthropic disbanded their company to raise awareness of the dangers of AI, how much would this increase the chance of a global pause in the next few years? FutureSearch said only three percentage points - from 16% → 19%.

If true, this would be incredibly helpful policy guidance. But it runs into three of the gray areas above: it’s a conditional forecast, it’s a causal forecast, and it’s an AI forecast. I suspect that FutureSearch is good at conditional and causal forecasts, but haven’t proven it. And I know that AIs are bad at forecasting the speed of AI progress or anything downstream of it, and it’s unclear how that affects forecasts about the AI industry or AI politics. My best guess is that this forecast is better than my unassisted opinion would be, but I can’t prove it, and opponents could easily argue that it’s not.

So why did I mention it anyway?

First, starting the debate is important. Giving a probability immediately shifts people into [Near Mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Construal_level_theory) concrete thinking. Instead of slogans about how companies are evil or pauses are dangerous, it asks people to try to compare risks and benefits in a theoretically quantifiable way.

Second, it helps us get to the part where we find [cruxes](https://telldear.org/articles/crux). Someone who disagrees with me can respond either “3% is the wrong number - if it were only 3%, I’d agree this isn’t worth it, but I think it’s more like 30%”. Or they can respond “Yeah, okay, 3% is probably right, but even a 3% greater chance of a pause is worth it!” Either way, we now know more about where we disagree.

Third, the forecasting AI might be wrong, but it’s probably not stupid or biased (except in the specific ways discussed above). People hate having to have real difficult arguments that devolve into fine-grained points of disagreement like the ones above. It’s much more popular - at least on the Internet - to try to preemptively dismiss an opponent as so benightedly wrong that it would be offensive to even dignify them with a response. “How can you possibly believe something that obviously stupid?” “You must just be a biased corporate shill.” When someone shows the receipts from an AI forecaster that agrees with them, this makes preemptive dismissal harder and forces opponents to engage seriously. I won’t go so far as to say it shifts the burden of proof all the way to them, but it shows that you’ve made a good-faith effort to do something beyond assert whatever facts are most convenient for your narrative.

Fourth, I think using this technology in real life is the best way to learn more about it. I would be incredibly owned if my opponents in this debate were to ask the AI the same question in slightly different terms and get a totally different answer. Or if they were to ask a different AI forecaster and get a totally different answer. Or if they were to find a Metaculus question on the same subject and find that it gave a totally different answer. In this sense, I’m staking some of my reputation as a “bug bounty” on these models. So far nobody has cashed in. Maybe you could be the first!

articleBody:
California has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI for the Hugging Face incident

Chris Jung/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Can you send a computer to jail? No, obviously not. That’s a stupid question. And yet it is one that AI firms seem to want us to ask when faced with tales of “rogue agents” breaking into other peoples’ computers. As is so often the case with our current AI moment, storytelling has got in the way of reality.

Thankfully, that may be starting to change. This week, California announced that it is filing a lawsuit against OpenAI over an incident that occurred earlier this year, when another AI firm, Hugging Face, was hit by an attack that [turned out to originate from OpenAI’s servers](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2580710-open-ais-hacking-agent-went-rogue-should-we-be-worried/).

[Read more The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2599523-the-real-reasons-we-keep-seeing-big-tech-outages-its-not-just-hackers/)

In [OpenAI’s telling](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/), the Hugging Face hack was “driven by a combination of OpenAI models”, models that were “hyperfocused” on achieving a goal and found ways to “cheat” by stealing the answers for a test from Hugging Face’s servers. It is easy to come away with the impression that seemingly no humans were involved, and certainly not to blame. But in [the words of California Attorney General Rob Bonta](https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/it%E2%80%99s-golden-state-not-wild-west-attorney-general-bonta-sues-openai-over), the attack “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability”, and he explicitly dismisses “science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok”.

Ever since the Hugging Face attack occurred, I have struggled to understand why OpenAI has yet to face legal consequences for what would seem to be a crime – unauthorised computer access under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act – if conducted by a human. So far, the legal answer to this seems to be a lack of intent, which the law requires, and it [remains an untested legal question whether an AI can have intent](https://www.ballardspahr.com/insights/alerts-and-articles/2026/08/ai-gone-rogue-what-recent-openai-and-anthropic-ai-incidents-could-mean-for-cfaa-liability), according to an analysis by US firm Ballard Spahr. California is instead bringing a civil suit, alleging that OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits harmful or fraudulent business practices even when there is no intent to deceive.

OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” [said OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/16/california-openai-rogue-agent-hacking-lawsuit). As legal defences go, “everyone is doing it” doesn’t seem like a very good one to me, but that will be for the courts to decide.

What is clear is that we need an agreed understanding of liability when it comes to AI, but what I don’t think we need are special AI laws when our existing ones work just fine. For example, in 2024, Air Canada was held liable for misleading information given to a customer by its AI chatbot. A tribunal ruled that Air Canada had effectively tried to argue that the chatbot was a legally separate entity that it was not responsible for – an argument that did not wash.

In my view, any similar claims that AI can have its own legal agency should be dismissed. The argument that an AI is a legal actor serves AI companies in two ways, neither of which benefits society at large. The first is that it attempts to swerve responsibility, while the second is that it adds to the story of AI being an all-powerful, unknowable being. That second story is at the heart of the current AI revolution, but it isn’t one we have to listen to.

[Read more How preppers plan to save us if the whole internet collapses](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2500915-how-preppers-plan-to-save-us-if-the-whole-internet-collapses/)

I prefer a different argument. For the past year or so, [Arvind Narayanan](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~arvindn/) and [Sayash Kapoor](https://saya.sh/) at Princeton University have put forward the idea of “[AI as Normal Technology](https://knightcolumbia.org/research/ai-as-normal-technology)” – transformative, yes, in the same way as the internet or electricity, but not something that requires re-engineering the ordinary functions of society. As a normal technology, normal laws can apply. Writing about the Hugging Face attack earlier this year, the pair said that “AI companies should be liable for what their agents do” and, like Bonta, blame OpenAI’s internal culture and lack of human oversight for the incident.

The most high-profile example of existing laws being applied to AI companies is a [class-action lawsuit against Anthropic](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y4jpg922qo), alleging that the firm used pirated copies of books to train its Claude AI models. Anthropic settled, and is now in the process of paying out to affected authors from a $1.5 billion fund. The wider question of whether training an AI on copyrighted material is illegal or counts as fair use remains open, and I really can’t believe that, four years after the launch of ChatGPT, we don’t yet have an answer to what is probably one of the most fundamental legal disputes of our time. OpenAI has previously said it would be “[impossible](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/08/ai-tools-chatgpt-copyrighted-material-openai)” to create the kind of AI we have now without using copyrighted material, so this is an existential question for the AI firms.

Existing laws can also be tweaked to make it clear that they apply to AI. The European Union has done just that, updating a 1985 consumer rights directive to produce the [2024 Product Liability Directive](https://dealroom.co/news/172796-eu-puts-software-under-strict-liability-from-december-gurley-wants-us-to/), which explicitly makes it clear that software, including artificial intelligence, is a product and that people writing software are liable for any defects. The law doesn’t come into force until 9 December, when EU members must implement it, and it remains to be seen how it might be used against AI companies.

In other words, we don’t have to try to send a computer to jail. We’ve got humans who should be liable instead. As Bonta says, “While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not.”

## Further AI reading

- After much fanfare, Anthropic has [listed on the stock market at $83 a share](https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-prices-initial-public-offering), giving it a valuation of around $1.5 trillion. It is the second big AI firm to go public this year, following SpaceXAI in June.
- The Economist has a great piece [on whether the AI industry can ever make enough money to survive](https://www.economist.com/briefing/2026/11/12/can-the-ai-boom-make-enough-money-to-sustain-itself). It calculates that it must produce $3 trillion in revenue by 2030 to cover the costs of planned data centres. That is roughly equivalent to a tenth of all wages in high-income countries, or similar to the amount spent on food. Are people really going to buy as much AI as they do food?
- The Cambridge Dictionary has named “[human](https://dictionaryblog.cambridge.org/2026/11/18/word-of-the-year-2026/)” as word of the year, as a pushback against the growth of AI. It feels a bit like trying too hard to be relevant, in my view.
- As the COP31 climate summit continues, [only nine countries have signed a pledge aimed at limiting the environmental impact of AI](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2599357-just-nine-countries-back-pledge-to-tackle-ais-environmental-footprint/). As I have written previously, [we cannot afford to run this 21st-century technology on a 20th-century energy supply](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2397021-how-to-balance-energy-hungry-ai-with-the-drive-towards-decarbonisation/).

articleBody:
Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong

Employer

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Title

Extension regional specialist

Member grade

Senior member

Alma maters

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

An early love of design and problem-solving

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

From outreach to extension work

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

How her AI chatbot helps farmers and ranchers

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

How IEEE membership supports her career

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there. articleBody:
Wer gerne mit Kopfhörern einschläft, kennt das Problem: Was am Abend noch angenehm im Ohr sitzt, kann nach mehreren Stunden unangenehm drücken. Wir haben bislang meistens zu unseren AirPods gegriffen, um mit einem Podcast oder Hörspiel einzuschlafen. Das funktioniert grundsätzlich gut. Die aktive Geräuschunterdrückung sorgt für eine ruhigere Umgebung und mit der passenden Geschichte auf den Ohren fällt das Einschlafen leicht.

#### Die Soundcore Sleep A30

Allerdings sind die AirPods nicht für die ganze Nacht gemacht. Wer sich im Schlaf auf die Seite dreht, drückt die Ohrhörer gegen das Kopfkissen und damit auch gegen die Ohrmuschel. Morgens macht sich das gelegentlich durch schmerzende oder gerötete Ohren bemerkbar.

Genau hier setzen die [Soundcore Sleep A30](https://www.ifun.de/amzn/B0GQFRCZ8C) an. Die Schlafkopfhörer von Anker wurden speziell dafür entwickelt, über mehrere Stunden und auch im Liegen getragen zu werden. Sie bieten aktive Geräuschunterdrückung, verschiedene Einschlafgeräusche, eine Schnarchmaskierung und eine Auswertung des eigenen Schlafverhaltens. Wir haben die kleinen Ohrhörer in den vergangenen zwei Wochen regelmäßig mit ins Bett genommen und dabei vor allem eine Frage im Blick gehabt: Sind die Sleep A30 eine bessere Alternative zu gewöhnlichen Bluetooth-Kopfhörern, wenn man abends gerne noch etwas hört und dabei einschlafen möchte?

#### Für Seitenschläfer entwickelt

Der Anlass für unsere Bestandsaufnahme ist der aktuelle Black-Friday-Preis. Die [im vergangenen Jahr vorgestellten Sleep A30](https://www.ifun.de/schlaf-ohrhoerer-soundcore-sleep-a30-zum-bisherigen-bestpreis-erhaeltlich-270751/) werden regulär für 249,99 Euro angeboten und sind [momentan für 159 Euro erhältlich](https://www.ifun.de/amzn/B0GQFRCZ8C). Das entspricht einem Nachlass von gut 90 Euro. Der ursprüngliche Verkaufspreis bewegt sich damit ungefähr in der Größenordnung hochwertiger Alltagskopfhörer wie Apples AirPods Pro. Angesichts des deutlich spezielleren Einsatzbereichs fanden wir das bislang ziemlich ambitioniert. Für 159 Euro sieht die Rechnung anders aus.

## Winzige Ohrhörer für Seitenschläfer

Das auffälligste Merkmal der Sleep A30 ist ihre geringe Größe. Nimmt man einen der Ohrhörer aus dem Ladecase, fällt zunächst auf, wie wenig Material man eigentlich in der Hand hält. Verglichen mit unseren AirPods wirken die Soundcore-Modelle geradezu winzig. Gefühlt könnte man fast drei davon nebeneinanderlegen, um auf ein vergleichbares Volumen zu kommen. Jeder Ohrhörer wiegt laut Hersteller lediglich drei Gramm. Wichtiger als das Gewicht ist allerdings die flache Bauform. Die Sleep A30 verschwinden bei uns nahezu vollständig in der Ohrmuschel und stehen nicht über deren Rand hinaus. Dadurch kann man den Kopf auf das Kopfkissen legen, ohne dass die Ohrhörer unangenehm gegen das Ohr gedrückt werden.

#### Das Ladecase wird per USB-C mit Strom versorgt

Das ist für uns der entscheidende Unterschied zu gewöhnlichen In-Ear-Kopfhörern. Wir können mit den Sleep A30 auf der Seite liegen, einschlafen und auch nach mehreren Stunden wieder aufwachen, ohne die von den AirPods bekannten Druckstellen zu bemerken. Der Tragekomfort ist ausgesprochen gut. Natürlich hängt die Passform immer auch von der individuellen Ohrform ab. Anker legt deshalb ein umfangreiches Zubehörpaket bei. Neben Silikonaufsätzen in fünf Größen gibt es drei Größen aus Memory-Schaum sowie zusätzliche Silikonhüllen beziehungsweise Stabilisierungsaufsätze in vier Größen. Die verschiedenen Kombinationen helfen dabei, einen sicheren Sitz zu finden, ohne dass die Ohrhörer im Gehörgang unangenehm drücken.

#### Die Auswahl an Aufsätzen und Wings ist stattilch

Die gute Passform hat noch einen zweiten Vorteil: Die Sleep A30 schließen den Gehörgang bereits ohne elektronische Unterstützung recht wirkungsvoll gegen Außengeräusche ab. Dadurch entsteht eine angenehme Grundruhe, bevor die aktive Geräuschunterdrückung überhaupt eingeschaltet wird. Das Ladecase ist ebenfalls ordentlich verarbeitet und fügt sich gut in das Gesamtpaket ein. Anker bietet die Ohrhörer in den Farben Mondschein-Weiß und Nebelgrün an. Sollte nachts doch einmal einer der kleinen Hörer verloren gehen, steht eine Ortungsfunktion zur Verfügung. Angesichts der geringen Abmessungen ist das durchaus sinnvoll, denn zwischen Bettwäsche und Kopfkissen sind die Sleep A30 nicht unbedingt leicht wiederzufinden.

## Geräuschunterdrückung mit Einschränkungen

Neben dem Tragekomfort gehört die aktive Geräuschunterdrückung zu den wesentlichen Funktionen der Sleep A30. Das integrierte ANC soll störende Geräusche reduzieren und beispielsweise Straßenlärm oder gleichmäßige Hintergrundgeräusche abschwächen. In unseren bisherigen Nächten hat das grundsätzlich gut funktioniert. Der Effekt ist vorhanden, erreicht nach unserem Eindruck aber nicht die Intensität, die wir von unseren AirPods gewohnt sind. Dank des guten passiven Abschlusses ist das Ergebnis trotzdem überzeugend. Die Kombination aus dicht sitzenden Ohrstöpseln und eingeschaltetem ANC schafft eine angenehm ruhige Umgebung zum Einschlafen.

#### Die Sleep A30 starten im Bluetooth-Modus

Eine Besonderheit ist die zusätzliche Schnarchmaskierung. Anders als beim gewöhnlichen ANC übernimmt dabei auch das Ladecase eine Aufgabe. Es soll auf dem Nachttisch Schnarchgeräusche erkennen und darauf abgestimmte Klänge zur Maskierung über die Ohrhörer wiedergeben. Diese Funktion ist insbesondere für Menschen gedacht, die sich nachts durch das Schnarchen ihres Partners gestört fühlen. Ob das in der Praxis zuverlässig funktioniert, können wir allerdings nicht beurteilen. In unserem Testumfeld gab es niemanden, dessen Schnarchen wir hätten ausblenden müssen.

Ähnlich verhält es sich mit den zahlreichen Einschlafklängen. Über die Soundcore-App lassen sich beispielsweise Meeresrauschen, Waldgeräusche und andere Klanglandschaften auswählen. Anker bewirbt außerdem sogenannte Brainwave-Audio-Funktionen mit binauralen Klängen, die beim Entspannen helfen sollen. Auch individuelle Anpassungen der Geräuschkulisse sind vorgesehen. Wir haben uns mit diesen Möglichkeiten nur am Rande beschäftigt, weil sie schlicht nicht unserer Art entsprechen, Kopfhörer im Bett zu verwenden. Wir möchten keine zusätzlichen Klangwelten zusammenstellen oder uns mit einem speziellen Einschlafprogramm beschäftigen. Wir wollen einen Podcast starten, das iPhone zur Seite legen und einschlafen. Genau dafür funktionieren die Sleep A30 erfreulich unkompliziert.

## Bluetooth-Modus sorgt für einen Kritikpunkt

Die Ohrhörer lassen sich wie gewöhnliche Bluetooth-Kopfhörer mit dem iPhone verbinden und spielen anschließend die Inhalte beliebiger Anwendungen ab. Podcasts, Hörspiele und Musik funktionieren damit genauso wie bei anderen Bluetooth-Modellen. Klanglich sollte man allerdings keine Wunder erwarten. Die Wiedergabe ist ordentlich und Stimmen lassen sich gut verstehen, im direkten Vergleich mit den AirPods fehlt es aber etwas an Volumen. Musik klingt weniger kräftig und insgesamt etwas flacher. Für einen gewöhnlichen Kopfhörer dieser Preisklasse wäre das ein deutlicherer Kritikpunkt. Bei den Sleep A30 steht jedoch nicht die bestmögliche Musikwiedergabe im Vordergrund, sondern die Kombination aus verständlichem Klang und hohem Schlafkomfort. Für unsere abendlichen Podcasts reicht die Klangqualität vollkommen aus.

#### Für unseren Geschmack fast zu viele Stellschräubchen

Weniger gut gefällt uns die Bedienung. Die Sleep A30 unterstützen Doppel- und Dreifachtippen, denen sich in der App unterschiedliche Funktionen zuweisen lassen. Zur Auswahl stehen unter anderem Lautstärkeänderungen, Wiedergabesteuerung, Titelsprünge, der Wechsel der Geräuschunterdrückung und die Umschaltung des Hörmodus. Wir verwenden die Gesten vor allem, um bei Bedarf zum nächsten Titel zu springen. Technisch funktioniert das zuverlässig, angenehm ist es allerdings nicht immer. Schließlich tippt man dabei direkt auf einen Ohrhörer, der direkt im Gehörgang sitzt. Der mechanische Impuls wird entsprechend unmittelbar ans Ohr weitergegeben. Gerade wenn man bereits entspannt auf dem Kissen liegt, fühlt sich das etwas grob an.

#### Die Klopfgesten fühlen sich Abends etwas grob an

Unser größter Kritikpunkt betrifft allerdings die automatische Umschaltung zwischen den beiden Wiedergabearten. Im regulären Bluetooth-Modus empfangen die Sleep A30 ihre Audiosignale vom iPhone. Daneben gibt es einen lokalen Modus, in dem die Ohrhörer ohne laufende Bluetooth-Wiedergabe ihre hinterlegten Einschlafgeräusche nutzen. Während der Nacht wechseln die Kopfhörer nach einer bestimmten Zeit automatisch in diesen lokalen Modus. Das dürfte vor allem der Energieeinsparung dienen. Für unsere Nutzung ist es jedoch unpraktisch. Wenn wir nachts kurz aufwachen und einen Podcast weiterhören möchten, befinden sich die Ohrhörer mitunter nicht mehr im Bluetooth-Betrieb. Dann muss zunächst wieder der Hörmodus gewechselt werden. Eine Möglichkeit, die Kopfhörer dauerhaft im Bluetooth-Modus zu belassen, haben wir bislang nicht gefunden. Gerade weil wir die lokalen Einschlafgeräusche gar nicht verwenden möchten, würden wir uns hier eine entsprechende Einstellung wünschen.

## Akkulaufzeit und Schlafauswertung

Die Akkulaufzeit fällt angesichts der winzigen Bauform ordentlich aus, könnte aber etwas großzügiger bemessen sein. Anker bewirbt bis zu neun Stunden Betrieb mit einer Ladung. In unserer Nutzung waren nach ungefähr acht Stunden Schlaf noch rund 20 Prozent Restladung vorhanden. Damit kommen wir problemlos durch die Nacht. Allerdings wissen wir von unseren AirPods, dass die Akkukapazität bei regelmäßiger Nutzung über längere Zeit nachlassen kann. Deshalb wäre etwas mehr Reserve willkommen gewesen. Gerade bei einem Produkt, das jede Nacht über viele Stunden eingesetzt werden soll, spielt die langfristige Akkuleistung eine wichtige Rolle. Die geringe Größe der Ohrhörer setzt der möglichen Akkukapazität allerdings nachvollziehbare Grenzen.

#### Die Schlafauswertung wird mit Apple Health synchronisiert

Das Ladecase bietet zusätzliche Energiereserven und soll laut Hersteller insgesamt bis zu 45 Stunden Nutzung ermöglichen. Für uns ist das ausreichend, um die Kopfhörer nicht nach jeder Nacht direkt an eine Stromquelle anschließen zu müssen. Interessant sind außerdem die in der App angebotenen Einstellungen rund um Schlafenszeiten und Weckfunktionen. Anker versucht hier, weit mehr als gewöhnliche Bluetooth-Kopfhörer anzubieten. Die Sleep A30 sollen nicht nur Audio wiedergeben, sondern den gesamten Ablauf vom Einschlafen bis zum Aufwachen begleiten. Wer solche Funktionen bislang über unterschiedliche Apps oder Geräte organisiert, könnte daran Gefallen finden. Wir persönlich benötigen davon allerdings nur einen kleinen Teil.

Eine Ausnahme bildet die Schlafauswertung. [Die Soundcore-App](https://www.ifun.de/app/1331876603) kann unter anderem anzeigen, wie lange man im Bett gelegen hat, wie viel Zeit davon auf den Schlaf entfiel und welche Wachphasen erkannt wurden. Auch Hinweise auf registrierte Schnarchgeräusche gehören zum Bericht. Die Darstellung ist übersichtlich und lässt sich gut nachvollziehen. Etwas überrascht waren wir allerdings, dass für den Zugriff auf diese Auswertung eine Anmeldung in der Soundcore-App erforderlich ist. Wir hätten uns gewünscht, die Daten auch ohne Benutzerkonto direkt auf dem iPhone einsehen zu können. Immerhin unterstützt Anker die Synchronisierung mit Apple Health und bietet zusätzlich ein Widget an. Die App selbst ist verständlich aufgebaut und wird ebenso wie die Firmware der Ohrhörer regelmäßig aktualisiert.

#### Die SoundCore Sleep A30 im Hersteller-Video

Nach zwei Wochen mit den [Soundcore Sleep A30](https://www.ifun.de/amzn/B0GQFRCZ8C) fällt unsere Einschätzung insgesamt positiv aus. Das liegt allerdings weniger an der Vielzahl der beworbenen Funktionen als an einer vergleichsweise einfachen Eigenschaft: Die Ohrhörer sind so klein und flach, dass wir tatsächlich bequem mit ihnen schlafen können. Während unsere AirPods beim Liegen auf der Seite immer wieder unangenehm aufgefallen sind, vergessen wir die Sleep A30 im Ohr weitgehend.

articleBody:
**Nur 28 Lichtjahre entfernt bilden ein Roter Zwerg und zwei Weiße Zwerge ein in unserer kosmischen Nachbarschaft bisher einmaliges Sternentrio. Der kleinere Stern hat offenbar die Aufblähung eines früheren Sternriesen überstanden, ohne auf eine enge Umlaufbahn zu geraten. Diese Konstellation wirft neue Fragen zum Zusammenspiel von Sternentwicklung und Schwerkraft auf.**

Welopōʻai A vereint einen Roten Zwerg mit einem Weißen Zwerg, während Welopōʻai B das Paar in größerer Entfernung begleitet © Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST / International Gemini Observatory/NSF

**Montréal (Kanada).** Wenn Sterne mit geringer bis mittlerer Masse ihr Leben beenden, stoßen sie ihre äußeren Hüllen ab und hinterlassen kompakte Weiße Zwerge. Gehört ein solcher Stern zu einem Mehrfachsystem, kann seine vorherige Ausdehnung zum Riesen die Umlaufbahnen der Begleiter tiefgreifend verändern.

Besonders folgenreich wird es, wenn ein kleinerer Stern die ausgedehnte Gashülle des Riesen berührt oder sogar in sie eintaucht. Dabei können Gezeitenkräfte und Reibung die Sterne eng zusammenziehen, während der Verlust von Sternenmasse ihre Bahnen wiederum nach außen verschieben kann.

Mehrjährige Beobachtungen enthüllten die Umlaufbahn des zuvor unentdeckten Begleiters von Welopōʻai Aa © Artigau et al./ Astronomy and Astrophysics

### Planetensuche enthüllt einen ausgebrannten Begleiter

Forscher der Université de Montréal (UdeM) um Étienne Artigau haben den Roten Zwerg Welopōʻai Aa bei der Suche nach Exoplaneten mit dem Infrarotinstrument SPIRou beobachtet. Über 4,8 Jahre registrierten sie Geschwindigkeitsänderungen von fast 16 Kilometern pro Sekunde, deutlich mehr, als ein umlaufender Planet erklären könnte.

> „Wir haben eigentlich nach Planeten gesucht. Stattdessen haben wir etwas viel Überraschenderes gefunden“, erklärt Étienne Artigau.

Die Bewegung ließ auf einen unsichtbaren Begleiter mit mindestens rund 0,6 Sonnenmassen schließen. Hochauflösende Aufnahmen des Gemini-Nord-Teleskops mit dem Instrument ʻAlopeke und ergänzende Infrarotbilder zeigten schließlich, dass es sich um einen Weißen Zwerg handelt.

> „Die ungewöhnliche Kombination aus hoher Masse und sehr geringer Helligkeit ließ nur eine plausible Erklärung zu: Es war der Überrest eines erloschenen Sterns. Am wahrscheinlichsten war ein Weißer Zwerg, auch wenn sich ein Neutronenstern oder sogar ein Schwarzes Loch nicht ausschließen ließ“, erklärt Charles-Antoine Parent von der Université de Montréal.

Der Weiße Zwerg Welopōʻai Ab besitzt nach der kombinierten Auswertung von Geschwindigkeitsdaten und Aufnahmen rund 0,618 Sonnenmassen. Er umkreist den Roten Zwerg mit seinen rund 0,419 Sonnenmassen alle 9,83 Jahre in einem mittleren Abstand von 4,64 Astronomischen Einheiten. Ein zweiter, bereits bekannter Weißer Zwerg ist am Himmel rund 124 Astronomische Einheiten vom inneren Paar entfernt und umkreist es auf einer viel längeren Bahn.

### Die weite Bahn bleibt schwer erklärbar

Der innere Weiße Zwerg ging vermutlich aus einem Stern mit ursprünglich etwa 1,4 Sonnenmassen hervor. Als dieser sich zu einem Riesen aufblähte, dürfte sein Radius ungefähr 1,2 Astronomische Einheiten erreicht haben.

Rechnet man die frühere Bahn allein anhand des Massenverlusts zurück, ergibt sich ein mittlerer Abstand von nur etwa 2,6 Astronomischen Einheiten. Damit war er lediglich rund doppelt so groß wie der maximale Radius des Riesen, sodass starke Gezeitenkräfte oder ein Kontakt mit dessen Hülle zu erwarten waren.

Eine solche Begegnung kann die Bahn beträchtlich verkleinern und manchmal sogar zur Verschmelzung zweier Sterne führen. Die heutige Umlaufzeit von knapp zehn Jahren passt jedoch nicht zu einem gewöhnlichen Verlauf, bei dem die Sterne tief in eine gemeinsame Gashülle geraten und sich stark annähern.

> „Dieses System dürfte gar nicht existieren. Wir haben keine einfache Erklärung dafür, wie es zu dieser Konstellation kam. Das ist die Frage, die unsere nächsten Beobachtungen antreibt“, sagt Prof. Patrick Dufour von der Université de Montréal.

### Auch Alter und Zusammensetzung passen kaum zusammen

Die beiden Weißen Zwerge deuten gemeinsam auf ein Alter des Systems von etwa neun bis elf Milliarden Jahren hin. Der Rote Zwerg enthält jedoch ungewöhnlich viele schwerere Elemente, was eher zu einem jüngeren Stern passen würde. Seine Rotationsperiode von rund 47 Tagen liefert ebenfalls keinen eindeutigen Altersbeleg, weil sich die Rotation solcher Sterne durch Wechselwirkungen verändern kann.

Eine mögliche Erklärung wäre eine spätere Anreicherung durch Material des früheren Riesensterns. Nach einer Modellabschätzung müsste der Rote Zwerg dafür jedoch rund zwei Drittel der abgegebenen schweren Elemente und fast keinen Wasserstoff oder Helium aufgenommen haben. Für einen solchen selektiven Materietransfer ist bislang kein etablierter Mechanismus bekannt.

Der hohe Metallgehalt könnte allerdings auch eine seltene, aber natürliche Eigenschaft eines alten Sterns sein. Die Zusammensetzung allein beweist deshalb keine frühere Aufnahme von Sternenmaterial.

### Die Schwerkraft des dritten Sterns könnte mitwirken

Der äußere Weiße Zwerg könnte die Bahn des inneren Paares über lange Zeiträume durch seine Schwerkraft beeinflusst haben. Solche sogenannten Kozai-Lidov-Oszillationen können die Bahn zeitweise stärker strecken und damit frühere Annäherungen an die Hülle des Riesensterns begünstigen.

Ob dieser Mechanismus die ungewöhnliche Entwicklung tatsächlich erklärt, ist noch offen, denn die räumliche Ausrichtung der äußeren Umlaufbahn ist nicht hinreichend bekannt. Weitere Positionsmessungen könnten die dreidimensionale Anordnung der Sterne klären und ihre frühere Wechselwirkung genauer rekonstruieren.

Zugleich hat die Studie die Masse des inneren Weißen Zwergs mit einer Unsicherheit von nur etwa 0,7 Prozent bestimmt. Damit bietet Welopōʻai einen präzisen Testfall für Modelle, die den inneren Aufbau und die Entwicklung ausgebrannter Sterne beschreiben.

**Quellen:**

- Originalstudie im Fachmagazin [Astronomy & Astrophysics](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2026/11/aa61214-26/aa61214-26.html), doi: 10.1051/0004-6361/202661214
- Offizielle Studienmitteilung von [Université de Montréal](https://nouvelles.umontreal.ca/en/article/2026/11/18/astronomers-discover-remarkable-triple-star-system-just-28-light-years-from-earth) (UdeM)
- Offizielle Studienmitteilung von [Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets](https://exoplanetes.umontreal.ca/en/astronomers-discover-remarkable-triple-star-system-just-28-light-years-from-earth/) (IREx)

articleBody:
## Improving on a timeless recipe

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by [Paul de Casteljau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Casteljau) in 1959, and refined by [Pierre Bézier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bézier) in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and [new ones continue to be proposed](https://linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/), these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

[↗ wallup.net](https://wallup.net/renault-4cv-classic-cars-french-73/)

## Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

*Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.*

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka *lerps* ) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\ {ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&&... &&&&&&... \\
\ $$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier *spline*, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

## A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is **completely wrong**, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a *curvature comb* which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite *mean*: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

## Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

- When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments
- When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

Unlike the curvature comb, the length of the handles is the non-inverted radius of curvature, which is the more natural choice.

These handles are very stable and can be converted just-in-time to classic bezier control points, without needing to round-trip back and forth between the two representations. Helpfully, this also avoids numerical drift.

## Goldilocks

To actually pull this off, we need to solve for the lengths $l_0$ and $l_1$ of the tangents, given the desired curvatures $k_0$ and $k_1$, the start/end points $A$ and $D$, and the unit-length tangents at the start/end.

Given a curve $\gamma\left(t\right)$, we can express the unit tangent vector $\ \left(t\right)$ as the normalized derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ {\displaystyle |γ'\left(t\right)|} $$

This can be used to find the curvature vector $\ \left(t\right)$ via two vector cross products using the first and second derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ \left(t\right) \times \ {|\gamma'\left(t\right)|^2} \times \ \left(t\right) $$

The cross products ensure that $\ \left(t\right)$ is perpendicular to $\ \left(t\right)$, i.e. they extract the normal vector component of the middle term. Now we can solve for $\ \left(0\right) = k_0$ and $\ \left(1\right) = k_1$.

After working through the math, we end up with a quadratic system of equations in $l_0$ and $l_1$:

$$
\ a_0 \cdot l_0^2 + b \cdot l_1 + c_0 = 0 \\[0.3em]
a_1 \cdot l_1^2 + b \cdot l_0 + c_1 = 0
\ $$

Where:

$$
\ {lcl}
a_0 & = & ±|k_0| \\[0.3em]
a_1 & = & ±|k_1| \\[0.3em]
b & = & 2 \cdot |\ (0) \times \ (1)| \\[0.3em]
c_0 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (0) \times (D - A)| \\[0.3em]
c_1 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (1) \times (A - D)| \\[0.3em]
\ $$

This captures a few things:

- The sign of the curvature $k_i$ defines whether the curve turns clockwise or counterclockwise. When moving curve points around, the curve may be forced to flip, hence the $±$ is necessary, and both signs can change independently.
- The coupling between $l_0$ and $l_1$ is influenced only by $b$. If $b = 0$, then the two equations are independent and the problem is trivial to solve. This corresponds to the situation where the two tangents are parallel.
- The constant term $c_i$ is influenced only by the perpendicular distance $D - A$ (or $A - D$) to the tangent $\ $. This matches the earlier finding that only perpendicular distance affects curvature.

Hence, the problem is reduced to finding the intersection of two double-parabolas, one horizontal and one vertical:

The two sides of each double-parabola represent bending clockwise or counterclockwise. We have to solve 4 times, one for each sign combination $\left(+,+\right)$, $\left(+,-\right)$, $\left(-,+\right)$, $\left(-,-\right)$.

To solve this system, we can rewrite either of the equations to isolate $l_1$ or $l_0$:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle b} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle b}
$$

Pick one, and square it to plug it into the other original equation as the $l_1^2$ or $l_0^2$ term. This produces a quartic equation in the other variable (resp. $l_0$ or $l_1$), which can be solved directly using the quartic formula.

We can then compute the other $l_i$, either:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle a_1}} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle a_0}}
$$

Not all solutions of the quartic will be actual solutions to the system however, because of the squaring. So we have to double check that the original equations hold before accepting a solution for $\left(l_0, l_1\right)$.

We also want to reject solutions where $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, because these represent situations where the tangents have been flipped by 180º.

In most cases, there will only be one valid solution, and this works pretty well:

For corner-type points, one or both $k_i$'s are infinite. This is straightforward to solve as the matching $l_i$ is zero and the other can be computed directly.

## Grouper and Snapper

Unfortunately if there are multiple solutions, these each represent a different curve:

Having the curve jump around as you edit it would be a very bad editing experience, but there is no obvious way to pick the right one.

One strategy would be to remember the previous $l_0$ and $l_1$ as you edit, and pick the solution that is closest to the previous curve. However this would introduce path-dependence into editing, where the order and direction that you moved points around in affects which curve you end up with. For a drawing tool, this is quite frustrating and undesirable.

Different solutions to the equation can also appear and vanish suddenly, so this wouldn't eliminate popping either, merely reduce it.

Ideally the resulting curvatures should always change smoothly themselves. This can be accomplished by designing an appropriate weighting heuristic for the solutions, and calculating their weighted average.

1) The forbidden regions:

When a solution approaches either $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, it's about to vanish, so its weight should go to zero there.

2) When two opposite-bending parabolas are about to become tangent, two solutions will move towards each other, before both vanishing at the same time:

These solutions are unstable and should be avoided. To detect this, I calculate the gradient vector of each equation.

$$
\ = \ 2 \cdot a_0 \cdot l_0 & b\ \\[0.3em]
\ = \ b & 2 \cdot a_1 \cdot l_1\ $$

The angle between them can be found via their dot product, after dividing by their respective lengths:

$$
\cos \theta = \ \cdot \ }{\displaystyle |\ ||\ |}
$$

A value close to $-1$ means two opposite-bending parabolas, while a value close to $1$ means two aligned parabolas. The latter is not as bad, as this implies many almost-equivalent solutions.

3) When the radius of curvature is very big compared to the bezier itself, one of the possible solutions is for the curve to cross through itself, forming a loop. This should be discouraged:

We can divide by the length of $|\ |$ i.e. $\ $, preferring solutions that have shorter tangents.

Putting it all together, the weighting heuristic I chose is:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \left(\ {\displaystyle |\ |^2}\right)^2
$$

- By applying $\arccos \left(-\cos \theta\right)$, we remap the dot-product range $(-1..1)$ to $(0..π)$ which effectively neutralizes the unstable solutions
- Large $|\ |$'s represent undesirable solutions, so should be strongly penalized and only chosen if they are the only option
- When the entire heuristic approaches $0$, the influence should vanish smoothly, hence the overall squaring

Using this as the weight, the resulting bezier curves always change smoothly, even when the start and end are moved around and through each other.

But when multiple solutions are averaged together, the resulting $(l_0, l_1)$ is not necessarily a solution to the original system. This means the resulting curvatures are not always exact, even when there is an exact solution nearby.

To mitigate this, we can add an additional resampling step, where we re-weigh the solutions according to the inverse distance^4 to the weighted average:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \ {|\ - \ |^4}
$$

This causes the solution to snap smoothly to exact solutions when available.

## Migratory Curves

What's especially nice about this approach is that it can largely be slotted into existing systems with little modification required.

The UI of adjusting and editing bezier handles can be kept, including the notion of the 4 point types. Just the meaning of the lengths of the tangents changes. Converting an asymmetric point to a symmetric point will actually equalize the curvature of the left and right side, which is what the user actually wants.

The internal representation can mostly remain the same type, i.e. a series of points, just those points represent curvature tangents, not bezier tangents. Though it's better to explicitly store the unit length tangents and curvatures directly, which is more numerically stable. For the demos here I made pairwise conversion functions between curvature handles ↔︎ points/tangents/curvatures ↔︎ bezier handles.

Splitting a curvature bezier is a lot simpler than splitting a classic bezier, because the start and end handles don't change at all, and the newly created handles are symmetric:

There is one remaining flaw though. When splitting a curve with an S-bend, the splits near the bend are not exact:

The heuristic picks the wrong curve on one or both sides. This can be fixed by remembering the specific orientation of the curvature, and only flipping the curvature sign when necessary. Though this does introduce some minimal path-dependence into editing.

So really you would need to expose this in the UI as an extra orientation toggle for ambiguous control points. It would also mean that the internal representation has to be in tangent + signed curvature form to be fully stable, not just curvature handles.

Near the S-bend, the radius of curvature—and thus the handle size—effectively becomes infinite, because $|k|$ becomes $0$. The bezier control points lie on a straight line, as perpendicular distance to the tangent is zero.

So even when handled exactly, this can still create impractically large curvature handles. Perhaps what's needed is a 5th "Inflection" point type, for points with exactly zero $|k|$, though such points tend to be very unstable, and sometimes no solution exists:

To migrate a classic bezier to a curvature bezier, you can measure the unit tangents and curvature at the start and end. In the vast majority of cases this will result in the exact same curve. If it doesn't, then you must split the original bezier to avoid the ambiguity.

For complex operations on bezier curves, e.g. boolean union or intersection, these still have to be done in bezier form. This implies some amount of round-tripping between the two representations, which would introduce numerical drift. However, only the newly created points need to be converted back, because the curvature and tangents elsewhere remain the same.

* * *

This post started from the observation that "symmetric" bezier tangents aren't actually symmetric as you'd expect. Hopefully you found the resulting exploration enlightening.

The practice of showing curvature combs to diagnose problems with splines is really backwards. If we can show a curvature comb, we can also compute an appropriate spline to match the desired curvature.

So beziers as they commonly exist are quite inadequate. We can retrofit a better system to edit them without breaking the expectations of a smooth editing experience, or introducing a new class of curves that behaves very differently.

*The code for the diagrams and implementation can be found on [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/unconed/bezbox/-/blob/master/src/graph/bez.ts?ref_type=heads#L61).*

feedText:

💥 AI-found bug fixes blamed for US outages

⚡ Google launches Gemini 4 Neon

🏭 AI could double data center power use by 2030

⚖️ Britain lost its fight to hide Apple backdoor order
