## How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/19/loan-out-companies/#termination-of-transfer)

There's a seeming paradox to copyright. For 50 years (starting with the 1976 Copyright Act) legislatures have monotonically expanded copyright, so that today, copyright lasts longer, covers more works, restricts more activities, and provides for harsher penalties for infringement, all in the name of protecting artists.

After 50 years of this, artists are, on average, *poorer* than we were in 1976, but the media companies we sell our work to are *much, much* richer. They're larger and more profitable, and yet our wealth (both in absolute terms and as a share of media company profits) has declined.

This may feel like a paradox, but it's actually easy to understand unless you've had the self-inflicted neurological injury we call "getting an econ degree." That's an injury that leaves the sufferer incapable of reasoning about or even perceiving *power*.

If you've avoided that fate, then you can see that when an artist sells to one of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies or one ebook/audiobook company, that artist has very little leverage. In that market, giving an artist more to bargain *with* is just giving them more to bargain *away*.

I have often compared giving more copyright to creative workers trapped in this oligopoly to giving a bullied schoolchild extra lunch money. No matter how much money you give that kid, they're not going to get fed. The bullies just take whatever money you give to the kid. Indeed, if you indirectly transfer enough money to the bullies, they'll pay for a global ad campaign: THINK OF THE HUNGRY SCHOOLCHILDREN! THEY NEED MORE LUNCH MONEY!

This is exactly what has happened with 50 years of successive copyright expansions. Every time Congress gave a new copyright to creative workers, the cartels we bargain with just amended their non-negotiable contracts to force us to hand over that new right for no extra payment. Then they used those new rights to get richer and more powerful, and to exert more control over the distribution channels we need to reach our audiences, which made us poorer. Then Congress heard their THINK OF THE STARVING ARTISTS pitch, and gave us more copyright…which we promptly handed over to our bosses. Lather, rinse, repeat.

If you want to feed a hungry schoolkid, you have to change the *structure* of the system. For example, you might open a credit account with the school lunchroom, so that the kid never has any cash for the bullies to take. Likewise, if you want to help artists get more money, you need to make a systemic change.

There are lots of ways to do this. In 2022, Rebecca Giblin and I co-wrote a book called *Chokepoint Capitalism*, and we devoted *half* of the book to detailed, shovel-ready proposals for ways to alter the copyright system to benefit artists, not our bosses:

[https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx](https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx)

That section includes a chapter on something called "termination of transfer," which was introduced with the 1976 Copyright Act. Under termination of transfer, any copyright contract (a "transfer") can be unilaterally canceled ("termination") by any creator after 35 years. So even if you sign away your copyrights for the entire term (your life plus 70 years), you can tear up that agreement after 35 years by notifying the company you sold your rights to and then filing some paperwork with the US Copyright Office:

[https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/](https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/)

We got *really* excited about termination. For one thing, Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject. In 2021, she co-authored the landmark study "U.S. Copyright Termination Notices 1977-2020: Introducing New Datasets," published in the *Journal of Empirical Legal Studies*:

[https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3880708](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3880708)

Termination is a uniquely efficient way to make artists richer at the expense of our bosses. The fact that you can only exercise it after 35 years produces some very interesting effects. First, consider that almost no copyrighted works are commercially viable after 35 years (most copyrighted works cease to generate income after 14 years or less, this being the original term of copyright in the USA). The rare works that continue to generate revenue 35 years after their release are the "perennial favorites" that drive a vast share of media industry profits.

Now consider that, between the realities of the human lifespan and the amount of time it takes most artists to master their craft, any given work you produced 35 years ago is almost certainly from the start of your career. That's the moment in which artists are typically *most* vulnerable. Artists at the start of their careers are unknown quantities and are often crammed into signing *terrible* deals, even worse than the "standard" media deal.

Put these two facts together and you'll see that termination is disproportionately applicable to a body of work that is wildly profitable for media companies, *but* the creators of those works are entitled to *even less* of the money it generates, thanks to the crummy contracts they were railroaded into because they were just starting out when they made them.

Termination lets creators cancel those crummy contracts, take back their rights, and bargain for a better deal with the old media company (or a new one). This time, they bargain from a position of unassailable strength, due to the fact that they're selling a property that's proven itself to be a perennial profit-generator.

Best of all, you can't bargain out of termination. Even if you sign a contract that says, "I promise I will not exercise my termination of transfer right," you can *still* exercise your termination right. This is a structural change, like the parent who opens a charge account with the school cafeteria so that their kid no longer has any lunch money to hand over to the bullies. The way Congress wrote termination into the 1976 Act, it doesn't matter how hard the media company you initially sign with twists your arm, you literally *can't* promise them you won't use your termination right 35 years after signing.

That's where that landmark study Rebecca co-authored comes in. Rebecca and her co-authors found that termination was working exactly the way Congress intended: it was making artists richer. It's particularly helpful to marginalized creative workers, for example, Black "heritage" musicians who were railroaded into terrible contracts that meant they never got a dime for decades of airplay, covers and samples of their hits. If this sounds familiar, you might be thinking of my 2024 technothriller *The Bezzle*, where I use this as a key plot point:

[https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250865878/thebezzle/](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250865878/thebezzle/)

Genre writers have really benefited from termination. The authors of massively popular YA series like *The Baby-Sitters Club* and *Sweet Valley High* claimed back their rights under termination. So did Peter Straub and Stephen King, who took back the rights to their early books and resold them on *much* more favorable terms. Just the *threat* of termination forced Disney to make giant payouts to Marvel's key creators, like Stan Lee, Steve Ditko and Jack Kirby:

[https://deadline.com/2023/12/marvel-court-termination-disney-spider-man-dr-strange-1234843941/](https://deadline.com/2023/12/marvel-court-termination-disney-spider-man-dr-strange-1234843941/)

In *Chokepoint Capitalism*, Rebecca and I point out that most of the 1976 Copyright Act (like longer copyright terms) has failed to help artists, but termination is the rare exception, a proven effective way to put money in artists' pockets. Which is weird, because in the 50 years since the 1976 Act, Congress has repeatedly doubled down on pretty much every measure in the Act, *except* the one thing that is empirically proven to be good for artists. Of course, all that failed stuff in the 1976 Act is good for giant media companies, and termination is bad for those companies, so it's not hard to see why there's been so little legislative appetite to beef up termination.

But it's also easy to see how we'd do that beefing up. In the original draft of the Copyright Act, termination was automatic, and kicked in after 20 years (meaning that 20 years after signing any contract, every creator would automatically get back all the rights they sold in the contract). The final version of the Act watered down termination so it kicks in after 35 years, and even then only after the artist does a ton of paperwork.

Giving artists the termination rights they were promised in the initial draft of the 1976 Act is a no-brainer. But that's not what we've gotten from Congress. To the extent that Congress acted on termination, it was to *take it away* from musicians. In 1999, an obscure Congressional staffer named Mitch Glazier snuck a clause into an unrelated bill that made it impossible for most recording artists to exercise their termination rights. This was such a scandal that Congress had to convene a special session to cancel this amendment and restore musicians' rights, and Glazier was drummed out of his Congressional job:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Glazier#Work_for_hire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Glazier#Work_for_hire)

Don't worry, Glazier landed on his feet: he was immediately hired by the RIAA (the record industry's lobbying arm) as their new CEO and there he perches even today, making more than $1.4m/year to do a job he continues to describe as "defending artists":

[https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131669037](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131669037)

With Glazier as the standard-bearer for "artists' rights," it's no wonder that creators haven't gotten a better deal on termination out of Congress.

Indeed, things are looking very bad for termination of transfer right now, thanks to a string of court decisions that pit a common tax strategy employed by freelance creatives against termination of transfer.

Like many freelancers, creative workers often incorporate limited liability companies that contract with the companies that employ them. These companies then pass the revenue on to creators as "partner distributions." There are lots of reasons to like this arrangement: it simplifies probate and estate planning, helps creators fund their pensions, and offers tax deductions for expenses like a home office or research trips.

This arrangement is especially common in Hollywood, where the companies that writers, directors, and other creative trades work through are called "loan-out companies" (because the company employs the creative, and "loans them out" to movie studios).

Movie studios and other media companies have recently seized on the existence of these loan-out companies to argue (with a great deal of success) that the existence of these loan-out companies nullifies termination of transfer.

You see, termination of transfer is only available for creative works that are independently produced and licensed through a copyright contract. Termination does *not* apply to "works made for hire," such as the emails and reports you might write in the course of your duties as an employee. The logic here is that termination of transfer is supposed to help artists get more out of their copyrights, but forcing (say) an insurance company to disgorge all the memos you wrote for them 35 years ago would introduce chaos and uncertainty without helping workers in any way (there's not exactly a market for 35-year-old insurance company memos).

The media companies' argument goes that creative workers are employees of their loan-out companies, so if you sell a script or a novel through your LLC, that is a "work made for hire" that the LLC owned, and that means that it can't exercise your termination of transfer rights to get that work back after 35 years.

Aaron Moss, who edits the Copyright Lately website, has been beating the drum about this for years, calling it "a ticking time bomb for copyright-intensive industries." He's been repeatedly vindicated, most recently through a bizarre dispute between Michael Mann, the director and writer of 1995's blockbuster *Heat*, and New Regency, the studio that released it:

[https://copyrightlately.com/michael-mann-heat-copyright-termination/](https://copyrightlately.com/michael-mann-heat-copyright-termination/)

Moss's article on the dispute is a very entertaining read, unpacking a decidedly weird gambit that Mann has deployed to regain the rights to *Heat*. But the most important part of the article is the way it describes the state of play for termination's ongoing collision with loan-out companies. The studios and labels have racked up a string of wins using this gambit, with creators settling their cases or losing outright. Take musician John Waite's bid to get his rights back from UMG: the judge ruled in UMG's favor, saying, "people cannot use a corporate structure for some purposes – eg taking advantage of tax benefits – and then disavow it for others":

[https://copyrightlately.com/copyright-termination-loan-out-corporations/](https://copyrightlately.com/copyright-termination-loan-out-corporations/)

This is a bad situation. Termination is a fantastic, artist-friendly legal doctrine, one that lets creators claim back some of our most cherished media. Termination gave George Clinton the rights back to his entire catalog (his sleazy ex-manager forged Clinton's signature on a rights assignment). It let Gary K Wolf take Roger Rabbit back from Disney:

[https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way](https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way)

It let the *Spinal Tap* crew get a *much* better deal out of their studio, and paved the way for 2025's (criminally underrated) *Spinal Tap II*:

[https://www.nme.com/news/film/this-is-spinal-tap-creators-and-studiocanal-settle-rights-dispute-2757087](https://www.nme.com/news/film/this-is-spinal-tap-creators-and-studiocanal-settle-rights-dispute-2757087)

The Wachowskis just announced that they're going to exercise their termination rights to get *The Matrix* back from Warner Brothers, which is now owned by Trump's cronies, thanks to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's decision to let the Warner-Paramount merger go through:

[https://puck.news/hollywood/2026/11/the-wachowskis-are-reclaiming-the-matrix](https://puck.news/hollywood/2026/11/the-wachowskis-are-reclaiming-the-matrix)

This clash between termination and loan-outs has been on my radar since 2021, when the artist-defending media lawyer Jeff Trexler told me about it over drinks at Comic-Con. I've since spoken to accountants and lawyers who think there might be a way to finesse this if creators set up contracts with their loan-outs that give the loan-outs the right to collect their royalties and advances, without assigning copyright to the loan-out companies. I don't have any definitive answers on this: if you're worried about it, you should talk to your own lawyers and accountants.

It's a dangerous erosion of one of the few bright spots in copyright, a rule that is an unambiguously good way to benefit artists, not media companies.

In the meantime, if you've got some 35-year-old copyrights you'd like to terminate, I've got a tip for you. The Authors Alliance is a nonprofit that defends the rights of authors (I volunteer for its advisory board); we've got a free online tool that will help you terminate your own transfers and get your rights back:

[https://www.authorsalliance.org/resources/termination-of-transfer/](https://www.authorsalliance.org/resources/termination-of-transfer/)

articleBody:
The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers.

The team estimates that additional air pollution from the electricity demands of data centers in 2023 resulted in about 650 premature deaths across the United States.

Some Midwestern states had among the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita attributable to data centers, even though much of the data center electricity demand was concentrated in Virginia and Texas.

The researchers built a modeling framework that captures how the electricity demanded by data centers propagates through the nation’s interconnected power grid. The model also considers how atmospheric conditions impact the formation of air pollution in different regions.

The framework identifies power plants across the country whose emissions increase in response to data center electricity demand. In parts of the Midwest, these emissions combine with atmospheric conditions that favor the formation of fine particulate matter, a pollutant that can cause heart attacks, stroke, and lung disease.

The researchers say these results underscore the importance of considering unintended regional health impacts of data centers, and how the location and operations of these facilities affect public health on a broader scale.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy; and senior author of the study.

Selin is joined on the paper by Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student; as well as others at MIT, the University of California at Irvine, and Yale University. The research [appears today in Environmental Research Letters](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/aebbd4).

**Capturing regional impacts**

The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory [estimated](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/32d6m0d1) that electricity demands of data centers represented about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and resulted in about 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions.

That proportion has likely increased as new data centers continue to be built at a rapid pace.

Many prior studies estimate impacts using average electricity-grid emissions. Like those studies, the researchers assume data centers draw power to run computing tasks 24/7. Their approach also identifies which generators respond to that additional demand hour by hour, allowing them to trace where the resulting emissions and health impacts occur, Chen explains.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” he says.

To drill down on regional health impacts, the MIT researchers developed a modeling approach that enables them to identify which generators are contributing to data center electricity demand within each modeled region.

This allows them to incorporate a spatial component into the analysis.

They built an electricity system model that simulates how much electricity each generator produces and pumps into the grid every hour. This model also considers how that electricity is transmitted between regions.

It gives the researchers data on emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) for each generator across the United States. NOx contributes to the formation of ground-level ozone, or smog, while both NOx and SO 2 contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) in the atmosphere.

“It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”

The researchers incorporated these data into a chemical transport model. This model simulates how pollutants form and travel through the atmosphere across regions.

From there, they translated the additional air pollution from data center operations into premature mortality rates using evidence from epidemiological literature.

The model estimates that emissions from data centers caused about 650 premature deaths in 2023 (513 from PM 2.5 and 137 from smog), which represents about 5.3 percent of the nation’s total electricity-related mortality.

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin says.

**A pollution mismatch**

The premature mortality rates were highest in Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas, but the bulk of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and in Texas. Premature mortality rates in Virginia and Texas are only about half as much as most Midwestern states.

One reason for this mismatch is the interconnected nature of the power grid, Chen says.

Generators that respond to the increased electricity demand in Virginia are likely located in the Ohio Valley, where there is a higher proportion of older power plants that generate more emissions from burning coal and natural gas.

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin says.

Plus, due to atmospheric conditions, many pollutants generated in these regions are transported to downwind states.

Midwest states like Nebraska and Iowa are traditionally agricultural regions. Additional ammonia in the atmosphere from fertilizer enhances the formation of PM 2.5. The estimated health impacts also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas, illustrating that the effects can reach states with relatively few data centers.

The study shows that rural populations are expected to have significantly higher mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations, Chen says.

“When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is important to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” he says. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”

In the future, the researchers want to consider air quality impacts of onsite generation — a growing trend where data centers incorporate power plants that supply electricity. They could also study the flexibility of data center operations, and how adaptively adjusting electricity demand could impact air quality.

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.

The paradigm of sexual differentiation holds that female embryos retain the Müllerian ducts, the precursor of the female reproductive tract, by default in the absence of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH). articleBody: The paradigm of sexual differentiation holds that female embryos retain the Müllerian ducts, the precursor of the female reproductive tract, by default in the absence of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH). However, whether Müllerian duct maintenance requires active signaling remains unknown. Here, using mouse genetic models, we discover that deletion of mesenchymal Gata2 causes selective regression of the cranial Müllerian duct, the precursor of the oviduct. This regression is not driven by ectopic AMH signaling but may instead result from the loss of region-specific NRG1 signaling. Deletion of mesenchymal Gata2 also causes uterine hypoplasia and vaginal atresia, whereas epithelial Gata2 is specifically required for uterine gland differentiation. These genetic mouse studies reveal a Gata2-dependent, region-specific program that actively maintains the Müllerian duct and promotes female reproductive tract differentiation. Extending these findings to humans, we report two individuals with GATA2 deficiency who exhibit utero-vaginal agenesis or hypoplasia, consistent with Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome. Collectively, our results identify Gata2/GATA2 as a critical regulator of Müllerian duct development, providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying female reproductive tract development and Müllerian anomalies.

articleBody:
*This is today’s edition of* [The Download](https://forms.technologyreview.com/newsletters/briefing-the-download/?_ga=2.179569122.736533416.1649661040-405833893.1649413289), *our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.*

### A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks.

They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs.

[Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/19/1148934/a-human-liver-has-been-kept-alive-outside-the-body-for-seven-weeks-setting-a-record/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*).

*—Antonio Regalado*

### What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market

After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion.

The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market. But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted. The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition.

[Find out what this deal reveals about the US battery industry](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/19/1148922/sila-panasonic-battery-deal/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*).

*—Casey Crownhart*

[This story](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/19/1148922/sila-panasonic-battery-deal/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*) **is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter.** [Sign up](https://forms.technologyreview.com/newsletters/climate-energy-the-spark/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*) **to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.**

### The AI Hype Index returns

Separating AI reality from hyped-up fiction isn’t always easy. That’s why we’ve created the AI Hype Index—a simple, at-a-glance summary of what’s shaping the industry right now.

The latest edition tracks AI’s spread across everything from literary prizes and cyberattacks to a Grok-ified version of *The Odyssey*. [See where it all landed on this month’s index](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/18/1148650/ai-hype-index-ai-is-everywhere/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*).

**The must-reads**

*I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.*

**1 Anthropic has raised $81 billion in the biggest-ever IPO** It eclipsed SpaceX as the largest stock-market debut. ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-18/anthropic-is-said-to-price-ipo-at-83-per-share) $)

#### China has approved the world’s first invasive brain-computer chip—here’s what’s next

Sitting in the courtyard of his house in China’s Henan province last October, Dong Hui decided to try holding a pen. Six years after a car accident left him paralyzed from the neck down, he slowly wrote his name, “Thank you,” and the date.

The breakthrough was made possible by a brain implant called NEO. In March, it became the world’s first invasive brain-computer interface approved for use beyond clinical trials. The approval is expected to accelerate China’s push to become a global leader in brain implants.

[Here’s how China reached the milestone—and what it means for the future of BCIs](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/06/01/1138133/china-world-first-brain-chip/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*).

articleBody:
**Between-States: Conversations About Bardo and Life**

*In Tibetan Buddhism, “bardo” is a between-state. The passage from death to rebirth is a bardo, as well as the journey from birth to death. The conversations in “* [Between-States](https://tricycle.org/tag/between-states/) ” explore bardo concepts like acceptance, interconnectedness, and impermanence in relation to children and parents, marriage and friendship, and work and creativity, illuminating the possibilities for discovering new ways of seeing and finding lasting happiness as we travel through life.

At the beginning of Ocean Vuong’s latest novel, [The Emperor of Gladness](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/752232/the-emperor-of-gladness-by-ocean-vuong/), 19-year-old Hai, a queer Vietnamese American grappling with addiction, stands on a bridge preparing to jump. Grazina, a Lithuanian immigrant with dementia and traumatic memories of war, persuades him to reconsider. They form an unlikely friendship, caring for each other in a world where just surviving day to day is a struggle. An exploration of displacement and intergenerational trauma, memory and immigrant identity, the novel illuminates the hardships of living in the margins, as well as the grace that can be found there. “My book is about being in bardo,” Vuong told me. “Everyone is in a liminal space.”

Born in 1988 in Saigon, Vuong came to the US with his family at the age of 2 and grew up in Hartford, Connecticut. His first novel, [On Earth We’re Briefly Gorgeous](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/600633/on-earth-were-briefly-gorgeous-by-ocean-vuong/) (2019), spent six weeks on the *New York Times* best-seller list and has sold more than 2 million copies. He is the author of two collections of poetry, [Time Is a Mothe r](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/689930/time-is-a-mother-by-ocean-vuong/) (2022) and [Night Sky with Exit Wounds](https://www.coppercanyonpress.org/books/night-sky-with-exit-wounds-by-ocean-vuong/) (2016), and his work has appeared in the *Atlantic, Granta, Harper’s*, and the *New Yorker*. His numerous awards and honors include a MacArthur Fellowship, the T.S. Eliot Prize, and the Whiting Award. Currently a Radcliffe Fellow at Harvard University, he teaches Modern Poetry and Poetics in the MFA Program at New York University.

Vuong spoke with me from his home in western Massachusetts about finding new possibilities in bardo, engaging with your true self, and why he looks forward to death.

**In bardo, new insights and possibilities are available to us if we have the right perspective. Is this something you’ve experienced?** One hundred percent. In bardo, we don’t have the grounding of the physical body, so our emotions and thoughts can be more chaotic. But the power of the bardo is that if we stay aware, we can see things in a new way.

It’s something I experienced with my mother. I took care of her for a long time, which was a kind of bodily experience because so many of my literary and career decisions were based on her material well-being. I was like, “How do I get my mother out of Section 8 housing? I need to become a professor, I need to write, I need to get a contract.” These were the things that were on my mind even though, like any young writer, I told myself, “Oh, innovation above all, forget about your career, blah blah blah.”

I didn’t know how much my anxiety was impacting me until my mother passed. Then, as she entered her bardo, I entered a creative one, where I was no longer tied to this obligation I put on myself to tend to her materially. After she was gone, I went through an intense, chaotic time, but I also thought, “Well, now that those bodily ties are cut, what happens? What can I be? What can I think?”

I didn’t know how much my anxiety was impacting me until my mother passed. Then, as she entered her bardo, I entered a creative one.

**You’ve said that writing** **The** **Emperor of Gladness** **was a way out of the grief you felt after your mother’s death. What role, if any, did the idea of bardo play in that writing process?** It’s such a great question. No one has asked yet about that. I used the whole novel, the writing of it, as a bardo, a liminal space of grieving, a place without landing. And the idea of bardo became fundamental to the story. You can even argue—I usually avoid telling this part because I’m not interested in explaining my books, but we’re talking about dharma, which has a different pressure for me—that there’s more than one possible understanding of what happens to Hai. One is that he jumps from the bridge, and the whole novel is his bardo hallucination before his death. Another is that he jumps, and the whole novel is his bardo hallucination in death, with the entire story taking place in the unconsciousness of the death state.

When I was writing the book, I also found that I wanted to really use Buddhist philosophy as a literary model. You expect canonical literary works to be models, and I have plenty of those, but I wanted to use Buddhist philosophy, including *The Tibetan Book of the Dead*, as a literary project as well.

**Can you say a bit more about that?** It’s so important to experience the canon as a made thing, to not get trapped by that curation and think those are all the books worth paying attention to. *The Tibetan Book of the Dead* is incredibly rich in imagery and metaphor. There’s so much poetry in it. I wanted to point to it as a book that one would put next to *The Brothers Karamazov* and *The Adventures of* *Huckleberry Finn*, as a way of saying, “These are the books that inspired my novel.”

**A central idea in** **The Tibetan Book of the Dead** **is that we’re the artists of our lives, shaping our trajectory with the choices we make. This idea is evoked in your novel when you write about Hai not taking certain paths that are “invisible until he’s long past their junction.” Do you feel that you’ve missed paths?** Oh, yeah. I think my missing paths was part of why I became an artist. I’m such a feeling person, and feeling and thinking are perhaps too present in my life, to the point where there have been times when a junction has come and I’ve failed to act, like with sexual awakening and understanding my queerness. There were so many opportunities when I was younger, with my friends and other people, and I never acted on them. I was too scared, or too much in the middle of processing it all.

**The Tibetan Book of the Dead** **speaks to this, describing dazzling lights we see in bardo that are the lights of our true nature. We turn away from their radiant beauty, drawn instead to the dull lights of our habitual propensities, the things we do that aren’t aligned with who we are and make us unhappy.** My work now is the psychic return to act things out on the page, to do the things I didn’t do. Things I should have said, conversations I should have had, things I should have done with family, with loved ones, as a teacher, all of it. The page becomes a way to recoup it and become who I always was.

Before I became a writer, the opportunities for the true self never arose, or if they did, were never rewarded. And so they were not sustainable. I can now participate in a truer self for longer periods, and what I’ve found is that when you engage with your true self, it’s not just this isolated, individual journey. When you engage with that light, other people see it. And they say, “Oh, what is that? How do you live this intellectual, emotionally rich life?” And I say, “Well, it wasn’t always there. I had to make room for it, just like anything else. I had to fight for it.”

When you engage with your true self, it’s not just this isolated, individual journey. When you engage with that light, other people see it.

**Becoming our true self is very much a question of attention, where what we pay attention to, what we engage with, determines the nature of our reality. There’s a lot of talk these days about how distracted we all are. How easy is it for you to pay attention?** My brain was formed in a different world, so it’s easier for me to not get distracted. My childhood was entirely analog. I remember what it was like to look at a tree or the sky for fifteen minutes. With nothing like an iPhone to lay your eyes on, your eyes search, they wander, they see things that otherwise go unnoticed.

**The Emperor of Gladness** **opens with an extended description of the fictional town of East Gladness, and that kind of detailed description is present throughout the book. It feels like a call to pay attention to what otherwise might go unnoticed, both the physical place and the people who live there.** The novel begins with seven pages of description. On one hand, a writing workshop instructor would say it’s a cardinal sin to start a book this way, like, are you kidding? But to invest in description and slow down linear progression is a way to upset or recalibrate value in the work. What you’re doing when you refuse or delay plot is saying, “Pay attention. This is important.” East Gladness is a place some novelists would pass by, some drivers would pass by. It’s a flyover town, which is a politically charged phrase because, of course, the people who live there don’t think they live in a flyover town.

**The bardo teachings urge us to accept reality but not give up, which is what the characters in your novel do, or try to do. The book draws on your own experiences of poverty and discrimination and addiction—how accepting do you feel of whatever is happening in your life?** I don’t know if you can say I’m good at acceptance, but I’ve just always had a predisposition to be fatalistic about things. Like, whatever happens is the present.

When I’m writing, I could be thinking, “Is there another version of this? Is there another story?” But I almost never think that. I just think that this is the inevitable result of my consciousness tending to these ideas and whatever comes out is like a volcano spewing magma.

To me, life is about waiting and watching where the magma cools. It’s like, “Oh, that’s where it ends, there was no other alternative.” I don’t say, “How do we reroute magma?” Instead, I think, “Once it cools, what can we do with it?” Sometimes it spills into the village. Sometimes it spills into the sea. I’m always living in the most fruitful site of action, which for me is in the aftermath, rather than in the attempt to control.

**We often find it hard to be fatalistic about endings, especially our own. How do you feel about death?** I’ve been a hardcore Buddhist since I was about 15. I thought I was prepared when my friends died. I thought I was prepared when my grandma died. I thought I was prepared when my uncle took his own life. But you’re never prepared. You can read all the books, you can have all the intellectual reasonings and justifications. But the words themselves become a hallucination because they’re still of this world. They’re still of the matrix of this body, of this realm. The veil is pierced only when we enter that final journey, which I look forward to.

**You look forward to your own death?** Yes, to learn. To see what it’s like, see if something will surprise me. I’m not in a hurry, though. I have a lot of work still to do here, and if I’m lucky, I’ll get to do it.

title: AlphaInterp: Revealing how AlphaFold 3 processes structure, confidence, and evolutionary information

articleBody: How does evolutionary information become structural knowledge? AlphaFold 3 predicts protein structures and biomolecular assemblies with remarkable accuracy, yet how it transforms comparative sequence information into three-dimensional structure remains poorly understood. Here, we use mechanistic interpretability to follow this transformation through AlphaFold 3 and identify a computational principle underlying its structural inference. By extracting single- and pair-representations across the model’s forward pass and combining representational-geometry analysis, linear probing, activation patching, and perturbation of the multiple-sequence alignment (MSA) and its phylogenetic diversity, we show that AlphaFold 3 does not simply infer structure from raw sequence nor from MSA depth. Instead, a small number of sufficiently divergent homologues provides enough comparative information to largely recover the structure predicted using the full MSA. The pairformer transforms this evolutionary signal into a compact latent space in which residue-pair distances, contacts, fold similarity, and structural confidence become progressively decodable. Removing the MSA disrupts these latent geometries. Replacing it with evolutionarily similar homologues provides substantially less information, while evolutionarily unrelated sequences fail to rescue prediction despite preserving the formal alignment input. In contrast, phylogenetically diverse MSA subsampling largely restores both prediction accuracy and representational coherence. These results suggest that AlphaFold 3 has learned to infer structure by constraining its geometric priors and structural hypotheses by the sequence variation of the MSA. This framework helps explain both the model’s remarkable predictive power and its characteristic failure modes, with direct implications for protein design, conformational diversity, out-of-distribution generalization, and the interpretation of model confidence.

articleBody:
Back in 2001, *Grand Theft Auto III* let players do something that shocked parents and thrilled teenage boys. You could pick up a prostitute in a stolen car, kill her, and take your money back. Critics were outraged. Predictably, sales soared.

The newly released *Grand Theft Auto VI*, out today, has done away with prostitutes. That is a marked departure from previous editions. This latest iteration of the game has two playable main characters, Jason and Lucia. Intimacy in the game is limited only to them. Players can shape their relationship through activities like going on dates, robbing banks together, and, presumably, sex.

The genius of *GTA* is that it supplies the unavailable. Back when young people were in relationships, or felt that relationships were within reach, the fantasy was the prostitute. Now that hookers and OnlyFans are everywhere, the fantasy is the stable girlfriend.

To understand what’s really going on, you have to understand something crucial about what a fantasy reveals about the person having it:

articleBody:
Bing Gordon is the former Chief Creative Officer of Electronic Arts and a partner at Kleiner Perkins.

He served on Amazon’s board for more than a decade, a seat he earned after giving Jeff Bezos five ideas. The first was Amazon Prime. Bing describes the week two directors told him they wanted to resign, and the fix he proposed: Bezos opens each meeting with what’s on his mind, and six-page memos replace slide decks.

He explains Bezos’s first rule for the board, “first, do no harm,” and the “institutional no” Bezos wanted the board to help Amazon avoid. He lays out the three behaviors Bezos looks for in people who are right a lot, why Bezos dropped one-on-ones, and how every Amazon candidate faces a seven-person interview loop built on the leadership principles.

Bing then turns to what games taught him. He explains why moving a game from an 80 to a 90 doubles sales, why Steven Spielberg recut films until nobody left their seat, and how expansion packs for The Sims shaped his pitch for Prime.

He shares the David Ogilvy lessons that never made the books, including that 90% of people who recall an ad remember the headline and only 25% remember the body copy.

articleBody:
People say that philosophers have been working on the same questions for thousands of years. True, we are persistent—thanks for noticing! But it’s also the case that philosophers are often working on *new* questions, ones that did not exist thousands or hundreds of years ago, or even decades ago. We’re inventive, too!

Today is [World Philosophy Day](https://www.unesco.org/en/days/philosophy). To mark the occasion, I thought it would be a good idea to let people know what philosophers are asking about *today*.

For that, I’ll need your help.

**Philosophers, please take a moment to write down, in a comment on this post, one question you are currently working on.**(Yes, just**one**. )

It would also help if you shared the post and encouraged other philosophers to comment with a question they’re working on. The result could be a picture of what philosophers are thinking about today, parts of which perhaps catch the attention of people who otherwise might have not realized they are interested in what philosophers are up to.

Thank you!

(Some readers may recall that I’ve posted this query several years ago. Unfortunately, the previous comments appear to have been lost, either in the recent hack or the resultant upgrade. I only recently noticed this, and am looking into whether they’re recoverable.)

Related: [The Intellectual Achievement of Creating Questions](https://dailynous.com/2017/08/23/intellectual-achievement-creating-questions/)

articleBody:
Canadian studio Sid Lee Architecture has created a curved-glass hotel that takes cues from the burgeoning wine region of Ontario.

The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

Drawings and photos

Previous

Next

Drawings and photos

Close

Floor plan of Clayfield Hotel by Sid Lee Architecture

Floor plan of Clayfield Hotel by Sid Lee Architecture

Floor plan of Clayfield Hotel by Sid Lee Architecture

Floor plan of Clayfield Hotel by Sid Lee Architecture

“The Clayfield was conceived as a new hub for Niagara-on-the-Lake, a place where wine culture and hospitality find a home,” Martin Leblanc, architect and co-founding partner of Sid Lee Architecture, told Dezeen.

“Its layered contours, rounded geometry and rhythmic wood elements translate the surrounding vineyard landscape into a building that celebrates the region’s contribution to Canadian winemaking."

The hotel was conceived as a pavilion set in the emerging townscape between vineyards and the Clayfield Commons housing development on an agricultural road.

The curved form allows access and connection to its surroundings in multiple directions.

“The hotel acts as a threshold between these typologies, connecting the vineyard and the denser village-like development around it,” Leblanc said.

“Its exterior wood elements recall the rhythm of the vine rows, the layered concrete refers to the clay soil and the reflective glass registers the changing light, sky and seasons.”

The studio said that the organic, natural flow of a hotel is essential to the lasting success of the design.

Working back and forth between the architecture and the interior design, the studio laid out spaces to progress from public to private and back again, integrating moments for visitors to discover the landscape.

“As visitors approach and circulate around the building, it frames changing views of the vines, the plaza and the emerging neighbourhood,” Leblanc said. “The lobby acts as a gateway to the vineyard, while the rooftop terrace reconnects the hotel experience with its broader surroundings.”

Meanwhile, the staircase acts as a connector, transition and centrepiece between the plaza, lobby and upper levels.

Read:

Sid Lee Architecture remodels offices at base of IM Pei skyscraper in Montreal

“Inside, we chose a palette that speaks to the natural beauty of Niagara’s wine country: walnut panelling, concrete, dark amaranth-coloured leather, greige limestone and woven fabrics,” Leblanc said, calling out the limestone registration desk chiselled from the Niagara Escarpment and the restaurant’s curved bar that resembles the shape of the building.

With mostly Teknion furniture, each space represents a season of the vineyard, from spring in the lobby to winter in the guest rooms with more quiet, reserved furnishings that complete the rooms that fan out from the rounded concrete strata.

Founded in 2009, Sid Lee Architecture has six offices across North America and Europe. The studio previously remodelled its own offices in an I.M. Pei office building, overhauled the interiors of the iconic Fairmont Queen Elizabeth Hotel and created an artisan-inspired workplace for video game designers – all in Montreal.

articleBody: Apoptotic cell clearance represents the final stage of apoptosis and involves phagosome formation, maturation, and digestion. Here, we found that SUMO modifications participate in apoptotic cell clearance by influencing phagosomal degradation activity in C. elegans. The SUMO E3 ligase, GEI-17, SUMOylates GDP dissociation inhibitor (GDI-1) at K270 to trigger phagosomal degradation. Upon SUMOylation, GDI-1 facilitates release of GDP-bound RAB-1, which is subsequently converted to the GTP-bound form in a manner dependent on GDI displacement factor, PRAF-3. RAB-1 conversion enables binding and translocation of RAB-7 from the endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to promote phagosome maturation and degradation activity. In the absence of GDI-1 SUMOylation, GDI-1 binds to GDP-RAB-1, sequestering it in the cytoplasm, resulting in impaired phagosomal degradation. Furthermore, we found SUMOylation of GDI1 at a conserved site plays a crucial role in efferocytosis regulation in mammals. This study defines a previously unrecognized mechanism by which SUMOylation drives apoptotic cell clearance.

title: The Amazing Inventions of Ancient Greece: From Plato’s Alarm Clock to Ancient Flamethrowers
subtitle: “It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece.
feedText: Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. articleBody:
“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in [the new video above from Lost in Time](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F20zQmyZa20) *,* a YouTube channel whose [look at ancient Roman technology](https://www.openculture.com/2025/09/the-advanced-technology-of-ancient-rome.html) we posted here on Open Culture last year.

Most of the others were invented for less gentle purposes: we have a nasty-looking flamethrower on wheels meant to breach stone fortresses; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapidly than any bowman; a nine-story-tall proto-tank fully stocked with catapults and soldiers ready to swarm a city; and a gigantic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and overturn invading warships. Yet as formidable as they sound, evidence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they functioned in actual battle — remains scarce.

Much clearer are records of the *Diolkos*, recently mentioned here when we featured [the megaprojects that even ancient Rome couldn’t pull off](https://www.openculture.com/2026/10/the-megaprojects-even-the-ancient-romans-couldnt-pull-off.html). Among those endeavors was a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth, which would save ships having to take the long way around the Peloponnesian peninsula. Or rather, it would save them having to be dragged by a couple hundred slaves over the *Diolkos*, a paved trackway built in the sixth century BC. Using ramps and winches, ships could be shifted onto a wheeled cart that ran in grooves the whole way, making the whole system a precursor of the railroad, or perhaps an inverted ancestor of the ferry still used to transport railway cars [across the Strait of Messina](https://www.openculture.com/2025/03/why-there-isnt-a-bridge-from-italy-to-sicily.html). Like the Romans, the Greeks also considered digging a canal, but to do so might have violated the intentions of Zeus, a better excuse not to build infrastructure than some of those we hear in the twenty-first century.

articleBody: Current diagnostic workflows for cervical lesions remain constrained by processing time, sampling representativeness, and limited molecular-level tissue assessment. Handheld Raman spectroscopy may provide label-free molecular profiling of ex vivo tissue specimens. In this methodological feasibility study, we evaluated a defined ex vivo acquisition workflow using a handheld 785-nm Raman spectrometer. We systematically evaluated laser power, integration time, and tissue thickness, and 128 mW laser power, 4000 ms integration time, and approximately 1-mm-thick tissue sections were selected as the working acquisition conditions for subsequent cervical measurements. The cervical cohort comprised 74 patients contributing 212 Raman spectra and was evaluated for two predefined primary binary classification tasks: invasive cervical cancer versus noncancer lesions (B1) and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) versus benign lesions plus low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL) (B2). Exploratory spectrum-level analyses yielded AUCs of 0.774 for B1 and 0.782 for B2. However, under repeated nested patient-grouped cross-validation of the previously selected model families, with all spectra from each patient retained within the same validation fold and hyperparameters optimized using training patients only, the mean patient-level AUC was 0.519 ± 0.051 for B1 and 0.639 ± 0.074 for B2. The corresponding median AUCs were 0.522 (IQR, 0.497–0.545) and 0.642 (IQR, 0.620–0.688), respectively. In patient-aware differential peak analysis, repeated measurements from the same patient were aggregated before statistical testing. Six prespecified Raman bands (1003, 1306, 1341, 1516, 1586, and 1638 cm-¹) remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction for B1, whereas no prespecified band remained significant after FDR correction for B2. These findings support the methodological feasibility of handheld Raman acquisition under the present defined ex vivo workflow and indicate the presence of lesion-associated spectral variation in cervical tissue, while also demonstrating substantial attenuation of classification performance under patient-independent validation. Handheld Raman spectroscopy should therefore currently be regarded as an exploratory adjunctive approach for ex vivo molecular tissue assessment rather than a standalone diagnostic method. Larger patient cohorts, spatially registered Raman–histology validation, fresh-tissue studies, and multicenter external validation are required before clinical translation.

articleBody:
In the Croatian village of Čigoč, some of the most conspicuous residents live above the rooftops. White storks build bulky nests on traditional wooden houses, sharing the settlement with the people below.

Situated in Lonjsko Polje Nature Park beside the Tišina oxbow of the Sava River, the village is surrounded by wet meadows, pastures, and pools. These habitats provide feeding grounds close to the nests, allowing adult birds to gather frogs, insects, and other small animals for their young.

In 1994, the conservation foundation EuroNatur named Čigoč the first European Stork Village. The designation recognised the village’s importance for white storks and its long-standing relationship between people, traditional farming, and wildlife. It also launched an initiative that would connect stork villages across Europe.

The wooden houses are part of this story. Their rooftops provide nesting places, while the surrounding agricultural landscape helps sustain the birds. During the breeding season, a walk through the village offers a chance to watch adults tending their nests and travelling between the rooftops and nearby feeding grounds.

articleBody:
Abstract: We report on our experience validating S3 Express One Zone, a high-performance Amazon S3 storage class launched in November 2023. We focused on its distributed metadata index, which implements a hierarchical namespace using distributed transactions. We check strong consistency and durability under crashes, network delays, and timeouts. Building on our prior work on lightweight formal methods, we combined executable reference models with property-based testing and stateless model checking. Applying these techniques to a production distributed system required three new techniques: a white-box approach to checking serializability; compositional validation of the data and control planes; and long-running canaries that use reference models to check correctness across deployments. We extended Shuttle, our open-source stateless checker, to support a production async Rust runtime and failure injection, including cancelled operations and timeouts. Our main finding is that this approach is sustainable at engineering scale. After launch, the engineering team took ownership of models and test infrastructure, increasing its share of validation commits from 41% to 84% and independently extending the models for conditional writes, object append, and atomic rename, with little involvement from the formal methods team.

### Was gibt’s Neues?

**Angela Ittel wirbt für eine „Wissenschafts-Nato“**

Die Präsidentin der TU Braunschweig, Angela Ittel, spricht sich für einen länderübergreifenden Beistand zum Schutz der Wissenschaftsfreiheit aus. Anlass sind Pläne der AfD, die Gleichstellungsarbeit an Hochschulen einzuschränken und Mittel für die Geschlechter- und Klimaforschung zu kürzen. Sollten die Gleichstellungsbeauftragten in Sachsen-Anhalt aus dem Hochschulgesetz gestrichen werden, erwartet Ittel von anderen Hochschulen und der Allianz der Wissenschaftsorganisationen öffentliche Rückendeckung und konkrete Unterstützung. Das sagte die Universitätspräsidentin [im Interview mit Anna-Lena Scholz](https://www.zeit.de/2026/48/gleichstellung-hochschulen-angela-ittel-afd?).

Den weiterhin großen Bedarf an Gleichstellungsarbeit begründet Ittel mit dem sinkenden Frauenanteil über die wissenschaftlichen Karrierestufen hinweg. In der Medizin liege der Anteil der Studentinnen teils bei 70 Prozent, während nur jede zehnte Professur mit einer Frau besetzt sei. 126 Hochschulen hätten 2024 eine Selbstverpflichtung der Hochschulrektorenkonferenz für Gleichstellungsmaßnahmen unterzeichnet. Nun würde bei Berufungen dokumentiert, wie viele Frauen sich bewerben, eingeladen werden und eine Stelle erhalten. Die Wirksamkeit einzelner Maßnahmen werde derzeit untersucht.

**NaWik-Trialog: Wie kommt Wissenschaft in die Politik?**

Wie arbeiten Wissenschaft und Politik optimal zusammen und welche Kompetenzen benötigen Wissenschaftler*innen, um ihre Erkenntnisse in die Politik zu tragen? Über diese Fragen diskutierten Armin Grunwald, Katrin Rehak-Nitsche und Richard Fuchs am 4. November beim [NaWik*-Trialog](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hj8qquMHEtU) „Politik & Wissenschaft“.

Dass politische Entscheidungen wissenschaftlich fundiert sein sollten, darüber waren sich alle drei Diskutant*innen einig. Doch wie gelingt es Wissenschaftler*innen ihre Expertise einzubringen? „Gute Politikberatung ist eine Langstrecke“, sagt Fuchs, Wissenschaftsjournalist, Medientrainer und Berater für Wissensorganisationen. Politische Autorität müssen sich Wissenschaftler*innen erarbeiten. Zunächst sollten sich Forschende klarmachen: „Wissenschaft und Politik ticken anders“. Wissenschaftliche Projekte hätten häufig einen langen Vorlauf, während Politik schnelle Ergebnisse wolle. Das könne für Wissenschaftler*innen frustrierend sein. Für eine erfolgreiche Politikberatung sollten Forschende die Arbeitsweise, Bedürfnisse und zeitlichen Zwänge politischer Entscheidungsträger*innen verstehen.

Grunwald, der das Institut für Technikfolgenabschätzung und das Büro für Technikfolgenabschätzung beim Bundestag am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* leitet, findet es zudem wichtig, die verschiedenen Rollen zu verstehen: „Wir wollen nicht, wir können nicht, wir dürfen nicht die besseren Politiker sein wollen.“ Forschende könnten Politiker*innen nur bei ihrer Entscheidungsfindung unterstützen. Dafür ist laut Fuchs ein Perspektivwechsel wichtig. Forscher*innen müssten sich überlegen, was Politiker*innen von ihnen benötigen.

Laut der Politikerin und Landtagsabgeordneten aus Rheinland-Pfalz, Rehak-Nitsche, werden vor allem konkrete Handlungsoptionen und Lösungsvorschläge benötigt. Forschende sollten dafür gezielt auf fachpolitische Sprecher*innen, Ausschüsse oder auch lokale Abgeordnete zugehen. Dabei sollten ihre wissenschaftlichen Ergebnisse aber realistischen Erwartungen entsprechen. Die Diskutierenden kritisierten überzogene wissenschaftliche Versprechen, da diese die Glaubwürdigkeit schmälern. Außerdem sollten die Ergebnisse priorisiert werden, zum Beispiel mit einer zentralen Botschaft pro Studie. Diese sollten Forschende verständlich kommunizieren können.

Wie das in der Praxis aussieht? Das lest ihr in unserem [Interview mit dem Politikwissenschaftler Daniel Wiesner](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wie-politik-wissenschaft-in-debatten-einsetzt-101497/) über wissenschaftliche Inhalte in österreichischen Parlamentsdebatten.

**Kritik am Impulspapier des Wissenschaftsrats**

Welchen Beitrag kann und soll Wissenschaft zur freiheitlich-demokratischen Gesellschaft leisten? Anfang November hat der Wissenschaftsrat zu dieser Frage ein [Impulspapier](https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/PM_2026/PM_2426?nn=68873b8321233a04bb97cedd&wt_zmc=nl.int.zonaudev.112331552451_555074179233.nl_ref) veröffentlicht. Zu den Impulsen zählen Fragen zur Balance zwischen wissenschaftlicher Selbstbestimmung und gesellschaftlichen Erwartungen sowie zu Werten und Wertekonflikten in der Wissenschaft. Der Rat sieht den Anlass darin, dass demokratische Institutionen und der gesellschaftliche Zusammenhalt zunehmend unter Druck stünden: „Wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse werden infrage gestellt, einzelne Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler bedrängt und angefeindet.“

Der Wissenschaftsrat versteht das Impulspapier als „Plädoyer und als Anstoß zur Debatte“, um Thesen, Anregungen und Spannungsverhältnisse offenzulegen. Diese sollen gemeinsam mit Wissenschaft, Politik und Gesellschaft erörtert werden. Gelegenheit dazu soll unter anderem ein gemeinsames Symposium im nächsten Frühjahr bieten. Bei [Table Media](https://table.media/research/thema-des-tages/wissenschaft-und-die-demokratie-welche-diskussionen-der-wissenschaftsrat-anstossen-moechte) bemängeln teils anonyme Kritiker*innen, dass das Papier vor allem Fragen stellt, wo längst Entscheidungen und Reformen gefragt wären. Johannes Vogel, Direktor des Naturkundemuseums Berlin, [fordert](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/m-weisskopf_wissenschaft-demokratie-symposium-share-7524013244613603328-UDsU/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAABrhP4ABM9rIpbs8S5tg0GHwDJPz18tv5aQ) etwa: „Die Diskussionen zu den genannten Themen führen wir teilweise seit zehn Jahren oder noch länger.“ Es sei nun keine Zeit mehr für teils systembewahrende Debatten, sondern für Experimente, Lernen, Mut und Handeln.

### Und sonst?

Ein KI-basiertes Tool könnte zukünftig Creator*innen beim **Factchecking** ihrer Inhalte unterstützen. Dabei würden Informationen eine Art „Nutri-Score für Social Media“ erhalten, die ihren Wahrheitsgehalt signalisieren sollen. [Im Podcast](https://www.podcast.de/episode/709350253/nutri-score-fuer-social-media-wer-bestimmt-kuenftig-was-im-feed-als-vertrauenswuerdig-gilt) spricht Journalist Martin Fehrensen mit der Gründerin Malina Wiethaus über das Tool „TrustScored“.

Die Verlagsgruppe Wort & Bild will in den nächsten zwei Jahren die **Redaktion der Apotheken Umschau halbieren**. Aktuell beschäftige die Redaktion insgesamt rund 120 Menschen. [Der Spiegel kommentiert](https://www.spiegel.de/kultur/apotheken-umschau-medienhaus-wort-bild-will-redaktion-halbieren-a-59b79ae8-97b8-4708-bd19-c1b4594081c4): „Das Geschäftsmodell des Wort-&-Bild-Verlags ist wegen des Rückgangs der Apotheken sowie des Printwerbegeschäfts unter Druck.“ Wir sprachen Anfang des Jahres [mit der Chefredakteurin Tina Haase](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/stuetzstrumpf-der-nation-betrachte-ich-als-kompliment-95119/) über das Magazin als „Hidden Champion“ der Wissenschaftskommunikation.

Eine **Kommission des Deutschen Bundestags** befragte Fachleute zur Wissenschaftskommunikation während der Coronapandemie. Ein Fazit der Anhörung, [schreibt die Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/de/corona-wie-kommunizierten-politik-wissenschaft-und-medien-in-der-pandemie/a-79844661): „Die Kommunikation von Politik, Medien und Wissenschaft muss besser werden.“

Der Call für die **Science X Media-Tandems** 2027 ist geöffnet. Mit diesem Programm fördert die Stiftung Charité innovative Projekte der Wissenschaftskommunikation. [Bewerbungen](https://www.stiftung-charite.de/en/funding/open-life-science/science-x-media-tandem-program) sind bis zum 25. Januar 2027 möglich.

Das Forschungsprojekt „Wikoko” des NaWik* sucht Wissenschaftler*innen, die an einem **kostenlosen Online-Training zu Grundlagen der Wissenschaftskommunikation** teilnehmen möchten. Im Rahmen des Projekts wird erforscht, welche Teilkompetenzen Wissenschaftler*innen für eine kompetente Wissenschaftskommunikation benötigen. Mehr Infos und die Teilnahmebedingungen gibt es [↗ nawik.de](https://www.nawik.de/wikoko-trainings/).

Der Facharzt **Nibras Naami** erhielt den diesjährigen [LifeScienceXplained | Sartorius-Preis für neue Kommunikation](https://www.sartorius.com/en/company-de/newsroom-de/corporate-news-de/1889636-1889636) für sein Instagram-Reel „Fall aus der Klinik: Krampfanfall im Supermarkt“. Ausgezeichnet wurde er für seine evidenzbasierte Wissenschaftsvermittlung, die laut Jury „auch im kurzen Social-Media-Format gelingen kann“.

Der Virologe Christian Drosten wird mit der **Mercator-Professur 2026** der Universität Duisburg-Essen [ausgezeichnet](https://www1.wdr.de/nrw/ruhrgebiet/christian-drosten-professur-duisburg-essen-100.amp). Die Professur wird an Persönlichkeiten vergeben, die das öffentliche Leben prägen und gesellschaftliche Debatten bereichern.

### Und die Forschung?

Von Wissenschaftler*innen wird zunehmend erwartet, sich in der Wissenschaftskommunikation zu engagieren. Aber reichen ihre Ressourcen aus, um die Anforderungen zu erfüllen? Anthony Dudo von der University of Texas at Austin und Josh T. L. Anderson von der University of Arizona haben dazu [mit Forschenden gesprochen](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10755470261489537?_gl=1*1mf6fw9*_up*MQ..*_ga*NzY4MDc3MDM5LjE3OTMxMTYyMDM.*_ga_60R758KFDG*czE3OTMxMTYyMDIkbzEkZzEkdDE3OTMxMTYyMDIkajYwJGwxJGgxNTI4ODg5MDk1), die zum Beispiel auf Social Media aktiv sind, öffentliche Vorträge halten oder von Journalist*innen interviewt werden. Die Wissenschaftler*innen berichteten von Zeitdruck, Belästigungen, Reputationsrisiken und teilweise von zu wenig Unterstützung vonseiten ihrer Institutionen. Die Gespräche zeigten, dass die Anforderungen größer seien als die vorhandenen Ressourcen, schlussfolgern die Autoren der Studie. Anzeichen für Burnout deuteten darauf hin, dass die aktuellen Bedingungen auf Dauer nicht tragbar seien.

Wie gestaltet China das Verhältnis zwischen Wissenschaft und Gesellschaft? Rongrong Ren, Bingyuan Chen und Zhaoyang Sun von der Northeastern University at Qinhuangdao haben die verschiedenen Fassungen des Gesetzes der Volksrepublik China über die Verbreitung von Wissenschaft und Technologie [(„das Gesetz“) aus den Jahren 2002 und 2024 untersucht.](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/09636625261486280?_gl=1*17fhma8*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTI3MjMwMzM5OC4xNzkzMTE2ODkx*_ga_60R758KFDG*czE3OTMxMTY4OTEkbzEkZzEkdDE3OTMxMTY4OTEkajYwJGwxJGg5MTA1OTAyMzc.) Drei Fallbeispiele für Popularisierungsprojekte in städtischen, ländlichen und mobilen Kontexten zeigen laut der Autor*innen, dass das Gesetz die Wissenschaftspopularisierung gestärkt habe. Allerdings werde auch deutlich, dass bei der Beteiligung der Öffentlichkeit hauptsächlich Besuchen und Erleben und nicht Problemerkennung, Entscheidungsfindung oder Mitgestaltung im Zentrum stünden. Die Autor*innen beschreiben das als hybride Form der Wissenschaftskommunikation mit Elementen des Defizitmodells und partizipativer Ansätze.

Dass mit indigenen Traditionen des Geschichtenerzählens wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse vermittelt werden können, zeigt Rachelle Warner von der University of Adelaide [in einem Praxiseinblick](https://jcom.sissa.it/article/pubid/JCOM_2506_2026_N05/). Anhand von Fallstudien der australischen „[National Science Week](https://www.scienceweek.net.au)“ zeigt sie, wie vielfältige Zielgruppen durch von Indigenen angeleitetes Geschichtenerzählen angesprochen werden und MINT-Inhalte zugänglich gemacht werden können. Warner gibt Tipps, wie kulturell verankerte Formen des Wissensaustauschs für eine inklusive Wissenschaftskommunikation genutzt werden können.

Hochschulen, Forschungsinstitutionen, Stiftungen und Co können ihre Stellenangebote direkt an Besucher*innen unseres Portals richten.

### Fundstück

Um einen neuen Gesellschaftsvertrag zwischen Wissenschaft und Gesellschaft zu gestalten, schlug der Wissenschaftsrat [fünf Handlungsfelder](https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/PM_2026/PM_2926) beim Falling Walls Science Summit in Berlin vor: Profile bilden und konsolidieren; Wissenschaft neben ihrer Exzellenz auch an ihrer Wirkung messen; Teilhabe als Leistungsfaktor begreifen; Lehre personalisieren; und die Handlungsfähigkeit der Wissenschaftspolitik stärken.

* Wissenschaft im Dialog (WiD), das Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT) und das Nationale Institut für Wissenschaftskommunikation (NaWik) sind die Träger des Portals Wissenschaftskommunikation.de.

articleBody:
Upon realizing his past self’s poor taste in music, Daniel Parris went looking for the [worst music subgenres in history](https://www.statsignificant.com/p/the-worst-trends-in-music-history).

> To qualify for this analysis, a subgenre has to have been popular (meaning its canonical artists graced the Billboard 200 album chart for a number of weeks) and retroactively disliked by people who rate stuff online.
> To do this, I compiled an exhaustive list of musical subgenres, each with at least 20 albums that reached the Billboard 200, then cross-referenced those albums’ composite scores on Best Ever Albums (which grades albums based on lists compiled by the site’s users and professional critics).

Teen pop and post-grunge topped the list of worst subgenres, but as noted by Parris, the biggest influence on the music we like is whatever was popular when we were young. Also, Matchbox Twenty is good, which I believe invalidates this analysis.

**Tags:** [Daniel Parris](https://flowingdata.com/tag/daniel-parris/), [music](https://flowingdata.com/tag/music/), [Stat Significant](https://flowingdata.com/tag/stat-significant/)

articleBody:
Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching

In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place.

It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back.

articleBody:
arXiv:2611.23322v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

title: How To Get A Friend To Leave An Abusive Relationship
subtitle: How do you get a friend to leave an abusive relationship?
feedText: If you talk to people who work at women's shelters, they will tell you, but there is something resigned about the way they do it: they know that it's too difficult an ask. Those who can do it reliably are often people who are unlucky enough to have had first-hand experience as victims.
